meaning: Titles and reading notes drafted by an AI agent in the register of the paper they annotate. No mathematician has reviewed them.

notes.TorusEuler.AmplificationCrossing.crossin: The time $2/\sqrt{\varepsilon\varepsilon_+}$ is the upper endpoint of the crossing interval in Proposition 2.8. The crossing argument assumes both coupling ratios are positive and this time lies within $[0,T]$. It sets the available time for reaching the successor ratio; it does not specify the crossing itself.
notes.TorusEuler.AmplificationCrossing.eight_d: If $0<\varepsilon_+\le\varepsilon/32$, the upper crossing endpoint is at least $8/\varepsilon$. Since Lemma 2.5 places the reference peak at or before $3/\varepsilon$, the crossing bracket in Proposition 2.8 has positive length. This estimate uses only the two positive coupling ratios and their size relation.
notes.TorusEuler.AmplificationCrossing.exists_: A continuous ratio satisfying the late bounds of Proposition 2.8 reaches $\varepsilon_+$ strictly between $\tau_m$ and $2/\sqrt{\varepsilon\varepsilon_+}$. At every crossing in $[\tau_m,T]$, it also gives $1/(4\varepsilon_+)\le\tan\varphi\le3/(2\varepsilon_+)$. The result assumes these ratio bounds and the peak bracket; it does not require the wave equations themselves or assert uniqueness of the crossing.
notes.TorusEuler.AmplificationCrossing.x_cross: At $\tau=2/\sqrt{\varepsilon\varepsilon_+}$, the reference angle satisfies $\tan\varphi=2/\varepsilon_+$. Both coupling ratios must be positive. In the proof of Proposition 2.8, substitution into the late upper bound shows that the successor ratio is already below its target at this endpoint.
notes.TorusEuler.AuxiliaryTerminalSmoothness: The auxiliary conclusion chooses the exponent, threshold and initial-frequency bound before choosing a construction for each sufficiently large initial frequency. It includes the time-derivative estimates and a singular Euler solution with a smooth periodic extension away from the origin. This supports Remark 1.2; the displayed conclusion does not itself state that the selected stages converge to the selected solution.
notes.TorusEuler.ChildFlow.graphDerivative_app: The derivative of a displacement restricted to $s=k_*\cdot a$ splits into a label derivative and a phase derivative multiplied by $k_*$. This is the chain rule behind $D\mathcal A_t-\operatorname{Id}=\partial_a\eta_a+\partial_s\eta_a\otimes k_*$ in Lemma 5.10. The formal identity includes the factors $\ell_*^{-1}$ and $h^{-1}$ arising from the scaled coordinates.
notes.TorusEuler.ChildFlow.labelTransition: This is the change of labels $\mathcal A_t$ obtained by starting the lifted flow on $s=k_*\cdot a$ and retaining its label component. Lemma 5.10 writes it as $a+\eta_a(t,a,k_*\cdot a)$. The formal definition also allows an arbitrary starting time, so the same construction describes the reverse transition.
notes.TorusEuler.ChildFlow.phaseDefect_transit: Along the lifted flow (5.54), the quantity $s-k_*\cdot a$ is constant. Consequently, a trajectory starting on the phase graph remains on it, as needed to identify the label change in Lemma 5.10. The statement applies in both time directions and assumes nonzero coordinate scales and the stated differential equation for the flow.
notes.TorusEuler.ChildFlow.physicalTransition: The physical transition is obtained by passing from a starting point to its parent label, evolving that label, and applying the parent flow at the final time. Starting at zero gives $Y(t,a)=X(t,\mathcal A_t(a))$, as in Lemma 5.10. This defines the composition; its identification with the required velocity field is proved separately.
notes.TorusEuler.ChildFlow.physicalTransition_: The chain rule bounds the derivative of the physical flow by the product of the parent deformation bound and the label transition bound. The same argument applies to the reverse transition. This supplies the last step of Lemma 5.10, once the corresponding differentiability and bounds have been established for both constituent maps.
notes.TorusEuler.ChildFlow.pullbackField: The label velocity is $c=(D_aX)^{-1}(W+v\circ X)$ in the proof of Lemma 5.10. Applying the derivative of the inverse parent flow converts the physical correction into motion of its labels. The formula has this interpretation for the smooth invertible parent flow used in the paper; the definition alone does not establish those properties.
notes.TorusEuler.ChildFlow.pullbackField_skewP: The velocity $c$ is unchanged under $(a,s)\mapsto(a+n,s+k_*\cdot n)$ for an integer lattice vector $n$. This is the continuation across cells used in Lemma 5.10. The conclusion follows from the translation laws of the parent flow and its inverse, the same law for the profile, and periodicity of the added perturbation.
notes.TorusEuler.ChildFlow.scaledField: In coordinates $(a/\ell_*,s/h)$, the lifted particle velocity is $(c/\ell_*,k_*\cdot c/h)$. Lemma 5.10 estimates its gradient before restricting to the phase graph. Keeping label and phase independent at this stage exposes the small gradient needed for the flow estimate; preservation of the graph is a separate result.
notes.TorusEuler.ChildFlow.slope_divergence_pu: The Piola identity transforms the divergence constraint on the physical perturbation into $(\nabla_a+k_*\partial_s)\cdot c=0$. Lemma 5.10 uses this equation to control the phase velocity by label derivatives. The formal statement requires a smooth volume-preserving parent flow and sufficient differentiability of the correction to justify both parts of the calculation.
notes.TorusEuler.EndpointCoefficientC1Bound: These are the coefficient bounds used in Theorem A.1: continuity in time with values in $C^{0,1/2}$, spatial differentiability, and uniform bounds on the coefficient and its first spatial derivative. The formal statement does not require continuity in time in $C^{1,1/2}$, as the paper does. Symmetry, ellipticity and the displacement energy bound are separate assumptions.
notes.TorusEuler.EndpointSobolevEnergyBound: This is assumption (A.2), written with $v=z_t$ and $z=Jv$. The test velocities are square integrable and have zero time integral, so their primitives vanish at both endpoints. At each label the energy must dominate $\mu\|v\|_{L^2_t}^2$. It is an assumption for Theorem A.1, not an existence assertion for the endpoint solution.
notes.TorusEuler.EulerSingularityWitness: These are the properties of the solution in Theorem 1.1: smooth odd periodic initial data, a positive finite maximal time, bounded velocity, divergent gradient and vorticity integrals, and central vorticity tending to infinity. Both velocity and its time derivative have spatial limits away from the origin. Uniqueness among maximal classical solutions is stated separately in the formal version of Theorem 1.1.
notes.TorusEuler.FiniteCoefficientMultiIndexPo: Equation (D.6) bounds each spatial derivative of a smooth coefficient by $C_m\mathsf D^{a(m+1)}$. Here the exponent is a nonnegative integer, and the constants are chosen for the fixed coefficient and parent parameter. Uniformity over varying coefficients or parent parameters must therefore be stated separately, as it is in Lemma D.2.
notes.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr: At positive retained depth, the constructed velocity, mean and pressure profiles vanish at unused levels. This justifies the finite expansion described in §1.3. The divergence correction belongs to the oscillation that produces it: in the paper's indexing, the initial vanishing correction is $C_1$, and the final retained correction is $C_{P+1}$. No infinite expansion is asserted.

For each retained level $2\le p\le P$, the construction satisfies its mean equation and its oscillatory equation. The parent residual enters the mean equation only at level two, as in §1.3. This result assumes that the required equations can be solved and organizes their algebra; identifying them with the physical material derivative and pressure terms requires the separate analytic construction.

The first velocity and pressure profiles are exactly the prescribed leading wave and its pressure, while the first mean velocity and mean pressure vanish. This supplies the starting level of the expansion in §1.3. The result assumes the leading transverse solution has already been supplied; its identification with the localized, activated wave is a separate step.

For each retained level $2\le p\le P$, the constructed $B_p$ and $\bar q_p$ are the selected solution of (5.11) with source $-\langle H_p\rangle_s$, including $-R_U\circ X$ at level two. This identifies the mean used by the recursion. Existence of the mean solution is supplied separately by the endpoint problem.

At each retained level $2\le p\le P$, the constructed $V_p$ and $\mathsf p_p$ solve the transverse problem with exactly the source $f_p+f_p^S$ of (5.27)–(5.28). Its phase average is zero. The new mean has already been chosen when this source is formed, preserving the order of construction required in §5.5.1.
notes.TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin: The first wave over the stationary shear starts with covector $\lambda e_1$ and amplitude in the positive $e_2$ direction. Its covector and amplitude solve the wave equations, remain nonzero and transverse, and attain the amplitude peak $\lambda^{-3/4}$ on $[0,T]$. These are the requirements used in §6.1; the existence of such a wave is proved separately.
notes.TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.first_couplin: For the first wave, the moving-frame coupling satisfies $\nu(t)\ge\pi$ throughout $[0,T]$ when $T|B_\rho|\le1/8$. This supplies the positivity needed in Lemma 6.1 and hence (5.5). The formal statement allows $|\rho|\le1$, including nonpositive values, whereas the construction chooses $0<\rho\le1$.
notes.TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.initial_coupl: The initial wave frame is $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ because the frequency and amplitude scale are positive. Substituting this frame into the stationary shear gives $\nu(0)=2\pi$ and $\eta(0)=2\pi\rho$, exactly as in (6.4). Their ratio supplies the amplification parameter for the second wave.
notes.TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.initial_proje: At time zero the transported covector is $\lambda e_1$ at every label, while the first seed points along $e_2$. The transverse projection in (5.4) therefore leaves the amplitude unchanged. This verifies the compatibility between the central normalization and the localized seed used in §6.1, including at labels away from the origin.
notes.TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.initial_stren: Under $T|B_\rho|\le1/8$, the first wave has initial strength between $\lambda^{1/4}/2$ and $\lambda^{1/4}$. The attained amplitude peak controls its value at time zero, and the initial covector has length $\lambda$. This is the strength estimate in Lemma 6.1; the formal estimate only requires $\lambda>0$.
notes.TorusEuler.FirstWaveOrigin.weighted_forw: On the short interval of Lemma 6.1, an amplitude solution satisfies $|\mathbf b(t)|/\gamma(t)\le\mathsf D|\mathbf b(t^{\prime})|/\gamma(t^{\prime})$ for $t^{\prime}\le t$ and every $\mathsf D\ge2$. Here $\gamma=\lambda^{3/4}|\mathbf a|$. The formal estimate does not require the test amplitude to be transverse, so it includes all the transverse solutions needed in (5.5).
notes.TorusEuler.GrowingCoupling.couplingNumer: Substituting the reference wave vector, amplitude ratio and strain into (2.20)–(2.21) gives their two coupling numerators. Multiplication by $\cos\varphi$ then yields the reference couplings divided by $\nu$. This algebraic step removes the terms proportional to $S^{-2}$; it is a reference calculation, not a claim that those terms vanish at finite shear.
notes.TorusEuler.GrowingCoupling.forcing: The quantities $f_1,f_2,f_3$ describe the strain acting on the amplitude after division by its second component, with the first and third outputs multiplied by $S$. In §2.2.4 they enter (2.20)–(2.21). The expression accepts the complete strain in the preceding frame; the preceding wave contributes to its shear entry.
notes.TorusEuler.GrowingCoupling.normalized_co: This identity gives (2.20)–(2.21) by evaluating $\nu_+$ and $\eta_+$ in the preceding wave’s oriented orthonormal frame. It requires a positive frequency and shear, $\alpha_2>0$, $\zeta_3\ne0$, and $k\cdot\mathbf a=0$. Those hypotheses justify the normalized amplitude and wave directions. The calculation supplies the algebraic starting point for Lemma 2.7, without yet estimating the couplings.

Adding the strain error $E_c$ changes each coupling divided by $\nu$ by at most $\|E_c\|/\nu$. The wave vector and amplitude must be nonzero and perpendicular, so their normalized directions form an orthonormal frame. In §2.2.4 this estimate accounts for the error omitted from the explicit formulas (2.20)–(2.21).

Under the wave geometry and coefficient bounds used in §2.2.4, this estimate controls the difference between each coupling divided by $\nu$ and its reference value. If the specified coordinate errors are at most $\kappa$, the bound is $256T^8\kappa+2\delta$. The estimates for the coordinates are inputs here; Lemmas 2.4 and 2.6 provide them before the smallness condition yields Lemma 2.7.
notes.TorusEuler.GrowingCoupling.referenceForc: The reference values of the three scaled strain components are $f_1=1/2$, $f_2=-Y$ and $f_3=\varepsilon/2$. They are substituted into the coupling formulas in §2.2.4 before the cancellation leading to (2.22). The expression itself only records these values; the reference equation and bounds on $Y$ enter later estimates.
notes.TorusEuler.HasOffOriginLimits: For every compact subset of $\mathbb T^3\setminus\{0\}$ and every order $m$, the field and all its derivatives through order $m$ converge uniformly to a $C^m$ field as $t\uparrow T_*$. This expresses the last conclusion of Theorem 1.1. Applied to the smooth solution with $T_*>0$, it gives spatial limits, without asserting smooth extension in time through $T_*$.
notes.TorusEuler.HasSmoothOffOriginExtension: The extension agrees with the original velocity before $T_*$ and is jointly smooth in space and time away from the torus origin. It is periodic and defined for every real time, a stronger extension requirement than the local continuation through $T_*$ in Remark 1.2. No Euler equation is imposed on this extended field after the singular time.
notes.TorusEuler.HierarchyLevelBound: The induction keeps the bounds (5.34)–(5.36) together with the sharper source and mean estimates (5.40). The latter contain no power of the parent scale, preventing losses from accumulating with the level. This declaration states the inequalities to be propagated; the subsequent induction proves them from the recurrence and the frequency smallness condition.
notes.TorusEuler.HierarchyMeasuredLevels.ofPro: These are the profile norms entering the numerical induction for Theorem 5.6. The oscillatory quantity combines velocity and $\lambda$ times pressure, while the means use unweighted norms on the whole interval. The source at level one is zero, and the first mean source includes the parent residual, exactly as in (5.27).
notes.TorusEuler.HierarchyOperators.level_two_: At level two, the mean forcing is the negative phase average of the quadratic wave terms minus the parent residual. This gives the sign and placement of the residual in the first correction described in §1.3. The algebra assumes the leading-level cancellations and the stated divergence-correction identity; solving the resulting endpoint equation is a separate analytic step.
notes.TorusEuler.HierarchyOperators.meanPhaseA: The supplementary source $f_p^S$ is determined by the profiles below level $p$ and the newly computed mean $B_p$. It needs no value of $V_p$. This is the dependency stated after (5.28): one first solves the endpoint problem for the mean, then forms the forcing for the transverse correction.

At a retained level $p\le P$, the mean phase-advection terms sum to $\sum_{i=2}^{p}(B_i\cdot\kappa)\partial_sY_{p+1-i}$. The supplementary source in (5.28) is its negative. In particular, the last term contains $B_p$ transporting $Y_1=V_1$, which explains why the current mean is needed before the transverse solve.
notes.TorusEuler.HierarchyOperators.momentum_e: Expanding the quadratic terms and substituting the mean and transverse equations cancels every retained level. The parent residual cancels at level two, leaving $R_P+R_{\widetilde\chi}$ as in (5.29). This is an algebraic identity conditional on the expansion equations and endpoint conventions; the construction of profiles satisfying those equations is established separately.
notes.TorusEuler.HierarchyOperators.remainder: The remainder contains $(\partial_t+M)C_{P+1}+\mathbf d\mathsf p_P$ and the quadratic interactions beyond the retained depth, as in (5.30). Phase advection is separated into contributions from corrections and means because $V_i\cdot\kappa=0$. Thus the alternative expression uses the same surviving interactions as the paper once the expansion constraints hold.
notes.TorusEuler.HierarchyOperators.sourceBefo: The preliminary source $H_p$ combines the preceding curl correction and pressure with label advection and phase advection by the curl corrections. At level two, the activation contribution is removed, giving (5.25); later levels give (5.26). Transport by the means is added separately after solving for $B_p$, through $f_p^S$.

Two profile families agreeing at every earlier level produce the same $H_p$ for $p\ge2$. Their divergence corrections are included in that agreement, each having already been determined from the preceding oscillation. This makes precise the sentence before (5.28): the preliminary source requires none of the new fields $V_p$, $B_p$, or $\mathsf p_p$.
notes.TorusEuler.HierarchyProfiles.velocity: This is the finite sum of the oscillatory profiles, their divergence corrections and the mean profiles. In the paper's notation it retains the final term $C_{P+1}$, as required in §1.3. Adding the parent after evaluating the profiles on the transported phase gives the approximate velocity. The sum alone makes no convergence claim about an infinite hierarchy.
notes.TorusEuler.HierarchyProfiles.velocity_eq: For positive depth and $C_1=0$, regrouping the finite perturbation gives $W=\sum_{p=1}^P Z_p+C_{P+1}$. The extra term completes the last oscillatory profile and must not be discarded. This is the bookkeeping identity used in §1.3 and §5.5; it requires no differential equation or estimate.
notes.TorusEuler.HierarchySmoothProfile.eq_zer: A smooth correction that vanishes before activation also vanishes at $t_0$, provided $0<t_0\le T$. This supplies the zero value at the beginning of the active interval in §5.4. When $t_0=0$, the same conclusion comes from the prescribed zero initial velocity, rather than from earlier vanishing.
notes.TorusEuler.HierarchySmoothProfile.moment: Evaluating the profile momentum on $a=X(t,\cdot)^{-1}(x)$ and $s=k_*\cdot a$ gives the residual of $U+W^\natural$, after adding the parent residual. This combines the material, advection, and pressure chain rules used in Lemma 5.8. The parent flow, its inverse, and the profile coefficients must have the stated smoothness and identities.
notes.TorusEuler.HierarchySmoothProfile.profil: This is the correction $C[V]=\mathbf d\times Q[V]$ in (3.5), formed by differentiating the wave potential at fixed phase. It supplies the additional velocity needed after localization in §3.1. The formula accepts a prescribed derivative matrix and nonzero wave covector; the identities that make the completed wave divergence free additionally require both to come from the same parent flow.

If a profile vanishes before activation and outside a fixed closed set of particle labels, its divergence correction vanishes there too. This is the support argument following (3.6): integration in phase preserves label support, and differentiation is local. The formal statement uses one closed support set throughout the time interval, rather than making a separate assertion for every instantaneous support.

For a transverse profile, this proves $\partial_s(\kappa\cdot C[V])=-\mathbf d\cdot V$, the step preceding the second identity in (3.6). The derivative matrix and covector must arise from one twice continuously differentiable inverse flow map. The zero-mean primitive is still needed to recover the identity for $\kappa\cdot C[V]$ itself; this result establishes its phase derivative.

The divergence correction is odd under simultaneous reflection of label and phase when the profile is odd and the derivative matrix and covector are even. Period one and zero phase mean are assumed, as is a nonzero covector. This proves the correction part of the parity argument in §3.1; composing with the odd inverse parent flow then gives an odd Eulerian velocity.

The correction $C[V]$ has zero phase mean because its potential has zero phase mean and averaging commutes with the curl at fixed phase. This justifies the normalization used to recover (3.6). The formal statement requires the derivative matrix to be independent of phase, as it is for the parent flow in §3.1.

The wave potential has zero average in $s$, the normalization used in (3.5) and (3.6). This conclusion holds for every smooth input profile with a nonzero covector because the primitive has its own mean subtracted. Periodicity is a separate issue: a periodic profile with zero phase mean also gives a periodic potential.

This identifies the curl at fixed phase with the label derivative of the potential, converted to Eulerian directions by the inverse flow derivative. It is the operation denoted $\mathbf d\times Q$ in §3.1. The identity explains why the divergence correction costs one label derivative; a quantitative estimate for that cost is supplied separately.

The divergence at fixed phase of $\mathbf d\times Q$ vanishes when $\mathbf d$ comes from a twice continuously differentiable inverse flow map. This proves the second cancellation used after (3.6). An arbitrary prescribed matrix of derivative directions would not suffice: the common coordinate map is what makes the usual divergence-of-curl identity applicable.
notes.TorusEuler.HierarchySmoothProfile.slabTi: For a profile evaluated along the parent flow, differentiation at fixed label and phase becomes $\partial_t+U\cdot\nabla$ in physical coordinates. The identity holds throughout the closed time interval for a smooth periodic parent. The auxiliary note uses it repeatedly to convert profile time estimates into bounds for derivatives at a fixed spatial point.
notes.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.Paren: The curl correction and $(\partial_t+M)C[V]+\mathbf d\mathsf p$ satisfy the $\lambda^{-1}$ estimates of Lemma 5.5, with one extra label derivative. The formal statement allows any positive continuous time weight, but requires zero phase averages on all of $[0,T]$, while the estimates concern $[t_0,T]$. Its parent exponent is independent of derivative order.

The unswitched leading velocity $A_1$, its pressure, and its curl correction satisfy the homogeneous form of Lemma 5.5 on $[t_0,T]$. The formal proof represents these fields by smooth profiles on the whole interval that agree there. This avoids requiring the unswitched leading wave itself to vanish before activation.
notes.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.Physi: The selected hierarchy yields smooth velocity and pressure, odd velocity, zero divergence, and the momentum identity (5.46). It assumes the smooth periodic parent and identifies the hierarchy residual with the physical residual of the parent. Evenness of the pressure is deduced from these relations, so no separate pressure symmetry assumption is needed.

The unswitched field $A_1+C[A_1]$ has scaled derivatives through order two bounded by a fixed parent power times $\lambda^{-5/4}\gamma(t)$. This is the input used in Lemma 5.8 to estimate $R_{\widetilde\chi}^\natural$. The bound is proved for the actual localized seed under the parent, envelope, and central-wave assumptions.

Before activation, or outside the transported label support, the oscillatory correction is zero. On that region the residual reduces to the remaining products of mean corrections. This gives the localization claimed in §1.3. It concerns the oscillations and their divergence corrections; the mean correction and the change introduced by Fourier truncation need not have that support.

The phase average of the finite velocity correction, evaluated in physical coordinates, equals the sum of its mean profiles. Since $B_1=0$, this is exactly $\bar W^\natural$ with $\bar W=\sum_{p=2}^{P}B_p$ in §5.6. The identity concerns the selected expansion, so the mean cannot be chosen independently of its oscillatory part.

The mean correction obeys the $C^{m,1/2}$ bound of (5.48), with decay $\lambda^{-5/2}$. It is obtained from actual level estimates and bounds on the inverse parent labels, with no fast phase derivative cost. The formal statement fixes a finite range of derivative orders and provides one coefficient controlling that range; the range is arbitrary.

Adding the selected mean equations gives the linearized Euler equation over $U$ for $\bar W^\natural$, with the corresponding sums of pressures and sources. Lemma 5.9 uses this equation to estimate the mean pressure. The relation holds throughout the closed time interval, with endpoint time derivatives taken from within that interval.

The summed mean pressure satisfies $\Delta\sum_p ar q_p^
atural=\operatorname{div}(\sum_p ar f_p)^
atural-2\operatorname{tr}(
abla U\,
abla ar W^
atural)$. This is the Poisson equation used in Lemma 5.9. It follows from the linearized momentum equation and incompressibility of the parent and the selected mean correction, with smoothness justifying the differentiated identities.

The derivatives at the origin of the nonleading oscillation and the mean have total size bounded by a parent power times $\lambda^{-5/12}$. This follows from their order-one profile estimates and the inverse deformation bounds. In Lemma 5.9, the smallness condition (5.43) then absorbs $\lambda^{-1/12}$ to obtain $|E_c|\le\lambda^{-1/3}$.

This is the physical field obtained from $W_{\rm osc}-V_1=\sum_{p=2}^{P}V_p+\sum_{p=2}^{P+1}C_p$ by evaluating on the inverse-label phase graph. Lemma 5.9 differentiates it at the origin to define part of $E_c$. The last curl correction remains in the sum even though there is no transverse velocity at level $P+1$.

The retained oscillations satisfy the supremum estimate (5.47). Their weighted profile bounds control physical values without any derivative cost because $\gamma\le1$; vanishing before activation extends the estimate to $[0,T]$. The constant must absorb the finite sum of levels, and the hypotheses explicitly provide the corresponding order-zero estimates.

The flow of $V+v$ and its inverse satisfy the $C_{\rm step}\lambda^{1/4}$ derivative bound of Lemma 5.10. The perturbation is smooth, periodic, divergence free, and bounded by $\lambda^{-5/2}$ through order two. The conclusion includes a flow with inverse transitions; its proof uses the actual hierarchy estimates and the smallness condition (5.43).

The assembled velocity and pressure satisfy (5.46), with residual equal to the transported expansion remainder plus the activation error. Smoothness, odd velocity, and zero divergence are included. This statement collects properties already established for the selected approximation; it relies on that prior construction rather than independently producing a new solution.

The oscillatory correction satisfies the $C^{m,1/2}$ bound in (5.48), with frequency power $3(m+1)/2-5/4$. The extra derivative needed for Hölder control explains the appearance of $m+1$. The estimate uses actual level bounds and inverse deformation estimates, and holds before activation because the oscillation vanishes there.

The higher oscillatory pressure Hessian is bounded by a parent power times $\lambda^{-5/12}$, while the mean pressure Hessian has the smaller scale $\lambda^{-5/2}$. These are the two nonleading estimates in Lemma 5.9. Both concern the same selected hierarchy and follow from its bounds through order two, together with parent coefficient estimates.

The three pressure contributions yield the one-sided Hessian bound (5.49), while the velocity gradient at the origin has the rank-one leading term and an error at most $\lambda^{-1/3}$ as in (5.50). This result combines previously supplied pressure and leading-gradient bounds with the actual level estimates; the smallness condition absorbs the remaining constants.

The source for the level-$p$ mean equation is $-\langle H_p\rangle_s$, with the additional term $-R_U\circ X$ only at $p=2$. This is exactly the distinction in (5.27). The source belongs to the same selected expansion as its mean correction and is the quantity estimated in the unweighted norms of Theorem 5.6.

The constructed profiles satisfy the finite-sum formulas, divergence constraint, and residual identity of Proposition 5.4. Their oscillatory parts and sources vanish on the inactive region, and the remainder is phase independent outside the envelope. The statement assumes the selected physical construction; existence and uniqueness among all families satisfying the recurrence are addressed by the numbered proposition.

Summing the retained level estimates yields (5.37): the oscillatory correction has scale $\lambda^{-5/4}$, while both the mean sum and its source sum have scale $\lambda^{-5/2}$. The formal bounds concern the constructed profiles and retain the parent residual in the first mean source. The finite number of levels enters the constants.

The pressure is $\Pi=p_U+\mathsf P^\natural$, using the same finite expansion and inverse parent labels as the velocity in §5.6. This fixes the pressure appearing in the exact residual identity (5.46). The zero-mean Poisson pressure assigned after Fourier truncation is a separate choice, compared with $\Pi$ in Proposition 5.11.

The finite hierarchy is obtained by successively applying the endpoint mean solve, transverse solve, and curl correction, starting from the chosen leading wave. The parent residual and activation terms are fixed inputs. These are the actual profiles used in Proposition 5.4; their estimates are subsequent conclusions of Theorem 5.6.

The physical residual splits into the transported remainder and $\widetilde\chi^{\prime}(A_1+C[A_1])^\natural$, as used in Lemma 5.8. The identity holds for any admissible time cutoff tied to the selected leading wave, throughout $[0,T]$. Thus the activation error is kept separate from the error controlled by the expansion depth.

The residual obeys the last estimate in (5.48), with $\|\widetilde\chi^{\prime}\gamma\|_\infty$ taken over the activation interval. The statement permits any admissible cutoff and uses the actual remainder estimate and the two-derivative bound for $A_1+C[A_1]$. It therefore preserves the dependence on the chosen activation, needed later in §6.

For the pullback with $v=0$, the oscillatory part has two scaled derivatives of size $O(\lambda^{-5/4})$, and the mean has one derivative of size $O(\lambda^{-5/2})$, up to parent powers. These suffice for the flow argument in Lemma 5.10. This statement does not include the displayed second-order mean bound or a general perturbation $v$.

The approximate velocity is $V=U+W^\natural$, with the depth-$P$ profile evaluated at the inverse parent labels and their phase. This is the definition at the start of §5.6. The profiles come from the selected recursion; smoothness, zero divergence, oddness, and the precise residual equation are established by the accompanying assembly theorem.

The approximate velocity is exactly the parent plus the leading wave, the higher oscillatory remainder and the mean correction. This is the decomposition used in §1.3 to explain the correction scheme. Positive retained depth is required. The identity identifies the four terms; their size, residual and support bounds come from separate estimates.

For the selected localized leading wave, the correction of $\widetilde\chi A_1$ equals $\widetilde\chi C[A_1]$, as in (3.7). The result also identifies the corresponding cutoff derivative as $\widetilde\chi' C[A_1]$. It applies to the constructed wave with its parent flow, regularity and parity assumptions, and supplies the correction component of the switching residual.

The leading wave and its divergence correction contribute exactly $\widetilde\chi'(A_1+C[A_1])$ when the time cutoff is differentiated. This is the residual $R_{\widetilde\chi}$ in (3.8), for the selected localized wave and parent flow. The identity accepts every admissible cutoff; estimating its size requires separate control of the wave during activation.
notes.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.Trans: The transverse solution consists of a velocity $V$ and pressure $\mathsf p$ satisfying (5.15), with $V(0)=0$ and zero phase mean for the pressure. Its pressure is the normalized primitive specified by (5.16). The formulation also records the support and reflection properties used in §5.5: vanishing of the source before activation or outside a label set passes to both fields.

The transverse equation gives $
abla_x\mathsf p_p^
atural=(\mathbf d\mathsf p_p+P_\kappa(f_p+f_p^S-2MV_p))^
atural$. Lemma 5.9 uses this identity before taking one further physical derivative. It avoids paying the fast derivative cost twice, which would lose the decay required for the higher oscillatory pressure Hessian.
notes.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.Trunc: The parent is supplied with the deformation and velocity bounds of (5.1), frequency bounds $2\mathsf D$ and $4\mathsf D$ for its velocity and residual, and the residual estimate (5.6). These are assumptions for the correction construction in §5, together with the geometry used by the endpoint problem. They do not assert that the parent already solves Euler exactly.

The velocity, pressure and flow satisfying the hypotheses of §5.1 determine coefficients for the mean and transverse equations. In particular, the coercivity assumption is the actual bound $D^2p_U-\nabla R_U\le\operatorname{Id}$, with $R_U$ the momentum residual. Fourier support and residual size are supplied explicitly; no exact Euler equation for the parent is required.

The inverse flow of a truncated parent satisfies both graph estimates of Lemma 5.7, including their phase-independent specialization. The constants are chosen before the parent, with $\ell_*=\mathsf D^{-a}$ and $h=\lambda^{-1/2}$. The formal statement allows arbitrary normed target spaces and positive continuous weights; its sums over derivative directions control the coordinate derivatives in the paper.

A physical expansion with the required leading-wave and correction estimates satisfies the level, finite-sum, and remainder bounds of Theorem 5.6. This statement takes that expansion and its leading estimates as inputs. The construction from a parent and central wave is supplied by further existence results, so this conditional estimate alone is not the whole construction.

A truncated parent and prescribed central wave determine a localized seed and a finite expansion satisfying the estimates of Theorem 5.6 at every derivative order. The constants are fixed before the parent data. This result uses the later-wave time cutoff; the more general construction subsequently allows any admissible cutoff after the seed has been chosen.

Under the parent bounds and $L^6\lambda^{-1/12}\le1$, with $L=\mathsf D^{2a+b_0}$, one localized seed works for every admissible smooth activation and every depth $P\ge2$. Each expansion satisfies all spatial derivative estimates. This makes the finite correction scheme of §1.3 precise: constants are chosen before the parent, and the seed before the activation and depth. The final residual estimate has no remaining power of the parent scale.

Given a localized seed satisfying the regularity and central-wave assumptions, the later-wave activation produces one expansion obeying the level, sum, and remainder bounds of Theorem 5.6. The construction derives the leading estimates from this seed. The same profiles satisfy every derivative order, rather than being chosen anew when the requested order changes.

Under the standing parent and central-wave assumptions and (5.43), one localized seed works for every admissible time cutoff. The resulting expansion satisfies all the physical conclusions of Lemmas 5.8–5.10. The common exponent and depth-dependent constants are fixed beforehand, ensuring the velocity, pressure, residual, central gradient, and flow estimates concern the same construction.

The truncated-parent assumptions supply the coefficient bounds needed to pass from profiles to physical fields in Lemma 5.7. They include derivatives of the inverse flow and its scaled deformation coefficients. The constants and exponent are selected before the parent; these estimates are derived from the standing assumptions, rather than imposed as new independent restrictions.
notes.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.ampli: The weighted norm of $(Z\cdot\kappa)\partial_sY$ is controlled by the unweighted norm of $Z$, the next weighted norm of $Y$, and the coefficient $h^{-1}\kappa$. This gives the second estimate of (5.39) after applying the parent bounds. With $h=\lambda^{-1/2}$, the resulting frequency cost is $\lambda^{3/2}$.
notes.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.avera: If $Y$ has zero phase average and $B$ is independent of phase, then $\langle(Y\cdot\mathbf d)B\rangle_s=0$. The parent deformation coefficients are also phase independent. This removes one kind of mixed product when averaging $H_p$ in the proof of Theorem 5.6, leaving only interactions between two oscillations or two means.

For a phase-independent $B$ and a zero-mean oscillation $Y$, the average of $(B\cdot\mathbf d)Y$ vanishes. Smoothness allows label differentiation to commute with phase averaging. Together with the reversed interaction, this supplies the mixed-product cancellation used after (5.42) to express the mean source using only the three displayed sums.

The phase average of $(B\cdot\kappa)\partial_sY$ is zero whenever $B$ and $\kappa$ are phase independent and $Y$ is periodic. No zero-mean condition on $Y$ is needed for this identity. Applying it to each term of (5.28) proves that the supplementary source is admissible for the transverse equation.

Periodic integration by parts and the divergence correction identity give $\langle(C[V]\cdot\kappa)\partial_sY\rangle_s=\langle(\mathbf d\cdot V)Y\rangle_s$. The profile $V$ must be transverse and have zero phase average, with coefficients supplied by the parent flow. This is the cancellation in (5.42) that avoids the fast derivative cost when estimating the mean source.

The preceding curl correction and oscillatory pressure have zero phase average, so their linear contribution to $H_p$ averages to zero. The activation term removed at level two also has zero average. This leaves the quadratic terms, together with the separately added parent residual at level two, as the forcing of the mean equation.

Averaging $H_p$ leaves label advection between oscillations, the label-divergence products obtained from (5.42), and label advection between means. The identity uses the actual transported coefficients and curl corrections, as well as the zero-mean and transversality constraints. It gives the three sums after (5.42); the source at level two additionally includes $R_U\circ X$.
notes.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.bound: The norm of $(Z\cdot\mathbf d)Z^{\prime}$ is bounded by the current-order norm of $Z$, the next-order norm of $Z^{\prime}$, and the scaled inverse deformation bound. This is part of (5.39). The formal estimate allows separate bounded time weights on the two factors, so the amplitude weight can be placed on either one.

The product $(\mathbf d\cdot V)Y$ is bounded using one extra derivative of $V$, the current-order norm of $Y$, and the scaled inverse deformation coefficients. This supplies the other slow product in (5.39). The formal statement also permits Hölder norms and distributes a bounded time weight between the two factors.
notes.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.const: If the parent coefficients are even and the leading velocity and residual are odd, parity-preserving mean, transverse, and curl operations propagate the reflection law under $(a,s)\mapsto(-a,-s)$. Every velocity correction is odd and each pressure is even. The statement also gives parity of the total correction and remainder used in §5.5.1.
notes.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.exist: For a sufficiently small envelope, the transverse estimates (5.20) and (5.21) hold with the fixed power $\mathsf D^{20}$. The first permits a nonzero initial value at $t_0$; the second estimates the zero-initial-value solution and its pressure when the source vanishes before activation. The radius is chosen before the derivative order, and the supported data remain near the origin modulo periodicity.

For a smooth source with zero phase mean, this result constructs a transverse solution of (5.15) with zero initial velocity and normalized pressure. It also supplies the support and reflection properties required by the finite expansion. The statement proves existence with these properties; uniqueness among all solutions is established separately.
notes.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.graph: The field $g^\natural$ is obtained by evaluating the profile at the inverse label and at $s=k_*\cdot a$, as in §5.6. Smoothness and the combined label-phase translation rule belong to the profile. Periodicity of the physical field also uses the lattice translation law of the chosen inverse-label map.
notes.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.inver: For an odd parent velocity, the inverse flow is odd. Therefore a profile that changes by a fixed sign under $(a,s)\mapsto(-a,-s)$ has the same parity after phase evaluation. In Lemma 5.8 this gives oddness of $W^\natural$; the same statement also applies to even pressure profiles.
notes.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.momen: The finite hierarchy identity becomes the Eulerian equation (5.46) once its residual profile is identified with $R_U\circ X$. The parent residual then cancels exactly, leaving the transported tail and the two leading activation terms. The statement assumes the smooth parent flow, its coefficient identities, and the constructed hierarchy at depth $P\ge2$.
notes.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.norm_: The factorially weighted time norm bounds its $i$th term by $i!T^{-i}$ times the whole norm, for $i\le q$ and $T>0$. This applies to either mean or oscillatory profiles with any chosen spatial seminorm. In the auxiliary note, the lower bound for $T$ converts this loss into a fixed power of the parent frequency.
notes.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.paper: A phase-independent profile satisfies the derivative and Hölder estimates of Lemma 5.7 on all of $[0,T]$, with only a power of $\mathsf D$ per derivative. The proof uses the constant weight one. Bounds on the inverse deformation coefficients are explicit inputs; the factor $\lambda^{3/2}$ does not occur because there is no phase dependence.

For a phase-independent profile, composing with inverse labels costs only parent powers, even in the weighted form of Lemma 5.7. The estimate retains $\gamma(t)$ and the corresponding weighted profile norm. Its assumptions give a positive continuous weight and inverse deformation bounds through the order required for the Hölder estimate.

The graph derivative and Hölder estimates hold on $[0,T]$ with weight one, as asserted after (5.45). The frequency cost remains $\lambda^{3/2}$ per physical derivative for a general oscillatory profile. The statement uses the prescribed width and wave vector bounds, together with smoothness and derivative bounds for the inverse-label coefficients.

Each physical derivative costs a parent power times $\lambda^{3/2}$, while a $C^{m,1/2}$ estimate uses one additional derivative, as in (5.44)–(5.45). The formal sum counts all ordered coordinate derivative sequences, which controls the multi-index sum in the paper. Order-dependent comparison factors enter $C_m$; the weight is positive and continuous on the active interval.
notes.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.physi: Before activation or outside the envelope, all transverse velocities, curl corrections, oscillatory pressures, and transverse sources vanish. There the remainder equals a sum of products $(B_i\cdot\mathbf d)B_j$. This proves the final support assertion of Proposition 5.4. The means may persist on that region because the endpoint problem selects their initial values globally in time.
notes.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.selec: For positive time order $q$, the selected mean correction is controlled using forcing derivatives only through order $q-1$, together with the endpoint inverse and bounds for the parent coefficients. The estimate uses the unweighted spatial norm and a factorially weighted sum of time derivatives. The auxiliary note then bounds these coefficients by parent-frequency powers to close its induction on time order.
notes.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.solve: This is the solution of (5.15) used at each level of the expansion: its velocity starts from zero and its pressure has zero phase mean. It is selected from the proved existence result for a smooth source with zero phase mean. Its equations and support properties therefore accompany the selected fields.
notes.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.termi: With $P=6K_{j+1}$ and $\lambda_{j+1}=\lambda_j^{K_{j+1}}$, the remainder factor becomes exactly $\lambda_j^{-5/4}\lambda_{j+1}^{-4}$. This is the arithmetic behind the depth choice in the auxiliary residual estimate. It identifies the decay supplied by the finite expansion after the analytic estimate for its remainder has been established.

If the label contribution is at most $\lambda^{1/2}$, multiplying it by the phase cost $\lambda^{3/2}$ gives a bound of $\lambda^2$. The auxiliary note obtains the required label inequality at sufficiently large stages from frequency separation. This arithmetic estimate concerns oscillatory profiles; the mean has its own bounds in powers of the parent frequency.
notes.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.timeD: This derivative holds the Lagrangian label and the independent phase fixed on a positive time interval. It is the time derivative used for the profile estimates in the auxiliary note. After evaluating the profile in physical space, it corresponds to the material derivative along the parent flow, rather than to differentiation at a fixed spatial point.
notes.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.timeJ: The time seminorm sums the spatial seminorms of derivatives through order $q$, with weights $T^i/i!$. The spatial seminorm can include the amplitude weight used for oscillations or be unweighted for means. Differentiation precedes division by the amplitude, so derivatives of that weight are not introduced. The auxiliary estimates use these factorial weights to control product expansions.
notes.TorusEuler.InductiveEulerParameters: The schedule records $q_1=1$, the frequency recurrence, the maximum rule for choosing the next order, and the positive threshold with its logarithmic lower bound. It also fixes the strength and comparison constants used throughout the construction. These are the assumptions on the common parameters in §1.5; separate existence results show that they can be met.
notes.TorusEuler.InductiveEulerParameters.Step: The auxiliary note enlarges the collection of constants bounded by $\mathcal B$ to include time derivatives as well as spatial orders and expansion depths. This construction retains the constants of the main argument and includes the additional derivative orders required by the time estimates. It is chosen before the initial frequency and the resulting sequence of approximate solutions.
notes.TorusEuler.InductiveEulerParameters.abs_: Each fixed-order constant in the auxiliary estimates is bounded by the enlarged threshold whenever its time order, spatial order and depth lie in the prescribed ranges. The bound follows by including its absolute value in a finite sum. This implements the auxiliary note’s choice of $\mathcal B$, with allowance for additional spatial derivatives arising from time differentiation.
notes.TorusEuler.InductiveEulerParameters.even: For every fixed $C,A$ and $\varepsilon>0$, the quantity $C\lambda_{j-1}^{A}\lambda_j^{-\varepsilon}$ is eventually at most one. The frequency exponents grow, so they absorb any fixed power of the parent frequency. The auxiliary note uses this fact to close the time-derivative recurrence; the first admissible stage may depend on the fixed constants and orders.
notes.TorusEuler.InductiveEulerParameters.exis: The constants of the main proof and the auxiliary time estimates fit a single frequency schedule once the initial frequency is sufficiently large. The threshold is fixed first, and the construction retains the original step inequalities and lifetime bounds. Each auxiliary constant within the admitted derivative ranges is then bounded by the parent frequency, as required in auxiliary equation (1.1).
notes.TorusEuler.InductiveEulerParameters.step: The expansion depth is chosen as $P=6K_{j+1}$ at wave $j$, as in (7.2). This ties the number of corrections to the frequency of the following wave. The definition fixes the depth; the separate estimate (7.11) shows how it makes the expansion residual small enough for the next step.
notes.TorusEuler.InductiveEulerParameters.term: The scheduled interval for the next wave satisfies $T^{-1}\le\lambda_{j-1}^{1/8}$ under the stated lower bound on the initial frequency and nonnegative activation time. Hence a fixed number of time differentiations introduces only a fixed parent-frequency power through factors such as $T^{-q}$. This supplies one of the numerical bounds used in the auxiliary note’s time estimates.
notes.TorusEuler.InductiveEulerStage.exists_re: Every time derivative of a stage residual remains supported on frequencies at most $4\lambda_j^5$ throughout the closed stage interval. The statement uses smoothness of the stage and positivity of the interval length. In the auxiliary note, this permits Bernstein estimates for spatial derivatives of the time-differentiated residual without enlarging its frequency scale.
notes.TorusEuler.InductiveEulerStage.exists_sl: A uniform bound for a time derivative of either the velocity or the residual gives an order-$m$ spatial bound with cost $C_m\lambda_j^{5m}$. The constants are fixed before the stage, time order and input bounds. This is the Bernstein step following auxiliary Lemma 1.3; the formal norm of a derivative is equivalent to the paper’s coordinate-derivative norm up to order-dependent constants.
notes.TorusEuler.InductiveEulerStage.exists_te: Bounds for velocity and residual through time order $q$ give a velocity bound through order $q+1$. Spatial derivatives of order $m$ cost an additional factor $C_m\lambda_j^{5m}$, while the residual retains its next-frequency decay through order $q$. The new velocity exponent is independent of $m$, which is essential for the auxiliary induction to control all spatial orders.
notes.TorusEuler.InductiveEulerStage.exists_ve: Every time derivative of a stage velocity remains supported on frequencies at most $2\lambda_j^5$ on its closed time interval. The stage is smooth and periodic, and the interval has positive length. Together with the analogous residual statement, this justifies using the same spatial Bernstein scale at each time order in the auxiliary note.
notes.TorusEuler.InductiveEulerStage.slabTimeJ: Differentiating the projected Euler equation gives the next velocity derivative as the preceding residual derivative minus the Leray projection of the binomial advection sum. Thus time order $q+1$ of the velocity uses residual derivatives only through order $q$. This is the identity in the auxiliary note that makes induction on time order possible.
notes.TorusEuler.InductiveEulerStages.HasTermi: For each fixed pair $(m,q)$, the correction $U_j-U_{j-1}-O_j$ eventually has time derivative of order $q$ bounded by $\lambda_j^{-1}$ in $C^{m,1/2}$ throughout the child interval. This records the bound in auxiliary Lemma 1.2, with an order-dependent starting stage. Continuity in time with values in that spatial norm is an additional part of the full lemma.
notes.TorusEuler.InductiveEulerStages.StageTim: At a fixed stage, velocity derivatives through time order $q$ are bounded by $\lambda_j^\psi$, and residual derivatives by $\lambda_{j+1}^{-5/2}$. These are uniform pointwise estimates on the closed time interval. Auxiliary Lemma 1.3 additionally chooses the exponent and a stage beyond which the bounds hold, and supplies continuity in the spatial supremum norm.
notes.TorusEuler.InductiveEulerStages.Terminal: The auxiliary induction needs two implications: lower time-order bounds give the next velocity and residual bounds, and they also give the next correction estimate at each fixed spatial order. Both implications are required only at sufficiently large stages. This records the hypotheses for that induction; the analytic work proving them is supplied by the profile and cutoff estimates.
notes.TorusEuler.InductiveEulerStages.eventual: Near any point away from the origin, the shrinking supports of the oscillations eventually disappear on the whole time interval. The mixed correction estimate then bounds the full velocity increment $U_j-U_{j-1}$ by $\lambda_j^{-1}$ at each fixed space and time order. A single spatial neighborhood works for all orders, although the starting stage may depend on them.
notes.TorusEuler.InductiveEulerStages.paper_pr: A compatible sequence of stages whose activation times tend to $T_*>0$ produces a smooth Euler solution on $[0,T_*)$. The initial data and velocities converge in every spatial $C^{m,1/2}$ norm on compact preterminal intervals, strengthening the introductory $C^m$ statement. The limit agrees with any maximal classical solution with the same data on their common interval. The stage estimates are hypotheses of this result.
notes.TorusEuler.InductiveEulerStages.stageMix: At time order zero, the correction estimate follows from the existing stage bound whenever $m\le q_j$. This starts the induction for auxiliary Lemma 1.2 without any new analytic estimate. Since the scheduled spatial orders tend to infinity, every fixed $m$ eventually satisfies the required restriction.
notes.TorusEuler.InductiveEulerStages.stageTim: The pointwise velocity and residual estimates imply the same bounds in the spatial supremum norm at every time of the stage interval. The derivative order remains at most $q$. This supplies the norm inequalities used in auxiliary Lemma 1.3; the eventual choice of stage and continuity with respect to time are established separately.

The main stage estimates give the auxiliary time bounds at order zero with velocity exponent one. The residual bound $\lambda_{j+1}^{-3}$ implies $\lambda_{j+1}^{-5/2}$ because the frequencies are at least one. This is the base case in the proof of auxiliary Lemma 1.3, and it holds at every stage of the fixed sequence.
notes.TorusEuler.InductiveEulerStages.terminal: Once the two analytic induction steps are available, induction on time order yields both the velocity-residual estimates and the mixed correction bounds. The spatial orders must tend to infinity, and all frequencies must be at least one. The resulting exponent and starting stage may depend on the time order, with the correction’s starting stage also depending on spatial order.

The mixed correction bounds, shrinking supports and summable inverse frequencies make the selected velocity limit jointly smooth up to the terminal time away from the origin. The same velocity must be the uniform limit on the closed common slab, whose enclosing stage intervals are nested. This supplies the boundary regularity needed for the auxiliary extension argument.

On a closed cylinder around each point away from the origin, the stage velocities converge uniformly with every joint space-time derivative. The mixed increment bounds and frequency growth give a summable majorant at each fixed order. The limit is identified with the same uniform velocity limit on the common slab, including its terminal boundary, as required in auxiliary Note 3.
notes.TorusEuler.IsEulerSolution: The velocity and pressure are jointly smooth and spatially periodic on $[0,T_*)$, where $T_*>0$, and satisfy the Euler equations pointwise. The pressure has zero spatial mean, fixing its additive freedom. This is the solution notion used in Theorem 1.1. It does not by itself impose initial data, oddness, maximality or blow-up; those are additional conclusions of the theorem.
notes.TorusEuler.IsEulerSolution.hasSmoothOffO: A preterminal Euler solution that is jointly smooth on the closed punctured slab admits a smooth periodic extension of its velocity through the terminal time away from the origin. The extension agrees with the original velocity before that time. This is the conclusion needed for the auxiliary theorem; the Euler equations are imposed only on the original time interval.
notes.TorusEuler.IsEulerSolution.isMaximal_of_: A smooth Euler solution whose central vorticity tends to infinity as $t\uparrow T_*$ cannot continue smoothly past $T_*$. A continuation would have bounded vorticity near this interior time, contradicting the limit. This is the maximality argument in Corollary 8.3; it does not itself establish divergence of either time integral in (1.2).
notes.TorusEuler.IsEulerSolution.velocity_eq_o: Two smooth periodic Euler velocities with the same initial data agree for $0\le t<\min(T_1,T_2)$. This is the classical uniqueness used when identifying the limit in the introduction and in Theorem 1.1. Neither solution must already be maximal, and the conclusion concerns the velocity on the common lifespan.
notes.TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn: This specifies particle motion by the trajectory equation and the condition that a particle starts at its assigned position. It allows an arbitrary starting time; choosing time zero gives $X(t,a)$ in §3.1. Smooth spatial dependence, invertibility and compatibility with lattice translations are further conclusions under hypotheses on the parent velocity, rather than part of this definition.
notes.TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.add_latticeVect: For a periodic velocity that is uniformly Lipschitz on the time interval, translating the initial particle by an integer vector translates its trajectory by the same vector. Thus the displacement of the lifted flow is periodic. This is the torus compatibility used for the Lagrangian localization in §1.1; the lifted particle position itself is not a periodic Euclidean-valued function.
notes.TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.det_labelDeriva: For a jointly $C^2$, periodic, divergence-free parent on a nontrivial closed time interval, the particle flow has Jacobian determinant one between any two times. This is the volume-preserving change of variables underlying the Lagrangian arguments in §§1.1–1.2. The conclusion concerns the derivative of the actual flow, rather than an independently specified matrix.
notes.TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.even_materialGr: An odd parent velocity has an even material gradient $M$ and an even transported wave vector $\kappa$ as functions of the label. The flow is assumed to be unique on the time interval through a common Lipschitz bound. These parity identities provide the symmetry of the coefficients used in §5.1 and the transverse correction equations.
notes.TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.hasDerivWithinA: For the parent flow, the covector $\kappa=(D_aX)^{-T}k_*$ satisfies $\kappa_t=-M^T\kappa$, with $M$ the velocity gradient along the particle path. This is the transport calculation in §3.1. The formal statement assumes a twice continuously differentiable periodic velocity on a nondegenerate closed time interval; oddness and incompressibility are unnecessary for this identity.
notes.TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.labelDerivative: The spatial derivative of the actual particle flow starts at the identity and satisfies $\partial_tD_aX=MD_aX$. This supplies the first identity in (4.2) and the displacement relation (4.4). The formal result needs only a twice continuously differentiable periodic parent; neither incompressibility nor the Euler equation is needed for this variational identity.

The derivatives of the forward and reverse particle maps compose to the identity, with the reverse derivative evaluated at the transported point. In §4.1 this makes $\xi(T)=0$ equivalent to $z(T)=0$. The formal result assumes a twice continuously differentiable periodic parent, but does not need incompressibility or the Euler equation.
notes.TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.labelJets_evolv: For a smooth periodic parent, every label derivative of $X$ evolves by the corresponding label derivative of $U\circ X$. The statement also supplies the continuity needed to integrate this equation in time. In Proposition 5.1, separating its highest-order linear term gives the variation-of-constants formula underlying (5.9).
notes.TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.norm_iteratedFD: At order $n\ge2$, the derivative of the flow is bounded by the partition sum in (5.9), with a factor $\mathsf D^2$ from the deformation. Every partition has at least two positive parts, so the flow derivatives on the right have order below $n$. The statement assumes their bounds and the differentiated flow equation before performing this induction step.
notes.TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.norm_labelWaveV: The bounds on $D_aX$ and its inverse give $\lVert k_*\rVert/\mathsf D\le\lVert\kappa\rVert\le\mathsf D\lVert k_*\rVert$. Applying this at the origin at activation, where $\lVert\kappa\rVert=\lambda$, bounds the constant wave vector. These estimates are the transport part of (5.3), independent of the seed amplitude.
notes.TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.norm_multilinea: A higher flow variation starting from zero, with forcing bounded by $C$, is bounded by $\mathsf D^2 C$. Both the forward and inverse deformation enter the propagator bound, and $T\le1$ removes the length of the integration interval. Proposition 5.1 uses this estimate after isolating the lower-order forcing in the differentiated flow equation.
notes.TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.norm_normalized: After imposing $\lVert\kappa(t_0,0)\rVert=\lambda$, the deformation bounds imply $\lVert k_*\rVert/\lambda\le\mathsf D$ and $\mathsf D^{-2}\le\lVert\kappa\rVert/\lambda\le\mathsf D^2$. These are the normalized bounds used in §5.1. The remaining lower bound on $\lVert k_*\rVert$ follows by applying the unnormalized transport estimate at activation.
notes.TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.odd: For an odd velocity with a common Lipschitz bound, the flow from any starting time is odd in its initial label. Uniqueness identifies the trajectory from $-a$ with the negative trajectory from $a$. In §5.1 this shows that the origin is fixed and allows evenness of the deformation coefficients to follow by differentiation.
notes.TorusEuler.IsMaximalEulerSolution: A smooth periodic Euler solution on $[0,T_*)$ is maximal when no solution on any longer interval agrees with its velocity before $T_*$. This is the noncontinuation conclusion in Theorem 1.1. Classical uniqueness separately identifies this solution with every other maximal solution from the same initial data; maximality alone is an extension condition.
notes.TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.CenterWave: The central wave vector and seed solve their transport equations on $[t_0,T]$, remain nonzero and perpendicular, and satisfy the two conditions in (5.5). The growth condition covers every transverse solution, not just the chosen seed. The coupling is written without division by amplitudes; nonvanishing makes it equivalent to the paper's normalized inequality. Frequency normalization is imposed separately.
notes.TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.SeedOn: The localized seed solves (3.2) with the projected initial data (5.4) and agrees with the central seed at the origin. In addition to the equation and transversality, this formulation includes quantitative comparison and positive coupling on $\lVert a\rVert\le2\ell_*$. These are conclusions of the localization construction, stronger than merely prescribing the seed equation.
notes.TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.SeedOn.eve: The selected seed remains even in its particle label when $M$ and $\kappa$ are even. Continuity in time and a nonzero covector ensure uniqueness for the amplitude equation. Opposite labels therefore carry the same amplitude throughout the active interval, providing the seed symmetry used to obtain an odd completed velocity in §3.1.
notes.TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.SeedOn.gen: On the centered label cell, the periodically extended leading profile equals $\widetilde\chi A_1$, as in (3.7). The selected envelope vanishes near the cell boundary, so extension does not change its values there. This statement uses the constructed seed, radial envelope and profile family; it permits any admissible time cutoff and any real initial wave vector.

The leading velocity satisfies $D_xV_1^\natural(t,0)=\widetilde\chi(t)\mathbf a(t,0)\otimes\kappa(t,0)$. Oddness of the parent fixes the origin, and $g(0)=F_h^{\prime}(0)=1$, $F_h(0)=0$ eliminate the other chain-rule terms. This is the exact leading contribution separated from $E_c$ in Lemma 5.9, for any admissible time cutoff.

On the centered label cell, the periodically extended pressure is $\widetilde\chi\mathsf p[A_1]$. This is the pressure identity in (3.7), for the selected radial envelope and zero-mean primitive $P_h$. Vanishing near the boundary makes the extension smooth and leaves the local formula unchanged; the statement is an identity, with pressure estimates established elsewhere.
notes.TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.SeedOn.lea: The leading oscillation is $A_1=g\mathbf a F_h$, the product in (3.3) with the particular radial envelope and profile family used in the construction. The paper first writes this formula for arbitrary suitable $g$ and $F_0$; this formal definition fixes the later choices. Smoothness and uniform estimates use a positive envelope radius and $0<h\le1$.

This is $\mathsf p[A_1]=-p_{\rm w}gP_h$, with $p_{\rm w}=2\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a/|\kappa|^2$, from (3.3). The formal definition uses the selected radial envelope, seed and normalized profile primitive. A nonzero covector is required for its use in the wave equations; the paper introduces the same formula before specializing its envelope and phase profile.
notes.TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.SeedOn.pap: For $0<h\le1$, the selected leading oscillation and pressure satisfy (3.4) throughout the active interval. The result also states transversality and zero phase mean for both velocity and pressure. This is the homogeneous equation before switching: after multiplication by $\widetilde\chi$, differentiating the cutoff produces the source described in (3.8).
notes.TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.SeedOn.wei: Dividing the leading velocity by $\gamma=\lambda^{3/4}\lVert\mathbf a(t,0)\rVert$ gives a bound $\lambda^{-5/4}$; the corresponding frequency-weighted pressure is bounded by $4\mathsf D^3\lambda^{-5/4}$. This is the zero-order estimate behind (5.22). It uses the nearby seed comparison, the lower bound on $\lVert\kappa\rVert$, and the bound on $M$.
notes.TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.coframeLif: The map $A_\perp$ is obtained by restricting the deformation to the fixed plane $k_*^\perp$. The formalization uses that plane with its Euclidean norm directly, while §5.4 chooses orthonormal coordinates in $\mathbb R^2$. For the paper's nonzero wave vector, these describe the same transported transverse plane.

The transported frame satisfies $\partial_tA_\perp=MA_\perp$ whenever the full deformation satisfies its corresponding evolution equation. This follows by restricting the deformation to the fixed transverse plane. In §5.4 the identity turns the equation for $V=A_\perp v$ into the fixed-plane equation (5.18), including the factor two in its coefficient.
notes.TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.coframePul: The map $A_\perp^\dagger$ first projects a physical vector onto $\kappa^\perp$, then applies the inverse deformation to return it to $k_*^\perp$. With mutually inverse deformations it satisfies the two identities used in §5.4. This gives the paper's projected inverse without choosing coordinates or explicitly inverting a Gram matrix.
notes.TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.coframe_id: For mutually inverse forward and backward deformations, $A_\perp^\dagger A_\perp=\operatorname{Id}$ on the fixed plane and $A_\perp A_\perp^\dagger=\operatorname{Id}-P_\kappa$ on physical vectors. These are the two identities preceding (5.18). They justify passing between transverse velocities and coordinates in the fixed plane, including the projected forcing.
notes.TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.exists_pap: The leading oscillation and its normalized pressure satisfy (5.22), with $\mathsf D^{20}$ as the parent factor, on $[t_0,T]$. The estimate assumes the localized seed's smoothness and periodicity as well as the central growth conditions and deformation bounds. It concerns $A_1$ before the time cutoff; label and phase derivatives are taken before division by $\gamma$.
notes.TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.exists_see: Starting from the central seed, this result constructs the solutions with projected initial data (5.4) at nearby labels. Bounds on the deformation and coefficient variation, together with central stability and positive coupling, control the perturbation. Explicit smallness conditions on the envelope yield both amplitude comparison and positive coupling, which are the conclusions used in (5.19).
notes.TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.norm_cofra: The norm of $A_\perp$ is at most the norm of the full deformation, because restricting a linear map to a Euclidean subspace cannot increase its operator norm. Thus (5.1) gives $\lVert A_\perp\rVert\le\mathsf D$ in §5.4. This particular inequality does not require invertibility of the deformation.

The norm of $A_\perp^\dagger$ is bounded by that of the inverse deformation: the orthogonal projections used to define it have norm at most one. Consequently, (5.1) gives $\lVert A_\perp^\dagger\rVert\le\mathsf D$ in the proof of Lemma 5.3, without estimating the inverse Gram matrix separately.
notes.TorusEuler.LocalizedAmplitude.paper_hier: On $[t_0,T]$ and $\lVert a\rVert\le2\ell_*$, the localized seed satisfies $\lVert\mathbf a(t,a)\rVert\le2\lVert\mathbf a(t,0)\rVert$ and $\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a>0$. These are exactly the two conclusions of (5.19). This result draws them from an already constructed seed with quantitative localization bounds; it does not repeat that construction.
notes.TorusEuler.MovingAmplitude.U: This records the negative of the paper's first scaled amplitude coordinate: $-S E_1\cdot\mathbf a=-\alpha_1$. The scaling makes the first two components comparable in the growing direction of §2.2.1. The sign convention matters when reading the formal coefficient matrices: returning to $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$ changes both off-diagonal signs, without changing the underlying amplitude equation.
notes.TorusEuler.MovingAmplitude.V: This is $E_2\cdot\mathbf a=\alpha_2$ in (2.3), the amplitude along the velocity direction of the preceding wave. Unlike the first and third components, it is not multiplied by $S$. The definition needs only the amplitude and frame; transversality and the wave equation enter when these coordinates are used to reduce the dynamics.
notes.TorusEuler.MovingAmplitude.amplitude_dec: The transverse amplitude is reconstructed from its first two scaled components using $\alpha_3=-(\zeta_1\alpha_1+\zeta_2\alpha_2)/\zeta_3$. This is the reduction immediately after (2.3). The formal statement assumes an orthonormal frame and nonzero $\lambda$, $S$ and $\zeta_3$; it is an identity for a given amplitude, before any estimates for its evolution.
notes.TorusEuler.MovingAmplitude.amplitude_pai: In the preceding orthonormal frame, $k\cdot\mathbf a=0$ gives $\alpha_3=-(\zeta_1\alpha_1+\zeta_2\alpha_2)/\zeta_3$. The frequency, shear and third wave-vector component must be nonzero. This identity is used in §2.2.3 to estimate the physical amplitude and in §2.2.4 to compute the couplings; it does not use an amplitude evolution equation.
notes.TorusEuler.MovingAmplitude.errorOperator: The coefficient error is bounded by a fixed polynomial in the size of the scaled inputs, multiplied by their discrepancy from the reference inputs. This justifies the polynomial comparison in the proof of Lemma 2.4. Bounds for $1/\zeta_3$ and $1/m$ are among the assumptions; the result does not itself establish that these denominators stay away from zero.
notes.TorusEuler.MovingAmplitude.norm_errorOpe: Adding the gradient error $E_c$ changes the reduced amplitude matrix by at most $6S|E_c|/r$ in normalized time. The formal statement assumes an orthonormal frame, $S\ge1$, $|\zeta_1|,|\zeta_2|\le S$ and $\zeta_3\ge1/2$. These are the coordinate bounds used at the end of Lemma 2.4 to absorb the contribution into $C\delta$.
notes.TorusEuler.MovingAmplitude.normalized_am: This derives the exact two-dimensional amplitude equation from the moving-frame equations and the full wave amplitude equation, assuming transversality and $\zeta_3\ne0$. It is the projection step in Lemma 2.4. The formal matrix acts on $(-\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$; changing back to the paper's coordinates gives the displayed matrix $N$, including any additional gradient error.
notes.TorusEuler.MovingAmplitude.pressureU: This is the coefficient of the negative first scaled amplitude in the pressure numerator. Consequently it equals $-F_1$ after specialization to the paper's setting without $E_c$. It is used when eliminating the third component in the proof of Lemma 2.4. The formula includes the full normalized gradient and requires $\zeta_3\ne0$ for that interpretation.
notes.TorusEuler.MovingAmplitude.pressureV: This is the coefficient multiplying $\alpha_2$ in the reduced pressure numerator. With $E_c=0$, it gives $F_2$ in the proof of Lemma 2.4; the more general formula allows the full normalized gradient. Its denominators arise from eliminating the third amplitude component, so its use in the amplitude equation requires $\zeta_3\ne0$.
notes.TorusEuler.MovingAmplitude.rawMatrix: The matrix combines the full gradient driving the wave with the older gradient driving its moving frame. It acts on $(-\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$; conjugating by $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1)$ gives the paper's matrix $N$. The displayed entries in Lemma 2.4 additionally set $E_c=0$. These coordinate and gradient choices explain the apparent sign and coefficient differences.
notes.TorusEuler.MovingAmplitude.referenceMatr: This gives the reference-system matrix in coordinates $(-\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$. Its diagonal damping is the same as in (2.5), while its two off-diagonal entries have the opposite signs. Changing back to the paper's coordinates recovers exactly (2.5). Defining this matrix identifies the candidate limit; convergence from finite shear is a separate result.
notes.TorusEuler.MovingAmplitude.scaledAmplitu: This collects scaled entries of the older and full gradients, the three wave-vector coordinates, and reciprocal factors $S^{-1}$, $\zeta_3^{-1}$ and $m^{-1}$. The list is used for the polynomial estimate in Lemma 2.4. The paper's list (2.9) is reduced by setting $E_c=0$; size and error bounds for the entries are proved separately.
notes.TorusEuler.MovingAmplitude.scaledMatrix_: Substituting $\zeta_0$, the reference gradient entries, $S^{-1}=0$ and $m^{-1}=\cos^2\varphi$ gives the reference amplitude matrix. This is the algebraic calculation near the end of Lemma 2.4. The formal matrix uses $(-\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$, so its off-diagonal signs reverse on returning to (2.5); the identity itself does not assert convergence as $S\to\infty$.
notes.TorusEuler.MovingAmplitude.scaledPressur: At the reference inputs, the pressure coefficients become $F_1=-\varepsilon\tau$, $F_2=(\tan\varphi+\varepsilon)/2$ and $m=1+\tan^2\varphi$. These are the expressions used in Lemma 2.4 to identify the limiting amplitude matrix. The first coefficient in the formal calculation has the opposite sign because it multiplies $-\alpha_1$; the pressure itself is unchanged.
notes.TorusEuler.MovingAmplitude.wave_norm_sq_: This proves $|k|^2=\lambda^2m$, with $m=\zeta_1^2+\zeta_2^2/S^2+\zeta_3^2$, as stated after (2.3). It assumes an orthonormal frame and nonzero scale factors $\lambda$ and $S$. The identity is algebraic: it does not require the wave equation or the small-error assumptions used later to compare $m$ with $\cos^{-2}\varphi$.
notes.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl: The data comprise a continuous trace-free older gradient, a continuous gradient error, and a nonzero transverse preceding wave satisfying the Craik–Criminale equations. The two activation couplings are positive. This is the setting of §2.2.1 with weaker regularity than the paper assumes; the formal time set is compact, and the active normalized interval must separately be placed inside it.

The new wave begins in the growing direction of §6.2 and is scaled to a prescribed amplitude peak. Its data include the first crossing of $\eta_+/\nu_+=\varepsilon_+$ within the bracket of Proposition 2.8, together with strength, coupling and early-amplitude estimates. The crossing occurs after the time cutoff has reached one. Existence requires the comparison bounds and is proved separately.

The change of variables is $t=t_0+\tau/r$, the inverse of the normalization in §2.2.1. The rate $r$ is positive and fixed at activation. The comparison theorem requires this change of variables to carry all of $[0,T]$ into the physical time interval; differentiating along it divides every physical rate by $r$.

The normalized clock is $\tau=r(t-t_0)$, with the growth rate $r$ fixed at activation. It lets §6.2 apply the wave comparison from Section 2 on the physical interval. The formula makes sense at every time; the estimates specify separately which part of the active interval is being considered.

The comparison assumptions (2.7), a normalized interval of length at least two, and $0<\varepsilon_+\le\varepsilon/32$ produce the growing wave of §6.2. The interval must also contain the crossing bracket. The result supplies the first crossing in that bracket, its strength and coupling bounds, and the early-amplitude estimate, for any positive carrier scale and prescribed positive peak.

The same wave used for the crossing satisfies the propagation and positive-coupling estimates (5.5). Under the comparison assumptions, it suffices that $\mathsf D\ge252eS$ and $\mathsf D\ge2/(\nu\varepsilon)$. The first bound applies to every transverse amplitude solution throughout the active interval; the second gives the lower bound on the new central coupling used in §6.2.

For any ordered pair of times in the active interval, the ratio $|\mathbf b|/|\mathbf a|$ grows by at most $252eS$ for a transverse amplitude solution $\mathbf b$. The seed is the same normalized growing wave used to choose the crossing in §6.2. The comparison smallness assumptions remain necessary; this is the first estimate in (6.7) with an explicit constant.

This is $\nu=E_1(t_0)\cdot B(t_0)E_2(t_0)>0$, the first coupling frozen in §2.2.1. It sets the growth rate together with the preceding shear strength. Later values of the corresponding matrix entry may vary: their relative deviation from $\nu$ contributes to the error $\delta$ in (2.6).
