Phase integration replaces the fast derivative in the mean source by a label divergence. One parent exponent suffices independently of derivative order and depth, while the order and finite-depth constants retain their allowed dependence.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.S5b.oddExpansions_of: Reflecting label and phase, changing the sign of velocities, and preserving pressure signs gives another admissible expansion with the same data. Proposition 5.4 makes the retained profiles unique, so the reflected velocities coincide with the originals. This proves oddness of the physical perturbation used in Lemma 5.8.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.S5b.uNorm_le_wNorm: For a profile vanishing before $t_0$, its unweighted norm on $[0,T]$ is at most its weighted norm on $[t_0,T]$ when $0<\gamma\le1$. The vanishing assumption matters because the time intervals differ. The remainder proof applies this to terms containing oscillations; products of two means are estimated directly in the unweighted norm.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.S5b.words_general: Iterating $\widetilde{\mathbf d}$ costs the inverse deformation coefficients and the sum of a label derivative cost and a phase derivative cost. With the parent bounds, these become the factor $\mathsf D^C\lambda^{3/2}$ in Lemma 5.7. The statement assumes finite profile and coefficient norms, positive scales, and a positive time weight.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.S5b.words_phaseIndep: For phase-independent profiles, repeated application of $\widetilde{\mathbf d}$ reduces to label differentiation through the inverse deformation. Every phase derivative vanishes, removing the fast frequency factor. This is the estimate behind the improved mean-field clause of Lemma 5.7, with positive scales and finite weighted profile and coefficient norms explicitly assumed.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Schedule.L: The gain parameter is $L_j=4\log\lambda_{j+1}$, as prescribed in §1.5. The shift is essential when reading Lemma 1.3: $L_{j+1}$ involves $\lambda_{j+2}$. Positivity of this gain is supplied by the frequency schedule, whose frequencies exceed one, rather than by the formula considered for arbitrary frequencies.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Schedule.ε: The ratio is $\varepsilon_j=L_{j+1}^{-2}$, equivalently $\varepsilon_{j-1}=L_j^{-2}$ in §1.5. It prescribes the orientation at which the next wave is launched. The ratio is therefore linked to the following gain, not the gain at the same index. Positive gains and the later schedule estimates supply the needed positivity and smallness.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Schedule.τ: The half-length is $\tau_j=\lambda_{j-1}^{-1/8}L_{j+1}^3$ for $j\ge1$, with $L_j=4\log\lambda_{j+1}$. Section 7 uses it to set $S_j=t_j+2\tau_j$, leaving room for the next crossing and all later activation times. Positivity and decay come from the prescribed frequency schedule and are established separately.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.SmoothTerminalExtension: There is a single smooth periodic field on an open neighborhood of $\{T_*\}\times(\mathbb T^3\setminus\{0\})$ that agrees with the velocity before $T_*$. This is the conclusion of the auxiliary theorem. It requires joint space-time regularity, beyond the separate spatial limits in Proposition 8.4, and imposes no Euler equation on the extended field after the singular time.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.Text.eq_5_13: Equation (5.13) holds for every positive $A\le\mathsf D^{C_A}$ once the radius exponent is sufficiently large. It bounds the scaled positive-order Hölder derivatives of $K$ and $\Omega$ first by $C_m\mathsf D^C\ell_*^{1/2}$, then by $C_m/A$. The radius threshold may depend on $C_A$, but not on the parent or derivative order; the bound on $A$ is a premise.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.Text.eq_5_14: For a solution of (5.11), write $B=D_aXv$ and $g=(D_aX)^T\bar f$. Equation (5.14) bounds $\lVert v\rVert_{[n],1/2}$ by $C_n\mathsf D^C\lVert g\rVert_{[n],1/2}$ and asserts finiteness of the output norm when the source norm is finite. The derivative order is unchanged; the loss in Proposition 5.2 occurs during the later comparison with supremum norms.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.Text.eq_5_59: The inequality (5.59) is stated for any bounded bilinear map $B$, with the necessary factor $\|B\|$ multiplying the two input Hölder norms. For each derivative order, the constant is independent of the fields, their target spaces and the chosen product. The conclusion also asserts the product has the required Hölder regularity, covering the tensor products in §5.7.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.Text.eq_D_2: For $0<\ell_*\le1$, (D.2) controls each Hölder derivative and the summed norm using one additional bounded spatial derivative. The formal statement supplies both inequalities and establishes Hölder finiteness. Its explicit constant is four for the maximum of the uniform and Hölder parts; using their customary sum changes the norm by at most a factor two, within the paper’s unspecified absolute constant.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.Text.section8: The formal statement asserts that some parameters, approximate velocities and terminal time satisfy the conclusions of Theorem 7.1. This supplies the common interval named at the start of Section 8. It does not state existence of the continuous limit $w$ or convergence on $[0,T_\infty]$; those further claims require the separate closed-interval convergence result.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.corollary_8_3: Given the construction of Theorem 7.1 and the conclusions of Propositions 8.1 and 8.2, Corollary 8.3 asserts maximality at $T_\infty$ and divergence of both integrals in (1.2). The formal proof uses the quantitative vorticity lower bound supplied with Proposition 8.2. Its conclusion agrees with the paper, although its integral argument does not invoke the general Beale–Kato–Majda criterion.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_1_3: Lemma 1.3 asserts $q_j\le q_{j+1}\le q_j+1$, $q_j\to\infty$, and $L_{j+1}\le(\log\lambda_{j-1})^2$ for the schedule of §1.5. The formal statement assumes the recurrence, the maximum rule, positivity and the logarithmic floor. It does not require the threshold to be nondecreasing or to dominate analytic costs, so the arithmetic conclusion applies more generally.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_1: This states Lemma 2.1 with weaker profile regularity: $F$ need only be differentiable and $P'=F$, without periodicity, oddness or mean normalization. It gives the Euler equations with the displayed pressure and propagates nonzero perpendicular data throughout the connected time interval, including earlier times. The background remains trace free, with $D'+D^2$ symmetric.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_2: This states the three frame equations and $(\log\sigma)'=B_{33}$ in (2.2), together with orthonormality. It assumes nonzero perpendicular wave vectors and a trace-free background, but no smoothness or time derivative of $B$. The paper's smooth interval setting is therefore covered by a statement using only the derivatives actually needed for the calculation.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_3: This states both parts of Lemma 2.3: the constant preceding strength and exact scaled equations, followed by uniform convergence to $\zeta_0$ and (2.5). For fixed $\varepsilon$ and $T$, the shear threshold is chosen before the model configuration. It also guarantees $\zeta_3\ne0$ throughout the interval for sufficiently large shear, making the reduced coefficients well defined.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_4: This states (2.10), (2.11) and the reduced amplitude equation with one error matrix valid for every amplitude. Absolute constants are chosen before the physical data, and the coefficient and exponent in the polynomial bound are recorded separately. Beyond the printed Lemma 2.4, it explicitly includes continuity of the error matrix and $|\sigma_p/\sigma-1|\le2T\delta$, both obtained in the paper's proof.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_5: For $0<\varepsilon\le1$, Lemma 2.5 gives a unique forward solution with $|Y|\le1$, the bounded deviation in (2.13), and the amplitude identity (2.14). Its unique zero satisfies $2\le\varepsilon\tau_m\le3$; the signs on either side make $a_{\rm ref}$ maximal there. The formal statement uses one function $e$ in both formulas and explicitly includes uniqueness of the initial value problem.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_6: Lemma 2.6 keeps $\alpha_2$ positive and proves (2.17)–(2.18), so the growing wave tracks the reference amplitude. It also gives invertible transport between the transverse planes, with bound $252\exp(1)S|\mathbf a(\tau_2)|/|\mathbf a(\tau_1)|$. The constants are independent of the physical data. The formal statement allows a larger compact interval on which the errors are measured, provided it contains the amplification interval.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_7: Lemma 2.7 gives $\nu_+\ge\varepsilon\nu/2$ throughout $[0,T]$ and both relative estimates in (2.19) when $\tau\ge\sqrt2/\varepsilon$. It assumes the growing initial amplitude and the common smallness condition (2.7), with an absolute threshold for $C_0$. The cosine is that of the reference angle; it need not be the exact angle of the perturbed wave vector.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_3_1: The formal statement of Lemma 3.1 identifies the particular bump-based families $F_h$ and $P_h$ used in the construction. It includes smoothness, oddness of $F_h$, period one, the zero-mean primitive, slope normalization and all derivative bounds for $0<h\le1$. This is more specific than the paper's existential assertion, while giving exactly the properties needed afterward.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_4_1: This is Lemma 4.1 with $z\in H^1_0$ represented as the primitive of a square-integrable velocity of zero time mean. Under $H^\#\le I$, the pressure term is at most half the displacement kinetic energy, and the label energy is at least that half. This formulation covers precisely the Sobolev test paths needed for Appendix A.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_5_10: Lemma 5.10 asserts existence of the flow of $V+v$ and bounds both its forward and inverse derivatives by $C_{\rm step}\lambda^{1/4}$. The formal statement assumes each spatial derivative of $v$ through order two is bounded by $\lambda^{-5/2}$, which follows from the displayed $C^2$ bound. Constants are chosen uniformly before the parent, expansion, and perturbation.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_5_3: Lemma 5.3 combines (5.19), the forced transverse bound (5.20), the zero-initial-value velocity and pressure estimate (5.21), and the leading-wave estimate (5.22). One parent exponent works at all derivative orders. In part (i), the formal statement uses smooth fields on $[0,T]$ and measures their restriction to $[t_0,T]$; the paper allows fields given only on the active interval.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_5_5: Lemma 5.5 retains the $\lambda^{-1}$ gain and one extra derivative in both estimates, and explicitly includes the homogeneous leading wave. For general $V$ and $f$, the formal statement requires zero phase average on all of $[0,T]$; transversality, pressure normalization, and the equation are required only on $[t_0,T]$. Its parent pressure and seed normalization conditions are broader than the fixed choices in §5.1.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_5_7: Lemma 5.7 gives both weighted and unweighted physical estimates and removes the fast factor for phase-independent fields. The formal statement works for any real normed target space and explicitly concludes Hölder regularity. Its sum over ordered coordinate derivatives controls the multi-index sum of (5.44), with order-dependent multiplicities absorbed into $C_m$.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_5_8: Lemma 5.8 states smoothness, oddness, incompressibility, the exact residual equation, and all estimates (5.47)–(5.48) for every admissible expansion. The formal version keeps the full weighted cutoff derivative contribution and chooses the exponent and depth-dependent constants before the parent. Uniform pointwise bounds in time express the time suprema used in the paper.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_5_9: Lemma 5.9 bounds $D_x^2\mathsf P^\natural$ from above as a quadratic form on the full interval. Its central-gradient estimate holds on $[t_0,T]$ and subtracts exactly $\widetilde\chi\mathbf a\otimes\kappa$, leaving norm at most $\lambda^{-1/3}$. The formal statement retains these distinctions and uniform choices of constants; it does not assert an absolute bound for the full pressure Hessian.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_6_1: For $0<\rho\le1$, $\lambda\ge1$ and $T>0$ with $T|B_\rho|\le1/8$, the formal Lemma 6.1 asserts existence of a normalized first wave and the required estimates for every such wave. These are the propagation and coupling conditions (5.5) and the initial strength bounds. The result concerns the central wave; spatial localization and corrections come later.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_A_2: Lemma A.2 covers $H=\mathbb R^3$ with $\mathcal R=\mathbb P$ and $H=L^2(I;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\mathcal R=\mathbb P\mathcal Q$. Coercivity and a spatial Lipschitz bound give an invertible projected coefficient map with a polynomial Hölder estimate. The paper assumes $C^{1,1/2}$ coefficients. Higher $C^{k,1/2}$ regularity is still required for the corresponding higher regularity conclusion.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_B_1: Lemma B.1 includes derivative commutation, parity, divergence freeness, frequency support, boundedness in $L^\infty$ and $C^{0,1/2}$, and estimates (B.1)–(B.2). The formal statement permits every $\Lambda>0$ and an even symbol, extending the paper’s radial setting with $\Lambda\ge1$. Its constants are fixed before the frequency and field; the real-velocity and complex-valued formulations provide the versions needed in §5.7.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_D_1: Lemma D.1 gives (D.3)–(D.5) and the phase-independent Hölder product estimate for smooth fields with finite norms and positive scales. Products are allowed to be any continuous bilinear map, with its operator norm included in the bound. Phase averaging requires periodicity, and the periodic primitive additionally requires zero mean; the formal constants include three for label differentiation and two for the primitive.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_D_2: Lemma D.2 closes (D.6) under products and inverses, then uses a sufficiently small label radius to retain one radius factor on every differentiated coefficient. The formal statement allows bilinear products and invertible elements of complete normed algebras. Its exponents are nonnegative integers, so replacing a fixed real exponent by its ceiling can require a smaller radius than the paper’s literal part (c).
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_D_3: Lemma D.3 lifts a uniform zero-order estimate to $\|v\|_{[n],\gamma}\le C_nC_{\rm low}\|f\|_{[n],\gamma}$. The formal version works with seminorms and a finite family of derivatives, requiring the coefficient bounds only through order $n$. Preserved constraints and equations modulo gradients are represented by the admissible solution and forcing spaces. It estimates existing solutions and makes no independent existence claim.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.proposition_2: Under Proposition 2.8’s hypotheses, a crossing occurs between $\tau_m$ and $2/\sqrt{\varepsilon\varepsilon_+}$. At every crossing in that bracket the normalized strength has lower coefficient $\exp(-1)/4$ and upper coefficient $18\exp(3)$, and (2.24) controls the early amplitude. The normalization uses the attained maximum of the actual amplitude over $[0,T]$; no uniqueness of the crossing is asserted.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.proposition_5: Proposition 5.1 bounds the six coefficient families, compositions with the parent flow, and their weighted finite norms in (5.8). The exponent is chosen before the parent and derivative order; composition constants may depend on the prescribed bounds for $f$. The formal statement uses operator norms of derivatives instead of sums of coordinate derivatives, whose order-dependent comparison factors are absorbed in $C_m$.

Proposition 5.11 supplies the truncated velocity and its zero-mean Poisson pressure, preserving oddness, incompressibility and the frequency bounds $2\Lambda$ and $4\Lambda$. It retains (5.56) and the one-sided Hessian estimate (5.57). The residual and pressure errors may be evaluated at independent times, so the conclusion bounds the sum of their time suprema. All constants precede the parent; the formal parent may use any smooth periodic pressure meeting the stated bounds. The nonzero seed need only stay below the prescribed peak, rather than attain it.

Every solution of the mean endpoint problem satisfies (5.12), with one additional derivative of $\bar f$ and a parent exponent independent of $n$. The norms are unweighted over all of $[0,T]$, allowing the mean to be present before activation. No central growing seed is required for this estimate; it depends on the parent and endpoint problem.

Proposition 5.4 gives a localized seed and an expansion at every depth $P\ge2$, then proves the identities and support properties for every such expansion. The formal statement explicitly makes the retained velocities, normalized pressures, and curl corrections unique. It preserves the final correction $C_{P+1}$ and the possibility that mean fields are nonzero before activation.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.proposition_8: For every construction satisfying Theorem 7.1, Proposition 8.1 produces velocity and pressure solving Euler before $T_\infty$, with convergence in every spatial Hölder order on earlier closed intervals. It compares this limit with any maximal solution of finite lifespan having the same initial data. Existence of a maximal continuation is not asserted here; Corollary 8.3 later establishes maximality at $T_\infty$.

For the same construction and Euler solution as in Theorem 7.1 and Proposition 8.1, the formal Proposition 8.2 gives bounded velocity and central vorticity tending to infinity. It also includes a lower bound throughout every sufficiently late activation interval. This additional quantitative conclusion lets the formal proof of Corollary 8.3 establish the divergent time integrals directly.

For the Euler limit of any construction satisfying Theorem 7.1, both velocity and its time derivative converge in $C^m(K)$ for every finite $m$ and every compact $K$ avoiding the torus origin. The local limiting extension may depend on $K$ and $m$. Proposition 8.4 does not itself assert a single smooth extension through the terminal time.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.remark_1_2: The formal statement of Remark 1.2 retains every conclusion of Theorem 1.1, including uniqueness of the maximal classical velocity, and adds a smooth periodic extension through $T_*$ away from the origin. It asserts that a solution can be chosen with this property. It neither requires every singular solution to have such an extension nor imposes Euler after $T_*$.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.theorem_1_1: Theorem 1.1 asks for smooth odd divergence-free data on $\mathbb T^3$ whose maximal classical solution develops unbounded central vorticity at a positive finite time while velocity stays bounded. It also includes the two divergent time integrals and both off-origin spatial limits. The formal statement explicitly says that any other maximal classical solution from those data has the same lifetime and velocity.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.theorem_4_2: Theorem 4.2 gives a unique solution of (4.9), its Hölder estimate, the smooth correction for a smooth force, and the fixed-time inverse. The formal bound uses uniform coefficient and first derivative bounds in place of the paper's full $C^{1,1/2}$ norms. Uniqueness concerns the displacement, velocity, constant field and pressure gradient; the scalar integrated potential retains its arbitrary time-dependent constant.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.theorem_5_6: Theorem 5.6 retains every frequency power in (5.34)–(5.38), including the leading level and the remainder bound without an extra parent factor. The exponent is independent of derivative order, level, and depth. Constants for level $p$ are chosen before the depth $P$, whereas finite-sum constants may depend on $P$; each admissible expansion satisfies all orders.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.theorem_7_1: The formal Theorem 7.1 retains the common sequence, the bounds (T1)–(T4), and equations connecting each step to Section 5. It permits the envelope exponent to be chosen above any prescribed lower bound and fixes the strength constant as $18e^3$. The conclusion identifies the central amplitude and oscillatory velocity, but does not explicitly identify the central covector with that of the localized step or restate the first-wave data (6.3). Those specific construction claims therefore need separate justification.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.theorem_A_1: This is Theorem A.1 on $[0,1]$, including uniqueness, (A.3), and smoothness for smooth data. The formal hypotheses require time continuity in $C^{0,1/2}$ and uniform first spatial derivative bounds, rather than the paper's time continuity in $C^{1,1/2}$. Positive ellipticity and displacement coercivity remain essential. The pressure gradient is unique; the scalar potential is not normalized.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Text.eq_5_13: This establishes (5.13) from Proposition 5.1, Lemma D.2 and the Hölder comparison (D.2). It is used to verify the coefficient condition (D.7) for the mean inverse. The conclusion applies to every positive $A$ with a supplied polynomial bound; the separate estimate for the endpoint inverse constant is still needed before applying it.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Text.eq_5_14: This proves (5.14) using the endpoint inverse of Theorem 4.2, the parent coefficient bounds, and Lemma D.3 with (5.13). For $v=z_t$ and $g=(D_aX)^T\bar f$, input and output have the same Hölder derivative order. The finite source norm is explicit, and the conclusion includes finiteness of the velocity norm.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Text.eq_5_59: Equation (5.59) holds for every bounded bilinear operation, including the tensor products used in §5.7. The formal estimate includes its operator norm and concludes Hölder regularity of the product. The constant depends only on derivative order, so changing the product or the target spaces does not alter it.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Text.eq_D_2: The formal proof establishes all of (D.2): the exact-order interpolation estimate, the lower comparison with the supremum norm, and the upper comparison with one extra derivative. Smoothness and boundedness through order $n+1$ imply the required Hölder finiteness. The explicit constant four uses the formal maximum convention; the paper’s unspecified absolute constant absorbs the equivalent sum convention.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Text.section8_setting: This theorem supplies a construction satisfying Theorem 7.1 and a positive common terminal time. It supports the opening clause of Section 8, which selects that sequence. It does not include the following assertion of a continuous limit on the closed interval; uniform convergence through $T_\infty$ is proved separately in the formalization.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Theorem71Conclusions: The formal conclusions collect (T1)–(T4), shrinking oscillation supports, summable increments, and activation times converging to $T_\infty>0$ below every endpoint. They also retain comparison bounds used in Section 8. The equations connecting the oscillation and central amplitude to the Section 5 expansion are supplied separately with each step. Neither set of conclusions explicitly identifies the central covector with the localized wave covector or restates (6.3). The spatial estimates hold uniformly at each time; smoothness is supplied with the step data.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Theorem71StepData: At wave $j$, the formalization specifies the parent scale $\mathsf D=\lambda_{j-1}^9$, the seed and cutoff, depth $P=6K_{j+1}$, and the approximate Euler equation. It identifies $U_j$ with the truncated approximate velocity, its normalized pressure, and $O_j$ with the oscillatory part of the expansion. The central amplitude is identified as well. The corresponding identity for the central covector and the first-wave initial data (6.3) are not included in this statement.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.Theorem71Steps: For every $j\ge1$, the construction supplies the parent, seed, sources and finite expansion with the equations relating them to $U_j$ and $O_j$. The Fourier cutoff and envelope exponent are shared across all steps. This adds the Section 5 construction identities to the size estimates of Theorem 7.1; it does not add the missing central-covector identity or restate the first-wave data.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.WaveOn: This records the two differential equations in (2.1), with the pressure coefficient given there. It does not by itself assert transversality, nonvanishing or the background conditions needed for an Euler solution. Lemmas 2.1 and 2.2 supply those assumptions separately; a reader should therefore distinguish the wave equations from the complete list of hypotheses in (2.1).
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.alpha: These are the coordinates $\alpha=(S E_1\cdot\mathbf a,E_2\cdot\mathbf a,S E_3\cdot\mathbf a)$ at physical time $t_0+\tau/r$, as in (2.3). The amplitude equation and transversality are separate hypotheses. Some intermediate calculations use $(-\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$, so their matrices require a change of sign in the first coordinate before comparison with the paper.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.corollary_8_3: Corollary 8.3 proves that the accumulation time is the finite maximal lifespan of the Euler limit and that both integrals in (1.2) diverge. The formal proof integrates the quantitative vorticity bounds retained in Proposition 8.2. The paper instead invokes the periodic Beale–Kato–Majda criterion; the stated conclusion is unchanged, but this theorem does not establish that general criterion.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_1_3: The formal proof establishes the three conclusions of Lemma 1.3 for the frequency and order schedule in §1.5. Orders increase by at most one, eventually reach every fixed order, and satisfy the displayed logarithmic gain bound. The proof requires the positive logarithmic floor but not the threshold's monotonicity or its separate role in bounding analytic costs.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_1: This proves Lemma 2.1, including the pressure formula, zero divergence and persistence of nonzero perpendicular wave data. The formal theorem works with differentiable profiles and arbitrary primitives, so the paper's smooth odd periodic choice is a special case. Persistence is proved throughout the connected time interval, rather than only after the selected initial time.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_2: This proves Lemma 2.2: the normalized wave vector, normalized amplitude and their cross product form an orthonormal frame satisfying (2.2). The logarithmic strength evolves by $B_{33}$. Only the two wave equations, nonzero transverse data and zero trace are required; the smooth background assumed in the paper is more regular than this calculation needs.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_3: Lemma 2.3 gives the normalized wave-vector and amplitude equations in the two-coupling model, then their uniform strong-shear limit on each fixed normalized interval. It also ensures that the third normalized wave-vector component stays nonzero for sufficiently strong shear. This supplies the reference model used in §1.1. The formal statement permits the physical interval to lie inside a larger compact observation interval.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_4: Lemma 2.4 controls the wave-vector coordinates, its squared norm and the common error in the amplitude equations under (2.7). This formal result also records continuity of that error and a bound on the variation of the preceding strength. These additional conclusions support the comparison argument in §2.2.3 and the coupling estimates in §2.2.4.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_5: This proves Lemma 2.5, including global forward existence, uniqueness, the bounded deviation, the amplitude formula and the unique turning time. The gain bound is $\log a_{\rm ref}(\tau_m)\ge\varepsilon^{-1/2}-1$. The result supplies the fixed reference trajectory for the subsequent amplitude and crossing arguments; its maximum concerns the reference amplitude, not the perturbed wave.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_6: This establishes Lemma 2.6 from Lemmas 2.4 and 2.5. The actual amplitude remains within factors $\exp(\pm\varepsilon)$ of $a_{\rm ref}$, and transverse amplitude transport is invertible with an explicit absolute constant in its bound. These conclusions justify both the size comparison and the control of arbitrary transverse amplitudes used later in the construction.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_7: This proves Lemma 2.7 from the wave-vector, reference and amplitude comparisons. The first coupling stays positive throughout the interval, while the successor ratio follows $\cos\varphi$ at late times. Here $\varphi$ is the reference angle of (2.5). The result supplies the positive denominator and late bounds needed to find a crossing in Proposition 2.8.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_3_1: This proves Lemma 3.1 for the explicit family built from a compactly supported bump. Its slope equals one at the origin, its negative slope and amplitude are bounded by a multiple of $h$, and higher derivatives obey the stated scaling. The accompanying primitive is smooth, periodic and has zero phase mean, as required for the leading pressure.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_4_1: Lemma 4.1 is established for every label and every displacement in $H^1_0$. The condition $H^\#\le I$ bounds its Hessian term by half the kinetic energy, and the identity (4.7) gives the complementary lower bound for the label form. These are the coercivity estimates used when Theorem 4.2 invokes Appendix A.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_5_10: The formal theorem proves Lemma 5.10 from the parent coefficient bounds, hierarchy estimates, and existence of the expansion. Every permitted small divergence-free perturbation gives a flow with forward and inverse derivative bounds $C_{\rm step}\lambda^{1/4}$. The assumptions bound each spatial derivative through order two, as implied by the $C^2$ condition in the paper.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_5_3: This proves the four conclusions of Lemma 5.3 from the profile, coefficient and finite-norm estimates. They retain the single parent exponent and the frequency-weighted pressure bound. The formal statement in part (i) quantifies over fields smooth on all of $[0,T]$, so its active-interval estimate does not by itself cover arbitrary fields defined only on $[t_0,T]$.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_5_5: The formal theorem proves both estimates of Lemma 5.5 and the source-free leading-wave case from Proposition 5.1 and Lemma D.1. The gain $\lambda^{-1}$ and single extra derivative are unchanged. For general velocity and forcing profiles, zero phase averages are required on the full interval, while transversality and the equation concern the active interval.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_5_7: The formal theorem proves Lemma 5.7 using Proposition 5.1 and Lemma D.1. Both weighted and unweighted bounds are present, and phase-independent fields incur no $\lambda^{3/2}$ derivative cost. The result includes Hölder regularity and allows arbitrary normed target spaces; the coordinate derivative counting differs only by order-dependent constants.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_5_8: The formal theorem proves Lemma 5.8 for every admissible expansion. It retains smoothness, oddness, zero divergence, the exact residual equation, and all velocity and residual estimates. The residual includes the actual weighted cutoff derivative on $[t_0,T]$, while the conclusions hold on $[0,T]$. Exponents and constant families are chosen uniformly before the parent and expansion.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_5_9: The formal theorem proves the upper pressure Hessian bound (5.49) and the central gradient estimate (5.50). The pressure bound is one-sided; the central error is bounded in operator norm by $\lambda^{-1/3}$. These concern the finite approximation before Fourier truncation, whose additional pressure and residual errors are handled in Proposition 5.11.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_6_1: Under the short-interval assumption $T|B_\rho|\le1/8$, with $0<\rho\le1$ and $\lambda\ge1$, Lemma 6.1 supplies a normalized first wave and proves (5.5) and the initial strength bounds for every such wave. Its frame starts in the coordinate directions, and the formal proof uses Lemma 2.2 to control the coupling throughout the interval.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_A_2: This establishes Lemma A.2 for both spatial vector fields and whole time paths. The inverse has a polynomial $C^{0,1/2}$ bound and preserves every $C^{k,1/2}$ class allowed by the coefficient. For the base estimate, the formal statement allows Lipschitz coefficients; the paper's stronger $C^{1,1/2}$ hypothesis therefore lies within its scope.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_B_1: Lemma B.1 gives derivative commutation, parity and divergence preservation, frequency support, the uniform Hölder bounds, Bernstein’s inequality and the high-frequency tail estimate. These are the cutoff tools used in §5.7. The formal statement admits any positive cutoff scale and a smooth even symbol, extending the paper’s range $\Lambda\ge1$ and its radial-symbol assumption.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_D_1: The formal proof supplies the full set of estimates in Lemma D.1, including the phase-independent Hölder product rule. Positive scales and amplitude weights are explicit, and every output has the required finite norm. The formulation extends ordinary products to continuous bilinear maps and gives the same averaging and zero-mean primitive estimates used in the mean and oscillatory corrections.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_D_2: The formal proof establishes all three parts of Lemma D.2 for nonnegative integer exponents: products, inverses and the weighted coefficient estimate. Invertibility is an explicit hypothesis. The constants remain uniform over the parent parameter and coefficient fields. A real exponent can be rounded upward for applications, but doing so may strengthen the radius condition and alter the powers in the literal conclusion of part (c).
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_D_3: The formal proof gives Lemma D.3 as a general estimate for linear equations with coefficient-dependent terms and seminorms. It needs the zero-order bound for every admissible solution and coefficient bounds through the requested order. Differentiating introduces lower-order solution terms, so the final estimate retains just one factor $C_{\rm low}$, as required by the Section 5 inverse bounds.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.meanDeformation: This is $D_aX(t,a)$, the deformation of the parent flow introduced in §3.1. It converts changes in the initial particle label into changes in current position. The formula alone does not assert invertibility; that property follows from the smooth parent flow and its inverse, and is used in defining the pulled-back spatial derivatives.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.meanDeformationInv: This differentiates the reverse parent flow at the particle's current position. For the smooth flow on the active interval, it equals $(D_aX(t,a))^{-1}$ and supplies the inverse deformation used in §3.1. The inverse identity is a consequence of the flow composition laws; it is not a property of an arbitrary pair of spatial maps.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.meanGradient: This is $M=(D_xU)\circ X$ in §3.1: the Eulerian velocity gradient evaluated along the parent trajectory. It drives the transported wave vector and seed amplitude when time derivatives hold the label fixed. Defining this coefficient uses the smooth parent and its flow, without requiring the parent itself to satisfy the Euler equations exactly.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.meanGradientRate: This is $M_t$ with the label $a$ held fixed, where $M=(\nabla u)\circ X$. It enters $H^\#=-(M_t+M^2)$ in (4.1). Derivatives at the endpoints are taken from within $[0,T]$. The smooth parent assumptions used in §4 provide the differentiability needed to interpret it.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.meanHsharp: The coefficient is $H^\#=-(M_t+M^2)$ along the parent flow, as in (4.1). For a general parent it need not be symmetric; Theorem 4.2 requires only an upper bound as a quadratic form. The identification with the pressure Hessian holds for an Euler solution, while (4.3) includes the residual correction for an approximate solution.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.meanKinetic: The kinetic coefficient is $K=(D_aX)^TD_aX$, the metric induced in particle labels. It appears in the endpoint equation (4.9) and its energy form. The formula alone gives nonnegativity; the bound on the inverse deformation gives the quantitative ellipticity $K\ge D_-^{-2}I$ used in Theorem 4.2.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.meanVorticity: The coefficient $\Omega=(D_aX)^T(M^T-M)D_aX$ is the vorticity form pulled back to labels in (4.1). No Euler equation is needed to define it. Together with the variational flow equation it gives $K_t-\Omega=2(D_aX)^T\partial_tD_aX$, which turns the integrated endpoint equation into the linearized momentum equation.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.modelEntries: The model matrix has entries $B_{12}=\nu$ and $B_{32}=\eta$, with every other entry zero, as assumed in Lemma 2.3. These are components in the preceding wave's moving frame. Requiring an actual older gradient to have these entries throughout the normalized interval is a separate model hypothesis.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_2_8: This proves Proposition 2.8 using Lemmas 2.4 through 2.7. It gives a crossing in the prescribed bracket, controls the strength at every crossing in that bracket, and proves the early-gain estimate (2.24). The maximum is taken over the actual amplitude on $[0,T]$. The conclusion guarantees existence of a crossing, without selecting a unique one.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_5_1: This proves Proposition 5.1 from Lemmas B.1 and D.2, retaining all six coefficient families and both composition bounds. The constants are uniform in the parent, with dependence on derivative order confined to $C_m$. The formal parent assumptions permit a broader pressure choice than the zero-mean Poisson pressure fixed in §5.1; that choice remains covered.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_5_11: Proposition 5.11 proves the cutoff and pressure estimates needed for the next parent, including the one-sided Hessian bound (5.57). It constructs the zero-mean Poisson pressure and gives the estimates for every truncation with that normalization. The residual contribution is retained in the pressure error, and independent time variables recover the sum of the two time suprema in (5.56). The parent pressure and seed normalization have the broader admissible ranges used throughout Section 5.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_5_2: This proves Proposition 5.2 from the parent bounds, the product inequality, (D.2), and (5.14). The result applies to every mean solution with zero displacement at both endpoints and gives precisely one additional source derivative. It is an estimate for existing solutions; existence for the mean problem is supplied through Theorem 4.2 and the expansion construction.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_5_4: The formal theorem proves Proposition 5.4 using Theorem 4.2. It supplies the localized seed, the retained profiles and normalized pressures, their uniqueness, and the residual and divergence identities. The oscillatory support and inactive-time conclusions are in label coordinates; a support statement in physical space additionally transports the envelope by the parent flow.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_8_1: Proposition 8.1 constructs a smooth odd Euler limit from every sequence satisfying Theorem 7.1, with convergence in all the stated Hölder norms before $T_\infty$. The formal result compares it with every maximal solution of finite lifespan from the limiting data. It leaves the existence and maximality of the terminal solution to Corollary 8.3.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_8_2: For the Euler limit supplied by Proposition 8.1, Proposition 8.2 proves bounded velocity and $|\operatorname{curl}u(t,0)|\to\infty$. The formal conclusion also retains a lower bound on every sufficiently late activation interval after passing from $U_j$ to $u$. This stronger quantitative statement is used to obtain the divergent integrals without invoking a formal general continuation criterion.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_8_4: Proposition 8.4 proves convergence of $u(t)$ and $\partial_tu(t)$ in $C^m(K)$ for every compact $K$ away from the origin and every finite $m$. The result applies to the Euler limit of the common construction. It is distinct from the joint smooth terminal extension in the auxiliary note, which controls all mixed time and space derivatives.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.referenceAmplitude: The reference amplitude is $a_{\rm ref}(\tau)=\exp(\int_0^\tau Y)$. For the reference solution of (2.12), continuity of $Y$ makes this integral well defined and gives $a_{\rm ref}^{\prime}=Ya_{\rm ref}$. Its positivity permits the normalization in (2.15), and Lemma 2.5 estimates its maximum and the gain inherited by the actual wave.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.referenceAngle: The reference angle is $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$, fixing the branch used in (2.4). For $\varepsilon\ge0$, it lies between zero and $\pi/2$. It describes the limiting wave vector as the preceding shear grows; it need not equal the exact turning angle of a perturbed finite-shear wave.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.referenceAngle_mem: For $\varepsilon\ge0$, the reference angle satisfies $0\le\varphi<\pi/2$ at every finite real time. This is the range specified in (2.4). In particular its cosine stays positive, allowing the trigonometric expressions in the reference system to be used without encountering a pole as the angle approaches a right angle.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.referenceSystemMatrix: This is the matrix in (2.5), acting directly on $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$ with second row $(-1,0)$. Its first row contains the turning-dependent damping and driving coefficients. It defines the reference system used in the amplification comparison; the assertion that finite-shear model coefficients converge to it is proved in Lemma 2.3.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.remark_1_2: The formal proof chooses a singular solution satisfying Theorem 1.1 and obtains a smooth extension through $T_*$ away from the origin. It uses the particular construction supplied by the auxiliary result. This proves the existential assertion of Remark 1.2, without claiming the broader auxiliary theorem for every admissible construction or an Euler continuation beyond $T_*$.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.scaledNormSq: This is $m=\zeta_1^2+\zeta_2^2/S^2+\zeta_3^2$, the factor in $|k|^2=\lambda^2m$ after (2.3). It is a weighted squared norm, not the ordinary squared norm of $\zeta$ unless $S=1$. In the amplitude formulas, positive $S$ and nonzero $\zeta_3$ ensure that $m$ is positive.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.strongShearMatrix: The four entries give the coefficient matrix for $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$ in Lemma 2.3 after expanding $\Pi$ and eliminating $\alpha_3$ by transversality. The formula contains denominators $S^2$, $\zeta_3$ and $m$. Its interpretation as the amplitude equation therefore uses the model hypotheses and nonzero third coordinate; the matrix definition alone supplies no solution.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.strongShearMatrix_mulVe: This expands the finite-shear matrix applied to $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$ into the two right-hand sides displayed in Lemma 2.3, including $\Pi$. It connects the coefficient matrix used in the convergence statement with the written differential equations. The identity is algebraic; the model assumptions and nonzero $\zeta_3$ justify applying it to a physical wave.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.strongShearPressure: This is $\Pi=(2\zeta_2\alpha_1+(\zeta_1+\varepsilon\zeta_3)\alpha_2)/m$ in Lemma 2.3. After the time and coordinate rescalings, it equals $\lambda S p_{\rm w}/r$. The formula is linear in the two remaining amplitude components; positive $m$, ensured by the nonzero third coordinate in the lemma, makes the pressure reduction valid.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.tan_referenceAngle: This proves $\tan\varphi=\varepsilon\tau^2/2$ for the chosen arctangent branch, the identity in (2.4). It permits the strong-shear calculations to move between trigonometric notation and explicit functions of normalized time. The identity holds for all real parameters; the range $0\le\varphi<\pi/2$ additionally uses $\varepsilon\ge0$.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_1_1: The formal proof of Theorem 1.1 combines the four terminal results in §8. It obtains the positive finite maximal time, bounded velocity, divergent central vorticity, divergent gradient and vorticity integrals, and spatial limits of velocity and its time derivative away from the origin. It also states uniqueness of the maximal classical velocity and its lifetime for the chosen smooth odd initial data.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_4_2: This establishes Theorem 4.2: the endpoint inverse, its Hölder estimate, smooth recovery of the physical correction, and the fixed-time inverse. Its proof uses Lemma 4.1 and the two results in Appendix A. The formal estimate depends only on coefficient and first derivative bounds, giving the paper's bound after enlarging the common polynomial constant.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_5_6: The formal theorem proves Theorem 5.6 at all derivative orders and retained levels under $\mathsf D^C\lambda^{-1/12}\le1$. The same exponent $C$ is independent of order, level, and depth. The level constants depend only on order and level, and the remainder retains the decay $\lambda^{-5/4}\lambda^{-2P/3}$ without an additional parent factor.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_7_1: Theorem 7.1 provides the common approximate sequence, the quantitative bounds, and each step’s relation to the Section 5 expansion and cutoff. The formalization fixes the strength constant at $18e^3$ and permits an arbitrarily large choice of envelope exponent. Its conclusion does not explicitly identify the central covector with the localized one or restate the first-wave data (6.3); the retained amplitude and oscillation identities do not supply those equalities by themselves.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_A_1: This establishes Theorem A.1 from Lemma A.2, including the polynomial velocity estimate and smoothness for smooth data. The formal coefficient assumptions need time continuity in $C^{0,1/2}$ and uniform first spatial derivative bounds. The stronger continuity in $C^{1,1/2}$ assumed in the paper is sufficient, but is not needed for this formal conclusion.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.zeta: These are the three components $\zeta$ in (2.3), evaluated at $t=t_0+\tau/r$. Projection onto $E_2$ is multiplied by $S$, and all components are divided by the initial frequency $\lambda$. In the amplification theorems $\lambda>0$ and the evaluation lies within the parent time interval; these conditions make the coordinate interpretation valid.
notes.TorusEuler.Paper.zetaRef: This defines $\zeta_0=(\tan\varphi,-\varepsilon\tau,1)$ in (2.4), the trajectory of the limiting triangular system. Its third coordinate is exactly one. Uniform closeness to this vector therefore keeps the third coordinate of an actual wave away from zero, which is needed to reduce the amplitude equation to two components.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.WaveOn: The wave vector and amplitude satisfy $k'=-D^Tk$ and $\mathbf a'=-D\mathbf a+p_{\rm w}k$, the equations introduced in §1.1. Derivatives at interval endpoints are taken from within the interval. Nonvanishing of the wave vector and perpendicularity of the two vectors are separate assumptions when these equations are used to construct an exact wave.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.additiveCompariso: This establishes a polynomial wave-vector comparison and one continuous error matrix valid for every transverse amplitude under (2.7). It is part of the content used for Lemma 2.4. The intermediate system uses $(-\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$, so its error matrix must be conjugated to recover the paper's coordinates; the relative squared-norm estimate is supplied separately.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.exactWave: The affine wave solves Euler with the pressure in Lemma 2.1, and nonzero perpendicular initial wave data remain so throughout the connected time interval. The formal statement needs only a differentiable profile and a primitive, without oddness or periodicity. Its persistence conclusion also includes times before the selected initial time, provided they lie in that interval.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.finiteComparison: Under the common smallness condition and growing initial data, this result combines the logarithmic amplitude comparison, the positive first coupling, the late coupling estimates and invertible transverse transport. These are the conclusions used from Lemmas 2.6 and 2.7. The reference solution is supplied as an input, and the propagator coefficient is explicitly $252\exp(1)S$.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.finiteReturn: This version of Proposition 2.8 places a crossing strictly between $\tau_m$ and $2/\sqrt{\varepsilon\varepsilon_+}$. It controls the strength at every crossing in the closed bracket with the common constant $18\exp(3)$ and proves the early-gain estimate. The amplitude maximum is taken over the whole prescribed interval. Neither the result nor the paper requires the crossing to be unique.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.movingFrameDeriva: For nonzero perpendicular wave data evolving over a trace-free background, the normalized axes form an orthonormal frame and satisfy Lemma 2.2's evolution equations. The strength also obeys $(\log\sigma)'=B_{33}$. The two-coupling example in §1.1 is a specialization: the general formula allows the additional entry $B_{13}$ and does not require the background itself to solve the affine Euler equations.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.referenceModel: For $0<\varepsilon\le1$, this result constructs a global forward Riccati solution, a deviation in $[0,\varepsilon/8]$, and a unique zero in the stated turning range. It includes the signs on both sides and the gain integral used in Lemma 2.5. This version constructs one solution; the full numbered lemma additionally states uniqueness among all reference solutions.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperFirstWaveConclusion: The first wave must control every transverse amplitude relative to $\gamma$, have coupling at least $\mathsf D^{-1}$ for every $\mathsf D\ge2$, and start with strength between $\lambda^{1/4}/2$ and $\lambda^{1/4}$. These are the conclusions of Lemma 6.1. Their proof uses the prescribed initial directions, peak normalization and the short-interval condition.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperLimitAgreement: The initial data converge in every $C^{m,1/2}$ norm, and the velocities converge in those norms uniformly on each compact interval before $T_*$. The velocity also has a continuous uniform limit on the closed terminal slab. This refines the introduction's convergence statement. Agreement with any other maximal classical solution from the same data is included as a separate conclusion.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperMeanIntegratedSolution: A continuous divergence-free velocity $v$ and a time-independent divergence-free field $c$ satisfy the Leray projection of (4.9), with $\int_0^T v\,dt=0$. Its primitive therefore vanishes at both endpoints. This is an intermediate formulation of the endpoint problem; existence comes from the inverse theorem, and the pressure gradient is recovered afterward.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperMeanIntegratedSolution.c: When $K(0)=I$ and $L(0)=0$, evaluating the projected endpoint equation at time zero gives $c=v(0)$. These are exactly the conditions for the force source in §4.3. Since the particle flow starts at the identity, the subsequent physical interpretation is $c=b(0)$, the initial correction selected by the endpoint conditions.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperMeanIntegratedSolution.e: A displacement satisfying $z_t=v$, both zero endpoint conditions and the integrated equation with a periodic pressure potential yields the projected endpoint solution with the same $v$ and $c$. This connects the original system (4.9) to the inverse used in Appendix A. Its primitive is the original displacement, so uniqueness in the projected problem applies without changing the endpoint data.

For time-continuous coefficients and source, the projected endpoint solution admits a periodic scalar potential completing (4.9). The formal result chooses this potential with zero spatial mean and proves continuity of its gradient in $C^{0,1/2}$. Appendix A needs that gradient; this assertion does not separately prescribe time differentiability of the scalar potential.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperMeanIntegratedSolution.p: If two integrated endpoint equations have the same velocity and the same time-independent field, subtracting them identifies their pressure gradients throughout the interval. This supplies the final part of uniqueness in Theorems 4.2 and A.1. Velocity uniqueness is an input here; the scalar potentials themselves may differ by a function of time.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperMeanParent: These are the geometric quantities used by the endpoint inverse: the deformation, its inverse, the parent gradient and its fixed-label time derivative. They obey the variational equation, the inverse-deformation and gradient bounds, and $H^\#\le I$. In §4 the quantities come from the actual parent flow; this formulation isolates the identities and bounds needed by the argument.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperMeanParent.exists_integr: A smooth periodic force expressed along particle trajectories gives the source $L=-\int_0^t(D_aX)^T(f\circ X)\,ds$ of Theorem 4.2. The formal result represents it as a smooth time-dependent $C^{0,1/2}$ field and identifies its value with that integral. This permits comparison of the smooth momentum equation with the integrated endpoint problem.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperPhysicalStepBudget.hiera: The inequality $C_{\rm step}\lambda^{-1/12}\le1$ implies the smallness condition used in Theorem 5.6 because the chosen step constant dominates its parent loss. This is the sentence following (5.43). The implication uses the previously fixed exponent and coefficient, without choosing a new frequency after the other estimates.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution: The mean problem uses label velocity $v$, label displacement $z$, physical mean $B=Fv$, and pressure, with $z_t=v$ and $z(0)=z(T)=0$. The momentum equation includes the transported pressure gradient. This is the endpoint selection introduced in §1.2 and developed in §4. The label displacement is $z$; the physical trajectory displacement is $\xi=Fz$.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution.euler: The change of variables $b=B\circ X^{-1}$ and $q=\mathsf q\circ X^{-1}$ turns the smooth label solution into smooth periodic fields satisfying (4.12). Incompressibility of the parent supplies the divergence identity, so $b$ is divergence free. The geometric coefficients must agree with the derivatives of the actual particle flow; arbitrary matrix fields are not enough for this conclusion.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution.exist: A smooth solution of the forced label equation also solves the projected integrated problem, with exactly the same label velocity. The source is the prescribed negative force primitive, and the zero displacement endpoints give zero time mean. This lets the uniqueness statement in Appendix A identify the smooth correction with the previously constructed Hölder solution.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution.mean_: On an interval $0<T\le1$, two smooth mean solutions with the same admissible parent, the same smooth periodic forcing and zero displacement at both endpoints have the same mean velocity. This is the uniqueness needed by the endpoint selection in §1.2. The result compares already existing solutions; the endpoint inverse separately establishes existence.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution.stron: A smooth endpoint correction obeys $Kv_t+\nabla_a\mathsf q=g-\mathcal Dv$, the equation (4.11). Here $g=(D_aX)^T(f\circ X)$ and $\mathcal D=2(D_aX)^T\partial_tD_aX$. The formal formula writes the latter using $\partial_tD_aX=MD_aX$. Time derivatives are interpreted from within the interval at its endpoints.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperTerminalOffOrigin: The terminal property in Proposition 8.4 requires limits for the velocity and its time derivative on every compact subset away from the origin, in every finite spatial order. It describes convergence as the terminal time is approached from below. It does not require a smooth time extension through that time; the auxiliary note addresses that stronger conclusion.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperTerminalTime: The terminal-time conclusion consists of a maximal Euler solution and divergence of the vorticity and velocity-gradient integrals over $[0,T_*)$. This records the properties asserted in Corollary 8.3. The common Section 8 result identifies the same time with the limit of activation times; the definition of these terminal properties does not itself prove continuation or blow-up.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperTerminalVelocityCurl: This is the pair of terminal properties in Proposition 8.2: one finite bound for the velocity throughout the lifespan, and the full limit $|\operatorname{curl}u(t,0)|\to\infty$ as $t\uparrow T_*$. The second condition holds at all sufficiently late times above each prescribed threshold, rather than merely along a sequence of times.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperTheorem71Conclusions: The conclusions of Theorem 7.1 collect the stage regularity, frequency support, residual and pressure bounds, central-gradient decomposition, crossing conditions and finite accumulation time. They also give the supported oscillations and small smooth corrections used in the introduction's convergence argument. These are requirements on one common sequence; the corresponding existence theorem constructs that sequence.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperWaveCutoff: The activation function is smooth on $[0,T]$, takes values in $[0,1]$, and vanishes before the launch time. This is the activation used in the finite correction scheme of §1.3. These requirements alone do not say that it eventually equals one. They also allow the constant-one cutoff for the first wave, which starts at time zero.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperWaveCutoff.derivativeSiz: This is $\|\widetilde\chi^{\prime}\gamma\|_\infty$ over $[t_0,T]$, the quantity appearing in (5.48). It retains both the rate of switching and the size of the leading wave during activation. For the continuous nonnegative weight used in the paper, the supremum is finite and controls each pointwise activation contribution.
notes.TorusEuler.PaperWaveCutoff.first: The first wave uses the constant activation function one on $[0,T]$. Since its launch time is zero, there are no earlier times in the construction interval at which it must vanish. This is the initial-wave case of the activation discussed in §1.3, and it contributes no time-switching derivative to the source.
notes.TorusEuler.ParentLabelJetBound: This records bounds of the form $\lVert D_a^m f\rVert\le C_m\mathsf D^{pm+c}$ throughout the time interval. The same slope $p$ and offset $c$ apply at every order. Proposition 5.1 uses such bounds before inserting the radius weights. Operator norms of derivatives replace coordinate sums, with the order-dependent comparison absorbed in $C_m$.
notes.TorusEuler.ParentLabelJetBound.weighted_: If $\lVert D_a^j f\rVert\le C_j\mathsf D^{pj+c}$ and $\ell_*\mathsf D^p\le1$, the weighted derivative sum is at most $(\sum_{j\le n}C_j)\mathsf D^c$. Thus the remaining exponent is independent of $n$. This is the final summation step behind (5.8); the polynomial derivative bound is an input to it.
notes.TorusEuler.RealTorusFourierBand: A continuous field on $\mathbb T^3$ is supported on frequencies at most the stated radius when every Fourier coefficient outside that ball vanishes. Frequencies on the boundary are retained. This is precisely the convention introduced in §5.1, used for the parent velocity in the $2\mathsf D$ ball and the residual in the $4\mathsf D$ ball.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.integrated: For $0\le\varepsilon\le1$, $T\ge2$ and a continuous rate with $|Y|\le1$, a constant coefficient-error bound $\eta\ge0$ gives an integrated normalized error at most $4T^3\eta$. This is the polynomial control required in §2.2.3. It uses $(\cos\varphi)^{-1}\le T^2$ and integration over an interval of length at most $T$.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.log_growin: If the normalized state is within $d\le1/2$ of $(1,0)$ and the stated wave-vector geometry holds, then $|\log(|\mathbf a|/a_{\rm ref})|\le2d+20T^4S^{-2}$. The two terms account for the error in $h$ and the transverse contribution to the physical norm. Lemma 2.6 bounds their sum by $\varepsilon$ to obtain (2.18).
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.normCorrec: The coordinate bounds used in Lemma 2.6 imply $(\alpha_1/\alpha_2)^2+(\alpha_3/\alpha_2)^2\le40T^4$. This requires $T\ge1$, $|\alpha_1/\alpha_2|\le2$, and the stated bounds on $\zeta$, including $\zeta_3\ge1/2$. Multiplication by $S^{-2}$ measures how little the two smaller physical components contribute to $|\mathbf a|/\alpha_2$.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.orthonorma: In an orthonormal frame, the scaled components give $|\mathbf a|=\alpha_2\sqrt{1+S^{-2}((\alpha_1/\alpha_2)^2+(\alpha_3/\alpha_2)^2)}$. The formal statement assumes $\alpha_2>0$, $S>0$ and a nonzero third wave-vector component. This algebraic identity underlies the norm comparison in (2.17); it does not require the amplitude evolution equation.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.raw_ratio_: If $(h,l)$ is within maximum-norm distance $d\le1/2$ of $(1,0)$, then $\alpha_2>0$ and $|\alpha_1/\alpha_2+Y|\le2d$. This step in Lemma 2.6 is purely algebraic: the positive reference amplitude and $h\ge1/2$ justify division. The evolution estimates are used earlier to establish the required closeness.

For $\alpha_2\ne0$, the coordinate identity is $\alpha_1/\alpha_2+Y=-l\cos\varphi/h$. Thus small $l$ and a lower bound for $h$ control the relative amplitude direction in (2.17). The identity needs no differential equation; the positive reference amplitude and cosine ensure that the normalization is legitimate.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceAmplitude.reference_: A positive amplitude $A$ satisfying $|\log(A/a_{\rm ref})|\le\varepsilon$ lies between $\exp(-\varepsilon)a_{\rm ref}$ and $\exp(\varepsilon)a_{\rm ref}$. This converts (2.18) into the two comparisons used in Proposition 2.8. It is a pointwise consequence of the logarithmic bound and positivity, without any further evolution assumption.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceComparison.hasDerivW: The perturbed amplitude equation becomes the triangular system (2.16) plus the matrix $R\mathcal E R^{-1}$ after the normalization (2.15). This identity uses the reference Riccati equation and both amplitude equations. In Lemma 2.6 it isolates the perturbation that must be integrated, separating it from the large reference growth already removed by $a_{\rm ref}$.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceComparison.norm_movi: Under the stated wave geometry, the maximum norm of $(h,l)$ and the physical amplitude satisfy $|\mathbf b|\le9a_{\rm ref}\max(|h|,|l|)$ and $\max(|h|,|l|)\le7S|\mathbf b|/a_{\rm ref}$. These bounds explain the factor $S$ in Lemma 2.6’s physical propagator. They assume transversality and the coordinate bounds, rather than proving the amplitude evolution.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceComparison.norm_norm: The transformed error matrix has norm at most $(1+|Y|)^2\|\mathcal E\|/\cos\varphi$, using the maximum norm on the pair of amplitude coordinates. With $|Y|\le1$ and $(\cos\varphi)^{-1}\le T^2$, this gives the polynomial loss used in §2.2.3. The bound is algebraic and does not assume an amplitude equation.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceComparison.normalize: This pair is $(h,l)$ from (2.15): $h=\alpha_2/a_{\rm ref}$ and $l=-(\alpha_1+Y\alpha_2)/(a_{\rm ref}\cos\varphi)$. The growing reference solution becomes $(1,0)$, making its perturbation easy to measure in Lemma 2.6. The formal estimates on this pair use the maximum norm; the physical amplitude retains its Euclidean norm.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceComparison.unscaledC: The map performs the coordinate change of §2.2.3 before division by $a_{\rm ref}$. It takes $(-\beta_1,\beta_2)$ as its input, whereas the paper’s matrix $R$ takes $(\beta_1,\beta_2)$. This reverses the lower-left matrix entry. Accounting for that first-coordinate sign gives exactly the same normalized coordinates $(h,l)$.

The inverse change of §2.2.3 returns $(Yh+l\cos\varphi,h)$ before multiplication by $a_{\rm ref}$. Its first output represents $-\beta_1$, so negating it recovers the paper’s inverse matrix. The difference is a coordinate convention, not a different amplitude equation; the positive reference cosine makes the change invertible.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferencePropagator.decay: The decay factor between two times is the exponential of minus twice the integral of $(1+e)\cos\varphi$. It multiplies $l$ in the explicit solution of (2.16). The expression allows arbitrary coefficient functions; its use as a forward decay factor requires ordered times, continuous coefficients, and the nonnegativity assumptions proved for the reference solution.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferencePropagator.hasDerivW: Differentiating (2.15) gives $h^{\prime}=l\cos\varphi$ and $l^{\prime}=-2(1+e)l\cos\varphi$, exactly (2.16). The formal result assumes the Riccati equation and the two reference amplitude equations on the prescribed interval. Derivatives at its endpoints are understood from within the interval. This triangular form supplies the uniform propagator bound used in Lemma 2.6.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferencePropagator.normalize: The coordinate $h=\alpha_2/a_{\rm ref}$ measures the second amplitude component relative to the reference growth. It equals one on the growing reference solution and appears in (2.15). The reference amplitude is positive. To deduce the evolution of $h$ or its proximity to one, the later comparison argument uses the amplitude and Riccati equations.

The coordinate $l=-(\alpha_1+Y\alpha_2)/(a_{\rm ref}\cos\varphi)$ vanishes on the growing reference solution. The extra factor $1/\cos\varphi$ gives both equations in (2.16) the same angular factor, which yields a uniform propagator bound. Both denominator factors are positive; bounds for $l$ itself are established by the subsequent evolution argument.

For any ordered times in $[0,T]$, the Euclidean norm of $(h,l)$ at the later time is at most twice its earlier norm. The result assumes a positive parameter, the reference initial value and the reference evolution equations. It proves the uniform bound stated after (2.16), with no growth in $T$ or $\varepsilon^{-1}$.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferencePropagator.triangula: For continuous nonnegative coefficients in the triangular system, the factor multiplying $l$ lies in $(0,1]$, and the transfer into $h$ is at most half the lost factor. In §2.2.2 this controls the change in $h$ by the decrease of $|l|$. The result applies to such triangular systems generally, without requiring the particular reference angle.

Along the triangular system, $|h|+|l|$ cannot increase between ordered times when the coefficients are continuous and nonnegative. Applied to (2.16), this gives the reference propagator bound after comparing the sum with the Euclidean norm. The formal result allows general nonnegative coefficients, so the Riccati construction supplies sufficient hypotheses for this application.

The solution of (2.16) expresses $l$ by its exponential integrating factor and $h$ by the integral of the resulting forcing. The formal result allows any continuous coefficients of this triangular form. Nonnegativity is needed only for the subsequent decay estimates; the explicit solution formula itself requires the equations and continuity on the interval.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.actual_coupl: Errors at most $\varepsilon/(8T^2)$ in both normalized reference couplings imply $\nu_+/\nu\ge\varepsilon/2$ and the late relative bounds of Lemma 2.7. The assumptions are $0<\varepsilon\le1/16$, $T\ge2$ and the bounded-deviation formula (2.13). This result translates established coupling errors into the final conclusions; it does not estimate those errors from the wave equations.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.amplitude_in: Using $Y\le1$, the reference gain and the multiplicative amplitude comparison, this estimate bounds $A(\tau)$ by $\exp(3-\varepsilon^{-1/2})A(\tau_m)$ for $0\le\tau\le1$. It assumes $2\varepsilon\le1$ and that both times lie in the interval of comparison. Proposition 2.8 replaces the amplitude at $\tau_m$ by the full-interval maximum to obtain (2.24).
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.amplitude_la: For $\tau\ge\tau_m$, the amplitude comparison, bounded reference deviation and wave-number estimates make the strength relative to the actual maximum comparable to $\sqrt{\tan\varphi/\varepsilon}$. The formal statement retains all comparison constants explicitly. In Proposition 2.8 the tangent bounds at a crossing then replace this scale by $(\varepsilon\varepsilon_+)^{-1/2}$.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.amplitude_ra: If $c\,a_{\rm ref}\le A\le C\,a_{\rm ref}$ with $c,C>0$, then the ratio of $A$ to its maximum is bounded by $c/C$ and $C/c$ times the reference ratio to its peak. This step of Proposition 2.8 assumes an attained maximum on $[0,T]$. It does not require the actual and reference maxima to occur at the same time.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.couplingRati: If $\tan\varphi\ge1$ and the successor ratio differs from $\cos\varphi$ by at most half its size, then $1/(4\tan\varphi)\le\eta_+/\nu_+\le3/(2\tan\varphi)$. These are the bounds used to bracket the crossing in Proposition 2.8. This pointwise estimate does not assume continuity or produce a crossing by itself.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.coupling_err: From $C_0T^{C_0}\delta\le\varepsilon$, one obtains $CT^p\delta\le\varepsilon/(8T^2)$ once $C_0\ge p+2$ and $C_0\ge8C$, with $T\ge2$ and $\delta\ge0$. This makes the final smallness step in Lemma 2.7 explicit. The absolute threshold must absorb both the multiplicative constant and the two powers needed to compare with $\cos\varphi$.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.deviation_ex: For $0<\varepsilon\le1$, there is one function $e$ on $\tau\ge0$ satisfying its differential equation, $e(0)=0$ and $0\le e\le\varepsilon/8$. This is the existence step in Lemma 2.5. Substitution into (2.13) constructs the global Riccati solution; a global solution is therefore obtained from the bounded deviation, rather than assumed in advance.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.deviation_ze: The change of variables (2.13) gives $e(0)=0$ whenever $Y(0)=1$, because the reference angle is zero at the initial time. This is the initial condition for the invariant-interval argument in Lemma 2.5. The identity follows from the substitution alone and does not require either differential equation.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.hasDerivAt_s: This differentiates the explicit reference cosine and yields $(\cos\varphi)^{\prime}=-\tfrac12\varepsilon\tau\sin(2\varphi)\cos\varphi$. Since the cosine is positive, division gives the logarithmic derivative used to integrate (2.13) into (2.14). The identity holds for every real parameter and time; it does not itself state a separate derivative formula for $\varphi$.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.hasDerivWith: Applying (2.13) to a Riccati solution gives $e^{\prime}=\cos\varphi(-2e-e^2+\tfrac12\varepsilon\sin\varphi\cos\varphi)$. Lemma 2.5 uses this equation to keep $e$ between zero and $\varepsilon/8$. The formal result is local and preserves the interval on which the original derivative is known, including one-sided derivatives at its endpoints.

For a continuous rate $Y$ on $\tau\ge0$, differentiation of the exponential integral gives $a_{\rm ref}^{\prime}=Ya_{\rm ref}$. With $\alpha_1=-Ya_{\rm ref}$ and $\alpha_2=a_{\rm ref}$, this is the second equation of (2.5). The result includes the right derivative at zero and does not need the Riccati equation for this step.

A solution of the deviation equation gives a Riccati solution after the substitution (2.13). This is the reconstruction step in Lemma 2.5: once the bounded deviation exists, it produces the reference rate $Y$. The identity itself needs no size or sign bound on $\varepsilon$; those bounds are used to construct the required deviation.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.inv_sq_windo: For $0\le\varepsilon\le1$, $T\ge2$ and $0\le\tau\le T$, the reference cosine satisfies $\cos\varphi\ge T^{-2}$. Equivalently, its reciprocal costs at most $T^2$. Lemma 2.6 uses this bound when changing to $(h,l)$, and Lemma 2.7 uses it to convert absolute coupling errors into relative errors.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.inv_two_mul_: Whenever $\tan\varphi\ge1$, the explicit reference angle gives $\cos\varphi\ge1/(2\tan\varphi)$. Together with the upper bound by the cotangent, this converts (2.19) into the bounds on $\eta_+/\nu_+$ used in Proposition 2.8. It is an algebraic estimate, independent of the amplitude or Riccati equations.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceEta: This is the reference value of $\eta_+/\nu$ in §2.2.4 before the cancellation in (2.22). It includes the common factor $\cos\varphi$. Its individual terms can be much larger than the final answer at late times; the bounded-deviation form of $Y$ is what exposes their cancellation and gives comparison with $\cos\varphi$.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceNu: This is $\sin\varphi+\varepsilon\cos\varphi+2\varepsilon\tau Y\cos\varphi$, the reference value of $\nu_+/\nu$ in §2.2.4. It is evaluated before the perturbation from the actual wave is estimated. The expression alone gives no positive lower bound; positivity and late-time closeness to one are proved using the reference solution.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceNu_: For $0<\varepsilon\le1$ and $0\le\tau\le\sqrt2/\varepsilon$, the reference value of $\nu_+/\nu$ is at least $\varepsilon$ whenever (2.13) holds with $e(\tau)\ge0$. This supplies the early-time lower bound in Lemma 2.7. The estimate is pointwise and does not separately require the deviation equation.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceU: This quantity is $Ya_{\rm ref}$, which is the negative of the paper’s first reference component $\alpha_1$. Together with $\alpha_2=a_{\rm ref}$, it reconstructs the reference solution described before Lemma 2.5. The sign convention matters when reading the amplitude equations or the change-of-coordinate matrices; the physical reference pair remains $(-Ya_{\rm ref},a_{\rm ref})$.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceU_z: When $Y(0)=1$, the quantity $Ya_{\rm ref}$ is one initially. Since it represents $-\alpha_1$, the paper’s first amplitude coordinate starts at $-1$. Combined with $\alpha_2(0)=1$, this gives the growing initial data used in §2.2.2. This initial-value calculation uses no differential equation.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceV: The positive function $a_{\rm ref}=\exp(\int_0^\tau Y)$ is the second reference component $\alpha_2$. In §2.2.2 it supplies the common growing factor removed from every amplitude by (2.15). Its growth equation requires continuity of $Y$, supplied for a Riccati solution; merely writing the exponential integral does not establish that regularity.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceV_l: If a continuous rate is nonnegative before a nonnegative time and nonpositive afterwards, its exponential integral is maximal at that time on the entire forward half-line. Lemma 2.5 applies this with the unique zero $\tau_m$ of $Y$. Proposition 2.8 needs only the resulting maximum on the finite interval $[0,T]$.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceV_r: For ordered nonnegative times, (2.13) gives an amplitude ratio equal to the square root of the cosine ratio times the exponential integral of $(1+e)\cos\varphi$. This is the decomposition used in Proposition 2.8 after the reference peak. The identity assumes continuity of $Y$ but does not need the bounds on $e$ used in the subsequent estimates.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceV_z: The exponential integral defining $a_{\rm ref}$ equals one at $\tau=0$, so the second reference component has the initial value required in §2.2.2. The integral over an interval of zero length vanishes. This identity does not assume the Riccati equation or continuity of the supplied rate.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceY: This is the expression $Y=(1+e)\cos\varphi-\tfrac14\varepsilon\tau\sin(2\varphi)$ in (2.13). It separates the leading positive rate from the correction caused by turning. The expression alone allows any function $e$; Lemma 2.5 constructs the particular bounded deviation whose equation makes this $Y$ solve the reference Riccati problem.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceY_n: If $0<\varepsilon\le1$, $\varepsilon\tau=3$ and $e(\tau)\le\varepsilon/8$, the expression (2.13) is negative. In Lemma 2.5 this supplies the upper endpoint of the bracket for the unique zero of $Y$. The formal statement records the final sign; the intermediate trigonometric inequalities belong to its proof.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.referenceY_p: With $\varepsilon\ge0$, $\varepsilon\tau\le2$ and $e(\tau)\ge0$, the rate in (2.13) is strictly positive. Lemma 2.5 uses this to place the reference peak after the initial growth interval. The estimate depends on the deviation’s value at that time; it does not assume that the deviation solves its equation.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.reference_am: If $Y$ solves the Riccati equation on $\tau\ge0$, then $(-Ya_{\rm ref},a_{\rm ref})$ solves both equations of the reference system (2.5). This justifies the reconstruction immediately before Lemma 2.5. The formal result does not impose $Y(0)=1$; that initial condition is supplied separately to select the growing reference solution.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.reference_co:
For $	au\ge\sqrt2/\varepsilon$, $0<\varepsilon\le1$ and $0\le e\le\varepsilon/8$, the reference value of $
u_+/
u$ differs from one by at most $7\varepsilon^2$. The reference value of $\eta_+/
u$, after division by $\cos\varphi$, differs from one by at most $2\varepsilon$. These quantify the two asymptotic estimates following (2.22).
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.reference_ta: From any time at or after $2/\varepsilon$, the integral of $(1+e)\cos\varphi$ to a later time lies between zero and two under the reference hypotheses. The bound is uniform in the later endpoint. Proposition 2.8 uses it to control the exponential factor in the amplitude ratio after $\tau_m$, leaving the cosine ratio to determine the strength scale.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.rhs: This is the right-hand side of (2.12): $\cos^2\varphi(1-\varepsilon\tan\varphi)-\varepsilon\tau\sin(2\varphi)Y-Y^2$. It specifies how the logarithmic reference growth rate evolves as the wave vector turns. The expression itself is not an existence assertion; Lemma 2.5 adds $0<\varepsilon\le1$, the initial value and the global bounds.
notes.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.riccati_abs_: Every forward solution of (2.12) with $Y(0)=1$ and $0<\varepsilon\le1$ satisfies $|Y|\le1$.
