notes.TorusEuler.hierarchyMixedDirection: The derivative directions are the three operators $\ell_*\partial_{a_i}$ and the phase operator $h\partial_s$. Thus mixed derivatives acquire exactly the weights $\ell_*^m h^j$ in (D.1). This is the scaling convention behind the finite expansion estimates; it specifies how derivatives are measured and is not itself a bound on a field.
notes.TorusEuler.hierarchyOscExponent: The oscillatory exponent at level $p$ is $-5/4-2(p-1)/3$. At the first discarded level, this gives $\lambda^{-5/4-2P/3}$ and hence the depth gain $\lambda^{-2P/3}$ emphasized in §1.3. The formula records how the powers are assigned; the hierarchy estimates separately prove that the constructed fields obey them.
notes.TorusEuler.hierarchyTailPairs: After cancellation through depth $P$, label interactions remain when $i+j\ge P+1$, and phase interactions remain when $i+j\ge P+2$. These are the ranges in (5.30), with positive indices up to the last correction level. The formal sum omits initial phase factors that are identically zero under the expansion conventions.
notes.TorusEuler.hierarchy_absorb_parent_loss: Under $\mathsf D^C\lambda^{-1/12}\le1$, any available decay of at least $\lambda^{-1/12}$ absorbs the fixed parent factor. This is the arithmetic behind the choice of $\lambda^{-2/3}$ decay per level in Theorem 5.6. The identity concerns numerical powers; the product and solve estimates supply the bounds to which it is applied.
notes.TorusEuler.hierarchy_advection_filtratio: The full quadratic sum splits exactly into the interactions at levels two through $P$ and the remaining tail. The same identity treats label and phase derivatives with their respective level conventions. In Proposition 5.4 the first group cancels against the solved equations, leaving the two quadratic sums in (5.30).
notes.TorusEuler.hierarchy_completion_previous: The correction generated by the preceding oscillatory profile has an exponent one-third below that of the current oscillation. Thus, in the paper's indexing, $C_p$ fits into level $p$ with an extra factor $\lambda^{-1/3}$. This is the exponent calculation used in the finite hierarchy of §1.3; it is not itself a bound on a constructed field.
notes.TorusEuler.hierarchy_fast_completion_exp: For an interaction with $i+j=p+1$, the phase cost $\lambda^{3/2}$ combined with $C_i$ and $Y_j$ leaves an extra factor $\lambda^{-1/12}$ beyond the target level-$p$ oscillatory bound. This is the weakest surplus in the induction for Theorem 5.6 and determines the frequency smallness needed to absorb the parent powers.
notes.TorusEuler.hierarchy_fast_mean_exponent: When $i+j=p+1$, the induction bound for $B_i$, the oscillatory bound for $Y_j$, and one fast derivative give the target level-$p$ exponent with an extra $\lambda^{-1/4}$. This includes the term involving $B_p$ and $V_1$. It is the frequency calculation used for $f_p^S$ near the end of the induction.
notes.TorusEuler.hierarchy_label_product_expon: Adding the oscillatory frequency exponents at levels $i$ and $j$ gives the mean exponent at level $i+j$. It also leaves a surplus $\lambda^{-7/12}$ relative to the oscillatory target at that level. This arithmetic supplies the power used for label-advection products in the proof of Theorem 5.6 after applying (5.39).
notes.TorusEuler.hierarchy_level_bounds: The numerical recurrence gives the source, velocity, mean, and correction estimates under its frequency smallness condition. An order-$n$ estimate at level $p$ requires the recurrence through order $n+3(p-1)+1$. Theorem 5.6 supplies these higher orders simultaneously. In particular, the propagated oscillatory source and induction mean bounds contain no remaining parent factor.
notes.TorusEuler.hierarchy_mean_inductive_shif: The exponent in the sharper mean estimate (5.35), increased by $1/12$, equals the mean exponent used in (5.40). Thus replacing a parent factor by $\lambda^{1/12}$ gives exactly the induction bound stated in the paper. This is an algebraic identity; the actual mean estimate is supplied by the endpoint solve.
notes.TorusEuler.hierarchy_mean_product_expone: Adding the induction exponents for two means gives the mean exponent at their combined level minus one. Once the label-advection estimate is applied, their product is therefore smaller by $\lambda^{-1}$ than the leading averaged oscillatory terms. This is the comparison of the third sum with the first two sums after (5.42).
notes.TorusEuler.hierarchy_phaseMean_supplemen: For a differentiable period-one profile, the phase average of $(B\cdot\kappa)\partial_sY$ vanishes when $B$ and $\kappa$ are independent of phase. This explains why the supplementary term in (1.12) belongs to the oscillatory equation rather than the mean equation. The result proves cancellation of the average, without estimating the size of the source.
notes.TorusEuler.higherPressureGradientBudget_: The finite sum of higher pressure-gradient bounds is controlled by the level-two scale $\lambda^{-23/12}$. The transverse equation supplies estimates in terms of forcing, velocity, and the slow pressure derivative. This numerical summation gives the bound preceding (5.52), with the number of retained levels absorbed into the depth-dependent constant.
notes.TorusEuler.inductionPressure_endpointHes: The accumulated pressure-Hessian upper bound and a residual-gradient bound of one-half together give the effective bound $H\le I$. Frequencies starting at least at four and doubling make the reciprocal-frequency sum at most one-half. This preserves the coercivity condition introduced in §1.2 when the parent is replaced by the next approximate solution.
notes.TorusEuler.inductionPressure_sum_le: If the positive frequencies at least double, every finite sum of their reciprocals is at most $2/\lambda_0=2/N$. Item 1 of §7.2 applies this to the pressure-Hessian bound (T3) when verifying the next endpoint problem. The formal result proves the numerical summation estimate; the pressure inequality is supplied separately by the induction.
notes.TorusEuler.induction_child_center_error_: For $\lambda_j\ge2^{12}$ and $\lambda_{j+1}\ge\lambda_j$, the sum $\lambda_j^{-1/3}+\lambda_{j+1}^{-5}$ is at most $\lambda_j^{-1/4}$. Item 6 of §7.2 uses this after truncation adds the gradient of the Fourier tail to the central error. The result supplies the numerical margin needed to preserve (T4).
notes.TorusEuler.induction_child_velocity_boun: The parent bound $\|U_{j-1}\|_\infty\le\mu$, the oscillation bound $\|O_j\|_\infty\le\lambda_j^{-1}$, and the same bound for the remaining increment give $\|U_j\|_\infty\le\lambda_j$ when $2\mu\le\lambda_j$ and $\mu\ge2$. This is the last velocity estimate in item 5 of §7.2, completing that part of (T2).
notes.TorusEuler.induction_comparison_error_bu: The physical error estimate (6.6), the older-gradient bounds, the correction bound and the growth-rate lower bound give the three terms used in item 2 of §7.2. They have sizes $\varepsilon^{-1}L_{j+1}^3\mu^{-1/16}$, $\mu^{-3/32}$ and $\mu^{-1/4}$. The formal numerical inequality keeps an explicit constant; the separate schedule estimates then establish comparison smallness.
notes.TorusEuler.induction_older_gradient_scal: Because $\mu=\lambda_{j-2}^{K_{j-1}}$ with $K_{j-1}\ge320$, the older bounds $\lambda_{j-2}^9$ and $\lambda_{j-2}^{18}$ are bounded by $\mu^{1/32}$ and $\mu^{1/16}$. Item 2 of §7.2 applies these comparisons to $B$ and $B_t$. The statement concerns the numerical bounds; the actual gradient estimates come from (7.6).
notes.TorusEuler.inductive_oscillations_eventu: If the oscillation supports shrink to the torus origin, all sufficiently late oscillations vanish on an open neighborhood of any compact set avoiding that point. The conclusion is uniform over the full closed time interval. Proposition 8.4 needs this neighborhood, rather than vanishing only on the compact set itself, to pass all spatial derivatives to the terminal limit.

When $t_j\to T_\infty$ and each later oscillation vanishes up to its activation time, all sufficiently late oscillations vanish on every fixed $[0,T]$ with $T<T_\infty$. Proposition 8.1 therefore needs to sum only the small remaining increments there. This is the time-local reason that convergence holds in every spatial Hölder order before blow-up.
notes.TorusEuler.inner_normalize_cross3_left: The curl contribution $\kappa\times\mathbf a$ is perpendicular to $\kappa$, so its component along the unit covector vanishes. Proposition 8.2 uses this cancellation to remove the newest rank-one wave term while retaining the preceding wave. For the actual wave the covector is nonzero; the cancellation is independent of the value of the time cutoff.
notes.TorusEuler.integral_endpointLabelEnergy_: For a continuously differentiable displacement vanishing at both ends, integrating the label energy gives $\int_I(|\xi_t|^2-H^\#\xi\cdot\xi)\,dt$. This is (4.7) at the continuous-derivative level. The formal statement includes the flow and gradient derivative identities; the full Sobolev coercivity result is obtained separately, so this identity alone should not be read as that extension.
notes.TorusEuler.integral_endpointLabelVelocit: With the inverse-deformation and gradient bounds, this gives the factor $D_-^2(1+\|M\|_\infty)^2$ in (4.6). The formal result here assumes continuous $v=z_t$ and the terminal condition $z(T)=0$. It proves the continuously differentiable case of the paper's estimate; the separate Sobolev result extends it to all square-integrable derivatives.
notes.TorusEuler.integral_inner_gradient_cente: The integral of $w\cdot\nabla q$ over the torus is zero when $w$ is divergence free and both fields are periodic and $C^1$. This is the pressure cancellation in the endpoint energy argument of §1.2. Opposite faces cancel the boundary terms; the remaining Jacobi and displacement identities are separate parts of that argument.
notes.TorusEuler.integral_norm_iteratedFDeriv_: For $K_\Lambda(y)=\Lambda^3K(\Lambda y)$, the integral of the absolute value of any order-$m$ derivative is $\Lambda^m$ times the corresponding integral for $K$. The kernel is Schwartz and $\Lambda>0$. In Appendix B, applying this with the cutoff scale $4\Lambda$ gives the derivative factor in the Bernstein estimate (B.1).
notes.TorusEuler.integral_norm_pow_scaledLiftK: The absolute moment of degree $k$ scales as $\int |y|^k|K_\Lambda(y)|\,\mathrm dy=\Lambda^{-k}\int |y|^k|K(y)|\,\mathrm dy$ for positive $\Lambda$. In Appendix B these moments are finite because $K$ is Schwartz. Taking $k=M-s$ gives the frequency factor in (B.2) after the Taylor polynomial has been canceled.
notes.TorusEuler.integral_scaledCutoffSchwartz: The scaled inverse Fourier kernel has integral $\psi(0)$ for every positive scale. The smoothness and support assumptions make this identity available before requiring the symbol to equal one near zero. The additional plateau condition in Appendix B gives unit mass, which cancels the constant term in the Taylor expansion used for the cutoff tail.

Every positive-degree coordinate monomial integrates to zero against the cutoff kernel because the symbol is identically one near the origin. Repeated coordinate factors are allowed, covering every multi-index in a Taylor polynomial. These are signed moments; Appendix B uses their cancellation together with finite absolute moments to estimate the remaining cutoff error.
notes.TorusEuler.inverseAdjoint_activationWave: The identity $F^{-T}(\lambda F^TE_3)=\lambda E_3$ for invertible $F$ justifies the choice $k_*=\lambda(D_aX(t_0,0))^TE_3(t_0)$ in §6.2. It ensures the transported covector at activation is exactly the desired direction and length. The formal result is this algebraic identity; the deformation of the parent supplies the required invertible matrix.
notes.TorusEuler.isEulerSolution_stationaryShe: The stationary shear $U_0(x)=\sin(2\pi x_2)(e_1+\rho e_3)$ solves the unforced Euler equations with pressure zero on every positive time interval. This verifies the starting flow in §1.1. The formal result permits any real tilt; positivity and smallness of $\rho$ are needed later for amplification, rather than for the Euler identity.
notes.TorusEuler.iteratedFDeriv_comp_sub_linea: The derivative of a composition, after subtracting the outer derivative applied to the highest inner derivative, is a sum indexed by partitions with at least two parts. Each term therefore involves lower-order inner derivatives. In Proposition 5.1, taking the composition $U\circ X$ produces the forcing $N_\beta$ in the higher variational equation.
notes.TorusEuler.kineticForm: The kinetic coefficient is the transpose of the deformation multiplied by the deformation, so its quadratic form is the squared norm of the deformed vector. For $D_aX$ this is $K$ in (4.1). Quantitative ellipticity does not follow from the formula alone; it uses the separate bound on the inverse deformation.
notes.TorusEuler.kineticForm_elliptic: If the deformation has a left inverse of norm at most $D_->0$, then $K\ge D_-^{-2}I$. This is the ellipticity used by both inverse applications in Theorem 4.2. The formal result is purely linear algebraic: it does not require a particle flow, a differential equation or a bound on the forward deformation.
notes.TorusEuler.labelFlow_firstVariation: Differentiating the particle flow with respect to the perturbation $u+\varepsilon b$ gives $\xi_t=M\xi+b\circ X$ with zero initial displacement. This is the first variation used in §4.1 to identify $D_aXz_t=b\circ X$. The formal result includes regularity and uniform bounds ensuring that $\xi$ is the actual perturbation derivative, not merely a solution of the proposed linear equation.
notes.TorusEuler.labelWaveVector: The wave covector along a trajectory is obtained by applying the transpose of the reverse-flow derivative to the initial covector. Once the inverse-flow identity is established, this is $\kappa=(D_aX)^{-T}k_*$. It is the Lagrangian wave vector used in §1.1 and §3.1. Its nonvanishing follows from invertibility and nonzero initial data, not from the displayed formula alone.
notes.TorusEuler.lemma31_waveProfile: The explicit families $F_h$ and $P_h$ satisfy all conclusions of Lemma 3.1 for $0<h\le1$: smoothness, the required parity and periodicity, the normalized primitive, unit central slope and derivative bounds. One constant works for the slope and amplitude estimates at every width, while each higher derivative has its own width-independent constant.
notes.TorusEuler.liftConvolution_cutoffSchwart: Convolving the periodic extension of a continuous torus field with $K_\Lambda$ gives the cutoff $S_\Lambda f$ defined by its Fourier multiplier. The symbol is smooth and compactly supported, and the scale is positive. This identity is the passage used in Appendix B from frequency support to the physical-space operator and tail estimates.
notes.TorusEuler.linearODE_ne_zero_of_mem: A solution of a homogeneous linear ordinary differential equation with continuous coefficients remains nonzero throughout a connected time interval if it is nonzero at one time. Applied first to $k$ and then to the amplitude equation, this gives the persistence step in Lemma 2.1. The conclusion includes both earlier and later times within that interval.
notes.TorusEuler.linearODE_variation_of_consta: For a linear equation with continuous coefficients and forcing, this gives the solution as transported initial data plus the integral of transported forcing. The fundamental evolution and its inverse are assumed to solve their equations and equal the identity at the starting time. Section 2.2.3 applies this formula to compare the perturbed normalized amplitude with the reference evolution.
notes.TorusEuler.localizedCoefficient_holderHa: The product $\chi(B(a_0)-B)$ has size $O(r)$ and a radius-independent Lipschitz bound, giving a $C^{0,1/2}$ bound of order $r^{1/2}$. These are the estimates used to absorb the near term in (A.7). The formal statement assumes Lipschitz difference estimates for the coefficient and cutoff; differentiability of the chosen cutoff is unnecessary.
notes.TorusEuler.localizedCompletedWave_proper: A smooth transverse profile whose potential vanishes near the label-cell boundary produces a smooth periodic divergence-free velocity by taking the curl of its localized potential. Inside the cell it equals the leading wave plus its slow curl correction. This implements the localization in §1.1 and §1.3, and allows arbitrary real wave vectors rather than only integer frequencies.
notes.TorusEuler.localizedTransportedProfile: The profile is evaluated on $s=k\cdot a$ inside one label cell, extended periodically, then composed with the inverse parent flow. This is the construction described in §1.1. Vanishing near the cell boundary supplies smooth matching across cells; periodicity does not require $k\in\mathbb Z^3$. Smoothness is a separate property to establish.
notes.TorusEuler.meanScalarBudget_le_power: With $\ell_*=\mathsf D^{-s}$, the inverse estimate, two deformation factors and the Hölder comparison costs can be bounded by a single power of $\mathsf D$. The exponent may depend on the fixed radius exponent $s$. It does not depend on the derivative order, which is the essential requirement in Proposition 5.2.
notes.TorusEuler.meanScalarRadius_absorbs_inve: If the inverse constant satisfies $A\le\mathsf D^a$ and $\ell_*=\mathsf D^{-s}$ with $s\ge2(a+9)$, then $A\mathsf D^9\sqrt{\ell_*}\le1$. This is the scalar smallness condition behind (5.13). The radius is chosen once from the inverse bound, rather than decreased separately at each derivative order.
notes.TorusEuler.momentumResidual: The momentum residual is $R_U=\partial_tU+(U\cdot\nabla)U+\nabla p$. It is the actual defect of the specified velocity and pressure in the unforced momentum equation. This is the source corrected in §1.3 and the term whose gradient enters the effective Hessian in §1.2. At endpoints of a parent interval, time derivatives are one-sided.
notes.TorusEuler.nonempty_truncatedChildStage: A smooth periodic odd divergence-free approximate solution, with its exact residual equation, admits a frequency-truncated velocity and smooth periodic zero-mean Poisson pressure. The construction includes the exact projected residual identity as well as frequency support and incompressibility. This supplies the fields used in §5.7; the quantitative error bounds require the additional cutoff estimates.
notes.TorusEuler.norm_complexFrozenInverseSymb: The inverse frozen symbol, acting on complex Fourier coefficients, has norm at most $\min(1,\mu)^{-1}$. This is the Lax–Milgram estimate used before (A.6). The formal result transfers the corresponding real operator estimate to a compatible complex Hilbert space; it also covers the zero frequency whenever its projection satisfies the same hypotheses.
notes.TorusEuler.norm_curlOfDerivative_ge_of_t: Two successive central-gradient decompositions, projected along the newest covector, give a lower bound for the newest stage’s curl. The leading curl of the newest wave cancels; the preceding wave contributes its signed projection, while the older gradient and both errors are subtracted. Proposition 8.2 then inserts the strength, angle and error estimates to obtain (8.2).
notes.TorusEuler.norm_iteratedFDeriv_labelJaco: An order-$n$ derivative of $D_aX$ is controlled by the order-$(n+1)$ derivative of $X$. The flow bound $\mathsf D^{5(n+1)-4}$ therefore becomes $\mathsf D^{5n+1}$ for the deformation. This is the conversion immediately after the induction in Proposition 5.1, before the other coefficients are bounded by products and inverses.
notes.TorusEuler.norm_operatorLiftConvolution_: A smooth compactly supported symbol vanishing at zero gives a convolution block bounded by the input's half-Hölder seminorm times $\lambda^{-1/2}$ and a kernel moment. For $\lambda=2^j$ this is the $2^{-j/2}$ gain in the proof of (A.6). The formal estimate retains the kernel moment explicitly; its uniform bound comes from the symbol estimates.
notes.TorusEuler.norm_phaseMean_le: The phase average has norm at most a uniform bound for the field over one period. Since the period has length one, no extra length factor appears. This is the zero-order estimate behind the averaging part of (D.5); commuting averaging with the label and phase derivatives gives the finite-order version.
notes.TorusEuler.norm_phasePrimitive_le: For a continuous periodic field of zero phase average, the normalized primitive is bounded by twice the field’s supremum over one period. The bound holds at every phase, using periodicity to reduce to that interval. This is the zero-order primitive estimate in (D.5), which extends to higher orders by commuting the relevant derivatives.
notes.TorusEuler.norm_sq_mul_oscillatoryPressu: For $\kappa\ne0$, the prescribed pressure slope obeys $\lVert\kappa\rVert^2\partial_s\mathsf p=\kappa\cdot f-2\kappa\cdot MV$, the identity (5.16). The result is algebraic and holds in a general real inner-product space. It determines the derivative in phase; taking the zero-mean primitive fixes the pressure itself.
notes.TorusEuler.norm_stationaryShearGradient_: The stationary shear gradient satisfies $|B_\rho|\le4\pi$ when $|\rho|\le1$. This follows from its rank-one form in (6.1) and is used to choose the short interval for Lemma 6.1. The formal statement also permits zero and negative $\rho$ of that size, beyond the positive parameter chosen in the paper.
notes.TorusEuler.norm_stationaryShear_le: The sine shear satisfies $|U_0(x)|\le2$ at every point when $|\rho|\le1$. This supplies the velocity part of the initial induction bounds in §7.2 once the base frequency is at least two. The estimate is uniform in space and includes the paper’s choice $\rho=\varepsilon_1$.
notes.TorusEuler.norm_sub_liftConvolution_scal: Applying the cutoff-error estimate to $f(\cdot+v)-f$ bounds increments of the error by increments of the highest derivative of $f$. The same kernel moment gives a factor $\Lambda^{-k}$ after $k$ derivatives. Choosing the derivative increment bound from its half-Hölder seminorm supplies the Hölder part of (B.2), alongside the separate uniform estimate.

For an integer $k\ge1$, a bounded field with $k$ continuous derivatives and a uniform bound on its $k$th derivative has cutoff error at most that bound times $\Lambda^{-k}\int |y|^k|K(y)|\,\mathrm dy$. The symbol equals one near zero, so its moments cancel the Taylor polynomial. Appendix B combines this pointwise estimate with derivative and increment bounds to prove (B.2).
notes.TorusEuler.norm_wavePotential_le: For a continuous periodic zero-mean profile bounded by $B$ and a nonzero covector, $|Q[V](s)|\le2B/|\kappa|$ at every phase. This is the inverse-frequency gain described after (3.6). Transversality is unnecessary for this norm estimate; the additional label derivative used to form the divergence correction is accounted for separately.
notes.TorusEuler.norm_wavePrimaryPressure_geom: After separating the signed rank-one term in (5.51), the other tensors are bounded in operator norm at a cost of at most $\lambda^{3/2}$ times the pressure profile bound, up to parent factors. This yields their $\lambda^{-3/4}$ decay in Lemma 5.9. The dominant tensor is deliberately treated by its sign instead.
notes.TorusEuler.norm_waveProfile_le: For $0<h\le1$, the constructed profile obeys $|F_h(s)|\le h/2$ at every phase. Multiplying by $|\mathbf a|$ gives the $O(h|\mathbf a|)$ velocity bound used in §1.2, with the explicit constant $1/2$. Together with $F_h'(0)=1$, it separates small velocity amplitude from large central velocity gradient.
notes.TorusEuler.odd_transportedProfile: If the inverse flow is odd and $f(t,-a,-s)=-f(t,a,s)$, then $f^\natural$ is odd in the spatial variable. This is the final evaluation step in the parity argument of §3.1. It holds for every real initial wave vector and needs no derivatives; localization and periodic extension are separate parts of the construction.
notes.TorusEuler.odd_waveProfile: The constructed $F_h$ is odd for every $0<h\le1$, because its normalized slope is even and the integral starts at zero. This is the parity step in Lemma 3.1. Periodicity and the existence of a periodic pressure primitive use additional zero-mean properties, so they are established separately from this reflection identity.
notes.TorusEuler.offOrigin: On the Euclidean lift, $\mathbb T^3\setminus\{0\}$ is represented by $\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb Z^3$. Every integer point is a representative of the same torus origin. This is the domain used for the compact-set limits in Theorem 1.1 and the smooth extension in Remark 1.2; removing just one Euclidean point would not represent the punctured torus.
notes.TorusEuler.oscillatoryPhasePressure_prim: The normalized phase pressure for the leading wave equals $-c_{\mathbf a}P_h$, as used at the start of Lemma 5.9. The calculation writes its phase derivative as a scalar multiple of $F_h$ and takes the zero-mean phase primitive. It therefore identifies the pressure selected by the transverse equation with the explicit profile in the paper.
notes.TorusEuler.oscillatoryPhasePressure_weig: The zero-mean primitive in (5.16) gives bounds for $\lambda\mathsf p$ in terms of the weighted velocity and source derivatives. Smoothness, phase periodicity and zero phase means are assumed, along with bounds for the normalized coefficients. Summing these derivative estimates and inserting the parent bounds yields (5.24), with no extra power of the frequency lost to pressure recovery.
notes.TorusEuler.oscillatoryTransverseProjecti: The orthogonal projection is $\operatorname{Id}-P_\kappa=\operatorname{Id}-\kappa\otimes\kappa/\lVert\kappa\rVert^2$ for nonzero $\kappa$. It gives the projected activation data (5.4) and the forcing in (5.17). In the paper, nonvanishing follows from the transported nonzero wave vector; the definition alone does not assert that the projected seed is nonzero.
notes.TorusEuler.oscillatory_transverse_of_ini: A transverse initial amplitude remains perpendicular to its nonzero transported covector on the connected time interval. The formal statement permits a projected forcing term in the amplitude equation, so the homogeneous seed equation (3.2) is a special case. This is the persistence assertion used in §3.1 to cancel the fast divergence of the leading oscillation.
notes.TorusEuler.paperA1_displacement_eq_primi: A displacement with $z(0)=0$ and continuous derivative $v$ equals $Jv$ throughout $[0,1]$. This is the fundamental theorem of calculus used in the uniqueness part of Theorem A.1. The endpoint derivative convention is one-sided; the assertion does not require an extension beyond the prescribed time interval.
notes.TorusEuler.paperA1_solution_of_unproject: Any solution of the unprojected equation in Theorem A.1 yields a solution of the projected endpoint problem with the same velocity and constant field. The periodic pressure gradient disappears under Leray projection, and $z=Jv$ preserves both endpoint conditions. This is the direction needed to transfer uniqueness of the projected inverse to the original formulation.
notes.TorusEuler.paperA2_wordNorm_le: The derivative estimates in Lemma A.2 form a triangular recurrence: each new solution derivative is bounded using only lower solution derivatives and known coefficient derivatives. This numerical induction bounds all derivatives through the chosen order by one constant times the source bound. The constant depends on the order and coefficient controls, while dependence on the source remains linear.
notes.TorusEuler.paperAppendixD_holderComparis: For $0<\ell_*\le1$, the finite supremum norm is bounded by the half-Hölder norm, which is at most $4\ell_*^{-1/2}$ times the supremum norm one order higher. Smoothness and finiteness of the derivative bounds are explicit. This is the comparison (D.2) responsible for the single source-derivative loss in Proposition 5.2.
notes.TorusEuler.paperHierarchyActiveVelocityN: This measures a field on $[t_0,T]$ in the scaled label and phase norm, divided by the positive amplitude weight $\gamma(t)$. Time indexes the supremum and is not differentiated. It is used in the version of (5.20) for data defined only after activation, without requiring fields at earlier times.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemma13_slowOrders: The frequency recurrence, maximum rule and positive logarithmic floor imply the conclusions of Lemma 1.3: adjacent orders differ by at most one, every fixed order is eventually reached, and $L_{j+1}\le(\log\lambda_{j-1})^2$. No monotonicity of $\mathcal B$ or domination of analytic costs is assumed in this arithmetic result.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemma31_waveProfile: This gives the existential form of Lemma 3.1: families $F_h$ and $P_h$ satisfy the full set of smoothness, parity, periodicity and quantitative estimates. The families and the common slope constant are chosen before $h$, and each higher-derivative constant is chosen before $h$ and the phase. Thus the bounds are uniform throughout $0<h\le1$.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemma57_periodicGraphFro: A profile agreeing with its smooth periodic mean near the label-cell faces gives a smooth periodic physical field after phase evaluation. The inverse labels must satisfy the lattice translation law. This implements the continuation assumed in Lemma 5.7 and preserves the derivative and Hölder bounds across the joining region; the compactly supported oscillation supplies the required collar.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemma61_exists_firstWave: For $0<\rho\le1$, $T\ge0$ and $\lambda>0$ with $T|B_\rho|\le1/8$, a normalized first wave exists and satisfies all the conclusions of Lemma 6.1. This combines the construction with the estimates, so the starting wave is not merely assumed. The formal parameter range includes shorter intervals and smaller positive frequencies than the numbered statement uses.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemma61_firstWave: Any first wave satisfying the prescribed equations, transverse initial directions and peak normalization obeys Lemma 6.1 under $0<\rho\le1$ and $T|B_\rho|\le1/8$. The formal estimate requires only $\lambda>0$. Existence of the input wave is separate; the conclusion supplies propagation, positive coupling and the initial strength range used in Section 7.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaA2_mixed_holder: This is the time-path case of Lemma A.2, with $H=L^2(I;\mathbb R^3)$ and $\mathcal R=\mathbb P\mathcal Q$. A $C^{1,1/2}$ coefficient coercive on zero-time-mean paths gives the bounded inverse on spatial $C^{0,1/2}$ fields of paths. The formal estimate fixes the polynomial exponent at $145$ and uses the coefficient and first derivative supremum bounds.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaA2_mixed_holder_bou: When the path-operator coefficient is spatially $C^{k,1/2}$, multiplication followed by $\mathbb P\mathcal Q$ is bounded in that same spatial class. Time remains an $L^2$ variable. This supplies the forward-map half of the higher regularity assertion in Lemma A.2; no coercivity or inverse estimate is needed for this direction.

For a coercive coefficient in $C^{k,1/2}$ with $k\ge1$, the mixed inverse maps data of that regularity to solutions in the same class, with a bound independent of the datum. This supplies the inverse estimate in the time-path case of Lemma A.2. Coercivity is imposed only on paths with zero time mean.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaA2_mixed_holder_res: The mixed projected coefficient map preserves each available $C^{k,1/2}$ spatial class, and every datum there has a unique preimage of the same regularity. This is the higher regularity existence and uniqueness part of Lemma A.2 for whole time paths. Separate estimates show boundedness of the map and inverse in that norm.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaA2_spatial_holder: This is the vector-field case of Lemma A.2. A $C^{1,1/2}$ coefficient with positive quadratic lower bound makes $v\mapsto\mathbb P(Bv)$ invertible on divergence-free $C^{0,1/2}$ fields. The formal estimate gives exponent $145$ and depends on the coefficient and first derivative supremum bounds, matching the paper's unspecified polynomial dependence.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaA2_spatial_holder_b: Multiplying by a $C^{k,1/2}$ coefficient and applying the Leray projection preserves $C^{k,1/2}$ and has a finite norm bound independent of the input. This gives the forward estimate in the higher regularity conclusion of Lemma A.2. Unlike the inverse direction, it does not require coercivity of the coefficient.

A coercive coefficient in $C^{k,1/2}$, with $k\ge1$, gives an inverse bounded in that same norm, with a constant independent of the datum. This supplies the spatial inverse estimate in the last assertion of Lemma A.2. The higher-order constant may depend on the coefficient and order; no uniform polynomial formula for all higher norms is claimed here.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaA2_spatial_holder_r: The spatial projected coefficient map preserves $C^{k,1/2}$ and every datum in that class has a unique preimage there, provided the coefficient has the same regularity and is coercive. This is the regularity and solvability part of the final assertion of Lemma A.2. Higher norm estimates for the map and inverse are proved separately.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaB1_bernstein: A field supported on frequencies at most $4\Lambda$ has its order-$m$ derivatives bounded by $C_m\Lambda^m\|f\|_\infty$. This version sums over all ordered coordinate differentiations and applies to complex Banach-valued fields. The paper’s multi-index sum counts each mixed derivative once; the corresponding real normed-space theorem gives precisely that form of (B.1).
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaB1_bernstein_real_m: For any real normed-space-valued field with frequencies at most $4\Lambda$, the multi-index derivative sum is bounded by $C_m\Lambda^m\|f\|_\infty$. Each multi-index is counted once, and completeness of the target is not required. The constant is chosen before the target space, frequency and field, matching the generality and uniformity of (B.1).
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaB1_cutoff_LInfinity: The cutoff satisfies $\|S_\Lambda f\|_{L^\infty}\le\|\check\psi\|_{L^1}\|f\|_{L^\infty}$ for essentially bounded measurable torus fields and every $\Lambda>0$. The kernel constant is independent of the frequency. This version of Lemma B.1 applies to complex Banach-valued fields and gives the genuine essential-supremum estimate, beyond the simpler statement for continuous inputs.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaB1_cutoff_aeBound: If an integrable torus field is bounded almost everywhere by $M\ge0$, its cutoff is bounded at every point by $\|\check\psi\|_{L^1}M$. The symbol is smooth and supported in the prescribed ball, and $\Lambda>0$. This estimate underlies the $L^\infty$ operator bound in Lemma B.1.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaB1_cutoff_commutes_: For a periodic field with $m$ continuous spatial derivatives, its order-$m$ cutoff derivative is convolution of the same kernel with the order-$m$ derivative of the field. This supplies the spatial commutation in Lemma B.1 without requiring a Hölder bound on the last derivative. Time differentiation is treated separately on the stage interval.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaB1_cutoff_derivativ: For a field in the required spatial Hölder class, differentiating its cutoff to order $m$ gives convolution with the corresponding derivative of the field. This version includes the boundedness and regularity needed for the estimates. Appendix B uses it to apply the same kernel argument at every derivative order in (B.2).
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaB1_cutoff_holder: The cutoff preserves $C^{0,1/2}$ and has norm at most $\|\check\psi\|_{L^1}$ in that space. Convolution bounds both field values and their spatial increments by the same constant. This proves the half-Hölder operator bound in Lemma B.1 and handles the equal-order case of the tail estimate.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaB1_cutoff_sup: For a continuous periodic field, the supremum norm of its cutoff is at most $\|\check\psi\|_{L^1}$ times the input supremum norm. The constant depends on the fixed smooth symbol and is independent of every positive cutoff frequency. This is the continuous-field form of the operator estimate used in Appendix B and §5.7.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaB1_cutoff_support_p: The cutoff has no frequencies beyond $2\Lambda$. If the symbol is even, it also preserves evenness and oddness of a continuous periodic field; the formal statement covers any scalar relation of the form $f(-x)=cf(x)$. These are the support and parity properties in Lemma B.1, used to retain odd symmetry through truncation.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaB1_cutoff_tail: For $0\le s\le M$, the tail obeys $\|(\operatorname{Id}-S_\Lambda)f\|_{C^{s,1/2}}\le C_M\Lambda^{s-M}\|f\|_{C^{M,1/2}}$. The constant is uniform in $s$, the field and $\Lambda\ge1$, and the conclusion includes the required regularity of the tail. This is (B.2), used to control the change in velocity when forming the next parent.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaB1_realBanachCutoff: The essential-supremum cutoff estimate also holds for fields taking values in any real Banach space. Using the real part of the spectral kernel gives the same bound by $\|\check\psi\|_{L^1}$ for all $\Lambda>0$. This supplies a real-target version of the $L^\infty$ estimate in Lemma B.1, including the velocity fields used in the construction.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaB1_realCutoff_LInfi: The real velocity cutoff has essential supremum at most $\|\check\psi\|_{L^1}$ times the input essential supremum for every positive scale. The input is assumed essentially bounded and measurable, without a continuity requirement. This supplies the real-vector version of the $L^\infty$ operator estimate in Lemma B.1.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaB1_realCutoff_admis: For a smooth periodic velocity and an even cutoff symbol, truncation preserves oddness and divergence freeness and restricts frequencies to at most $2\Lambda$. Each preserved property follows from the corresponding property of the input. These are the qualitative conclusions of Lemma B.1 used in §5.7 when the truncated approximate solution becomes the next parent.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaB1_realCutoff_parit: An even symbol preserves any relation $f(-x)=cf(x)$ for a continuous real vector field on the torus. Taking $c=1$ or $c=-1$ gives evenness or oddness. This is the parity part of Lemma B.1, ensuring that the spatial symmetry of the approximate velocity survives frequency truncation.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaB1_realCutoff_sup: The uniform norm of the real velocity cutoff is bounded by $\|\check\psi\|_{L^1}$ times the input norm, independently of every positive cutoff scale. The field is continuous and periodic, and the symbol is smooth with the prescribed compact support. This is the operator estimate used for the real velocities in Appendix B and §5.7.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaD1_derivatives: In (D.3), one label derivative costs $\ell_*^{-1}$ and one phase derivative costs $h^{-1}$, using the norm one order higher. Summing the three label directions gives the explicit factor three. Smoothness and bounded derivatives through order $n+1$ are required. Applying this to $f/\gamma(t)$ gives the amplitude-weighted version because the weight depends only on time.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaD1_phaseAverage: Phase averaging has norm at most one in the finite derivative norm, and subtracting the average has norm at most two. The field is smooth and periodic in phase, with bounded derivatives through the required order. The constant derivative directions can include the label and phase scales, giving the first two inequalities in (D.5).
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaD1_phasePrimitive: The normalized periodic primitive has finite derivative norm at most twice that of the original field. The input must be smooth, phase periodic and of zero phase average, with bounded derivatives through the required order. Applying the estimate after division by the time-dependent amplitude gives the primitive bound in (D.5).
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaD1_product: The finite-norm product estimate applies to any continuous bilinear map, with its operator norm included in the constant. One factor carries the time-only amplitude weight, as in (D.4). The estimate is available for supremum and half-Hölder norms under the corresponding smoothness and boundedness assumptions, covering the scalar, vector and matrix products used in Section 5.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaD2_inverse: If a coefficient satisfies (D.6) with exponent $a$ and its pointwise inverse is bounded by $\mathsf D^a$, the inverse satisfies the corresponding derivative bounds with exponent $3a$. The coefficient is explicitly required to be invertible, and $\mathsf D\ge1$. This is the inverse estimate of Lemma D.2; invertibility alone would not give the uniform bound required here.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaD2_inverse_multiInd: The inverse coefficient satisfies the coordinate-derivative version of (D.6) with exponent $3a$, assuming pointwise invertibility and the bound $|c^{-1}|\le\mathsf D^a$. Converting between derivative operator norms and coordinate sums changes only the order-dependent constants. Thus the inverse estimate in Lemma D.2 retains its absolute exponent in the paper’s norm convention.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaD2_mul: The product of two coefficients satisfying (D.6) with exponent $a$ satisfies the same kind of bound with exponent $2a$. Leibniz’s rule changes the order-dependent constants while the power of $\mathsf D$ still grows linearly with derivative order. This is the product step of Lemma D.2 for coefficients in a real normed algebra.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaD2_mul_multiIndex: The product estimate of Lemma D.2 is also stated directly using the paper’s coordinate-derivative sums. If both coefficients have polynomial exponent $a$, their product has exponent $2a$ when $\mathsf D\ge1$. Each multi-index is counted once, and changing the derivative norm affects only the order-dependent constants.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaD2_weighted: If $\ell_*\mathsf D^a\le1$, the scaled coefficient derivatives are bounded by order-dependent multiples of $\mathsf D^a$. At positive order the estimate retains the smaller factor $\mathsf D^{2a}\ell_*$. This is the gain in Lemma D.2(c) that controls differentiated coefficients in the inverse argument. The formal estimate also admits zero radius; the paper uses a positive envelope radius.
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaD2_weighted_multiIn: Under $\ell_*\mathsf D^a\le1$, summing the weighted coordinate derivatives through order $n$ gives a bound by $C_n\mathsf D^a$. Each positive-order term also satisfies $\ell_*^m|c|_m\le C_m\mathsf D^{2a}\ell_*$. This is the coordinate-sum form of Lemma D.2(c), including the radius factor later used in (D.7).
notes.TorusEuler.paperLemmaD3_lifting: For a linear equation with the stated commutation and product rules, coefficient bounds through order $n$ lift the uniform zero-order estimate to the finite derivative norm. The conclusion contains one factor $C_{\rm low}$; the remaining constant is determined by the order and coefficient bounds. This is the general estimate behind Lemma D.3, with constraints and prescribed data incorporated in the solution and forcing spaces.
notes.TorusEuler.paperMeanIntegratedMomentum: This is the left side $K(t)v(t)-J(\Omega v)(t)+L(t)$ of (4.9). The velocity is divergence free, but the expression need not be; its gradient part becomes the integrated pressure. The formula by itself imposes neither the endpoint conditions nor an equation. Those conditions are added in the endpoint solution.
notes.TorusEuler.paperMean_inverse_scale: The reciprocal ellipticity and coercivity constants are bounded by a fixed fourth power of the sum of the parent controls. This is the algebraic comparison used to turn the Appendix A estimate into (4.10). The assumptions include $D_-\ge1$ and nonnegative coefficient bounds, ensuring the common scale is at least one.
notes.TorusEuler.paperMean_projection_C1_gradi: If a $C^{0,1/2}$ field is the gradient of a continuously differentiable periodic scalar potential, its Leray projection is zero. Appendix A uses this to pass from the integrated pressure equation to the projected inverse. Periodicity is essential to this torus statement; a gradient of an arbitrary nonperiodic potential need not be removed.
notes.TorusEuler.paperPhysicalStepExponent: The exponent $b$ is chosen explicitly to dominate the parent powers arising from the hierarchy, inverse labels, mean estimates, and flow calculation. It is a sufficient choice for the common constant $C_{\rm step}$ in §5.6, independent of expansion depth. The separate coefficient choice supplies $\Gamma_P$, which may depend on that depth.
notes.TorusEuler.paperProposition511_physicalC: A smooth even Fourier cutoff gives a truncated velocity with controlled residual, controlled change in pressure Hessian, and the inherited upper pressure bound. This is Proposition 5.11, used in the scheme outlined in §1.3. The assumptions concern the actual smooth periodic approximation and its residual; the estimates keep pressure control alongside the small velocity truncation error.
notes.TorusEuler.paperProposition51_parentCoef: The six families in Proposition 5.1 satisfy derivative bounds with common power $\mathsf D^{16m+16}$. The velocity derivative bounds, deformation bounds and activation normalization are supplied first. After weighting by a sufficiently small radius, the remaining power is independent of derivative order. This result isolates that coefficient conclusion from the separate composition estimate.
notes.TorusEuler.paperProposition51_parentComp: If $f$ has the derivative bounds assumed in Proposition 5.1, composition with the parent flow gives $\lVert D_a^m(f\circ X)\rVert\le C_m A_f\mathsf D^{6m}$. The constants depend on the prescribed derivative bounds, not on the chosen parent or field. This supplies (5.7) before the radius weights are inserted.
notes.TorusEuler.paperProposition51_weightedCo: Once the composed field has derivative growth $\mathsf D^{6m}$, the condition $\ell_*\mathsf D^6\le1$ bounds its finite weighted sum by $C_nA_f$. This is the second estimate in (5.8). The theorem performs the summation of an already established derivative bound; composition with the flow is handled by the preceding estimate.
notes.TorusEuler.paperTheorem71: One exponent and one nondecreasing threshold work for every sufficiently large initial frequency, producing a common sequence with the conclusions used in §§1.3–1.5. The strength constant is $18\exp(3)$. This existence result selects its threshold; the paper's later Theorem 7.1 allows every admissible threshold above a chosen majorant and adds the stated connections to the finite expansion.
notes.TorusEuler.paperTheoremA1: The endpoint problem on $[0,1]$ has a unique velocity, displacement, constant field and pressure gradient, with a polynomial velocity bound of exponent $291$. A zero-mean potential is also constructed, and smooth data give smooth conclusions. This formal result underlying Theorem A.1 does not separately require symmetry of $K$ or skew-symmetry of $\Omega$; the ellipticity and energy assumptions suffice.
notes.TorusEuler.paper_mean_columns: For every smooth mean solution of the endpoint problem and every sufficiently large fixed radius exponent $s$, the estimate has the form $\lVert B\rVert_{[n]}\le C_n\mathsf D^{b+2+2s}\lVert\bar f\rVert_{[n+1]}$. The constants and threshold are chosen before the parent. Fixing $s$ therefore gives Proposition 5.2's parent exponent independent of $n$.
notes.TorusEuler.paper_mean_hardy: Under $H^\#\le I$ and $0<T\le1$, the Hessian term is at most half the displacement kinetic energy, while the label energy is at least that half. This is the general result applied in Lemma 4.1. The formal theorem works in any complete real Hilbert space and represents $H^1_0$ paths by square-integrable derivatives with zero time mean.
notes.TorusEuler.paper_mean_inverse: For admissible geometric parent data, every continuous Hölder source has an endpoint solution, and the fixed-time projected kinetic operator is also invertible. One polynomial in the parent controls bounds both inverses, as required in Theorem 4.2. The formal result gives exponent $1164$, constructs a normalized periodic potential, and states uniqueness of the endpoint velocity and constant field.
notes.TorusEuler.paper_mean_inverse_smooth_for: A smooth periodic force in label coordinates gives a smooth mean correction, zero displacement at both endpoints, and a zero-mean label pressure. This is the smooth inverse used in Theorem 4.2. To obtain the Eulerian equation, the supplied deformation and gradient must additionally be identified with the derivatives of the actual parent flow.

For a smooth periodic divergence-free parent on $0<T\le1$, the flow bounds and effective-Hessian upper bound give a smooth periodic correction solving the forced linearized Euler equation. The construction first solves the zero-displacement endpoint problem in labels and then returns to physical space. This supplies the analytic mean correction introduced in §1.2 and used in §1.3.
notes.TorusEuler.paper_section_8_of_inductiveE: For sufficiently large initial frequency, compatible approximate stages and central waves give a single Euler limit with all four conclusions of Section 8. These include convergence before accumulation, bounded velocity and central blow-up, maximality and divergent integrals, and both local terminal limits away from the origin. The same positive time is the activation limit in every conclusion.
notes.TorusEuler.parentResidualFourierBand_of_: A parent velocity supported on frequencies at most $2\mathsf D$ has projected momentum residual supported on frequencies at most $4\mathsf D$. The result assumes the residual is identified with that projected momentum expression. Products double the frequency bound and the Leray projection preserves it, supplying the residual support statement in §5.1.
notes.TorusEuler.periodicL2Coefficient_sub_rea: At every Fourier frequency, the part removed by the Leray projection is the gradient of the scalar potential $\Delta^{-1}\operatorname{div}v$. This is the projection formula in the introduction's conventions, here for real square-integrable torus fields. Setting the scalar zero mode to zero fixes its mean, while retaining constant divergence-free velocity modes.
notes.TorusEuler.periodicPoissonPressure_uniqu: Two smooth periodic pressures with the same Laplacian and zero spatial mean are equal. Their difference is a periodic harmonic function, hence constant, and the normalization removes that constant. Proposition 5.11 uses this at each time to identify the constructed pressure with the zero-mean Poisson pressure specified by the paper.
notes.TorusEuler.periodic_phasePrimitive: The normalized primitive of a continuous, period-one, zero-mean phase profile is again period one. This is the compatibility required for $\partial_s^{-1}$ in (3.5). A nonzero phase average would produce a linear drift in an ordinary primitive; subtracting the primitive's additive mean fixes its normalization but does not remove that drift.
notes.TorusEuler.periodic_wavePressurePrimitiv: For $0<h\le1$, the pressure primitive $P_h$ has period one. The proof uses continuity, period one and zero phase mean of $F_h$, as in the construction of Lemma 3.1. This is the compatibility needed for the phase pressure; the separate zero-mean normalization fixes the primitive's otherwise arbitrary additive constant.
notes.TorusEuler.periodic_waveProfile: For every admissible width, $F_h$ has period one because the normalized slope has zero integral over a period. This is the periodicity step in the proof of Lemma 3.1. Evenness of the slope gives oddness of the profile separately; the zero-mean condition is what prevents a drift from one period to the next.
notes.TorusEuler.phaseMean: The phase average is $\langle f\rangle_s=\int_0^1f(s)\,ds$, with time and particle label held fixed. It is the average used to split the forcing in §1.3 into the mean equation and the transverse equation. It is not a spatial torus average or an integration over the particle labels.
notes.TorusEuler.phaseMean_phasePrimitive: The normalized primitive has zero phase average because the average of its indefinite integral is subtracted. This holds for every continuous input. It supplies the normalization in (D.5); obtaining a periodic primitive also uses periodicity and zero average of the input, which are hypotheses of the separate periodicity result.
notes.TorusEuler.phaseMean_wavePressurePrimiti: The primitive $P_h$ has zero mean in the phase variable for $0<h\le1$, as required in Lemma 3.1. This normalization selects one primitive from those differing by an additive constant. It concerns the scalar phase profile; it does not assert that the full localized Eulerian pressure has zero spatial mean.
notes.TorusEuler.phaseOscillation: The oscillatory part of a profile is $f-\langle f\rangle_s$. This is the subtraction appearing in $H_2-\langle H_2\rangle_s$ in (1.12), which separates the transverse forcing from the mean forcing. For the smooth periodic profiles used in the paper, the resulting oscillatory part is periodic and has zero phase average.
notes.TorusEuler.phaseOscillation_longitudinal: The equation $(\nabla_a+k_*\partial_s)\cdot c=0$ gives $k_*\cdot c_{\rm osc}=-\partial_s^{-1}\operatorname{div}_a c_{\rm osc}$ and makes the mean label velocity divergence free. Smoothness and phase periodicity justify averaging and taking the primitive. Lemma 5.10 uses this to control the oscillatory phase velocity without paying directly for the large carrier $k_*$.
notes.TorusEuler.phasePrimitive: The operator $\partial_s^{-1}$ is formed by integrating from phase zero and then subtracting the mean of that integral over one period. It is used in the wave potential (3.5). For continuous periodic input of zero mean, it gives the normalized periodic primitive; those conditions are needed for the claimed derivative and periodicity properties.
notes.TorusEuler.physicalHierarchy_graph_cost: The bounds $\ell_*^{-1}\le\mathsf D^a$, $h=\lambda^{-1/2}$, and $|k_*|\le\mathsf D\lambda$ give $\ell_*^{-1}+h^{-1}|k_*|\le2\mathsf D^{\max(a,1)}\lambda^{3/2}$. This is the numerical derivative cost in Lemma 5.7. The inverse deformation contributes the additional parent factor when the profile is composed with the inverse flow.
notes.TorusEuler.planeWave_selfAdvection: For $w=F(k\cdot x)\mathbf a$ with $k\cdot\mathbf a=0$, the self-advection $(w\cdot\nabla)w$ vanishes. This is the exact cancellation used for the Craik–Criminale wave in §1.1. The calculation only requires differentiability of the profile at the phase in question and no time-evolution equation for the wave coefficients.
notes.TorusEuler.preceding_strength_retained_o: On an interval of length at most $\mu^{-1/16}$, a nonzero transverse wave over a trace-free gradient bounded by $\mu^{1/32}$ retains at least $e^{-1}$ times its initial strength. Proposition 8.2 uses this estimate throughout $[t_j,t_{j+1}]$, not only at its endpoints. It makes the fixed multiplicative loss in the paper’s argument explicit.
notes.TorusEuler.pressureCorrectionMode: At each integer frequency, the scalar correction has multiplier $\Delta^{-1}\operatorname{div}$. Its gradient is the part removed by the Leray projection in the introduction's conventions. The inverse Laplacian is normalized by setting its zero mode to zero, giving a mean-zero potential. A separate Fourier identity relates these individual coefficients to the spatial projection.
notes.TorusEuler.pressureCorrectionMode_zero: The scalar correction at zero Fourier frequency is zero. This is the mean-zero normalization of the potential in the Leray projection used in the introduction. It applies regardless of the vector coefficient being projected and does not force the velocity to have zero mean: constant divergence-free velocities remain after projection.
notes.TorusEuler.pressureHessianMultiplier: The periodic operator $D^2\Delta^{-1}$ maps scalar $C^{0,1/2}$ fields to matrix-valued $C^{0,1/2}$ fields continuously. Lemma 5.9 applies this operator to the Poisson equation for the summed mean pressure. Its identification with a particular pressure Hessian requires that pressure equation; boundedness alone does not identify the field being estimated.
notes.TorusEuler.projected_residual_of_cutoff: Applying the cutoff and Leray projection to the approximate equation gives (5.58), with tensors $v_\Lambda\otimes u$, $V\otimes v_\Lambda$ and $(\operatorname{Id}-S_\Lambda)(V\otimes V)$. The formal result proves this algebra for general linear projections and bilinear products once derivative commutation and removal of the pressure gradient are supplied. It does not itself prove the analytic bounds for those operators.
notes.TorusEuler.pulledBackCurl_material_eq: Differentiating the transported curl gives the curl of $\partial_tQ[V]$, the commutator $[\partial_t,\mathbf d\times]Q[V]$, and the strain contribution. This is the decomposition used after (5.33) to estimate $(\partial_t+M)C[V]$. The inverse deformation evolves according to its flow equation, and the derivatives must exist on the stated time interval.
notes.TorusEuler.radialEnvelope: The envelope is $g(a)=\chi(\lVert a\rVert/\ell_*)$, using one fixed admissible cutoff. It equals one near the origin and vanishes outside the outer ball, as specified in §5.1. The support and smoothness statements require $\ell_*>0$; the later parameter choices provide this positive radius.
notes.TorusEuler.radialEnvelope_eq_one: For a positive radius, the radial envelope equals one on $\lVert a\rVert\le\ell_*$. This is the plateau required in §5.1, preserving the seed and its leading contribution near the origin. It concerns localization in label space; the separate time cutoff determines when the wave becomes active.
notes.TorusEuler.reciprocal_inductive_frequenc: When $\lambda_0\ge2$ and each frequency grows at least by squaring, the reciprocal frequencies are summable and $\sum_{k\ge0}\lambda_{j+k}^{-1}\le2\lambda_j^{-1}$. Section 8 uses this estimate for velocity convergence and the derivative tail. The formal conclusion includes summability itself, as well as the explicit bound needed in the limit arguments.
notes.TorusEuler.referenceCouplingNumerators: Substituting (2.13) reduces the second reference coupling numerator to $1+4e+2e^2+\varepsilon\sin\varphi\cos\varphi$ and simplifies the first numerator as well. Multiplication by $\cos\varphi$ gives (2.22). This algebraic cancellation explains the small late transverse coupling in §2.2.4; it requires the angle and deviation identities, but no differential equation or smallness estimate.
notes.TorusEuler.scaledFlow_fderiv_and_displac: If the lifted vector-field gradient times the interval length is at most $1/2$, every flow transition has derivative norm at most two. The projected displacement also has a derivative bound proportional to the elapsed time and projected velocity gradient. Both time directions are included, giving the forward and inverse estimates used in Lemma 5.10.
notes.TorusEuler.scaledLiftKernel: The scaled kernel is $K_\Lambda(y)=\Lambda^3K(\Lambda y)$ on three-dimensional space. The factor $\Lambda^3$ compensates for the volume change under positive dilation. Appendix B uses this normalization to keep the $L^1$ operator bound independent of frequency and to obtain the derivative and moment scaling factors in the Bernstein and tail estimates.
notes.TorusEuler.scaledMultiplierKernel_decay: At frequency scale $\lambda>0$, the kernel and its first derivative are bounded by a coefficient depending on symbol derivatives, times $\lambda^{3+d}(1+\lambda|y|)^{-5}$ for $d=0,1$. Taking $\lambda=2^j$ gives the kernel estimate in Lemma A.2. Annular localization and control of the symbol derivative integrals are separate ingredients.
notes.TorusEuler.slabTimeJet: These are Eulerian time derivatives: the spatial point is held fixed while the field is differentiated on the closed time interval. Smoothness of the constructed fields gives their usual interpretation, including one-sided derivatives at the endpoints. The auxiliary note distinguishes these derivatives from profile derivatives at fixed label and phase, converting between them through the parent flow.
notes.TorusEuler.slabTimeJet_cutoffResidual_ra: The cutoff residual has time derivatives bounded by $\lambda_{j+1}^{-5/2}$ once the preceding residual estimate, cutoff error bound and stated frequency inequalities are supplied. The next frequency is a sufficiently high power of the current one, absorbing the fixed time-order losses. This is the numerical final step in auxiliary Lemma 1.3; the hierarchy provides its analytic premises at sufficiently large stages.
notes.TorusEuler.smoothFourierCutoff: The operator $S_\Lambda$ is formed from the finitely many torus modes with frequencies at most $2\Lambda$, each multiplied by $\psi(\xi/\Lambda)$. With the symbol’s prescribed support, this agrees with the multiplier definition in Appendix B. Its boundedness and preservation of parity and divergence freeness are separate conclusions of Lemma B.1.
notes.TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_cutoffP: The difference $D^2(p-\Pi)$ is controlled in $C^{0,1/2}$ by the product of the velocity-gradient difference and the two velocity-gradient sizes, together with $\|R_V\|_{C^{1,1/2}}$. This is the pressure estimate in the proof of Proposition 5.11. The formal statement keeps the residual term, which is necessary because $\Pi$ belongs to an approximate solution.
notes.TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_cutoffV: For $m\le P$, the cutoff difference satisfies $\|S_\Lambda V-V\|_{C^{m,1/2}}\le C_P\Lambda^{m-P}\|V\|_{C^{P,1/2}}$ and has the asserted Hölder regularity. This is the tail estimate used in §5.7 and item 5 of §7.2. The formal result works for every $\Lambda>0$, extending the paper’s cutoff range $\Lambda\ge1$.
notes.TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_le_of_u: Uniform bounds through derivative order $m+1$ control the full $C^{m,1/2}$ norm, with the explicit factor $3(m+1)$ in the formal convention. The proof combines a bounded function and its bounded first derivative at each order. Lemma 5.7 uses this elementary estimate to pass from (5.44) to (5.45).
notes.TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalfNorm_realVec: The real velocity cutoff satisfies the tail estimate (B.2) for every $0\le s\le M$, including regularity of the error in $C^{s,1/2}$. The formal statement permits every positive cutoff frequency, extending the paper’s range $\Lambda\ge1$. Its constant depends on the fixed symbol and the highest derivative order, providing the estimate used for physical velocities in §5.7.
notes.TorusEuler.spatialHolderHalf_bilinear: A bounded bilinear map $B$ sends two $C^{m,1/2}$ fields to another such field, with norm bounded by $3(m+1)2^m\|B\|$ times their norm product. This proves (5.59) and covers the tensor products in the cutoff residual. The operator-norm factor allows the same constant to apply uniformly to different products and target spaces.
notes.TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_localizedTr: The periodically extended evaluated profile is spatially periodic whenever the inverse label map commutes with integer translations. This holds for arbitrary real $k_*$ and explains the extension procedure in §3.1. Periodicity alone requires no boundary vanishing; the collar where the profile vanishes is needed separately to preserve smoothness across the cell boundary.
notes.TorusEuler.spatiallyPeriodic_modOne_line: The phase $k_*\cdot a$ modulo one is invariant under all integer label translations exactly when $k_*\in\mathbb Z^3$. This is the lattice obstruction stated in §3.1. The construction permits other real wave vectors by evaluating localized oscillations on one label cell and then extending the resulting fields periodically.
notes.TorusEuler.stationaryShear: The starting velocity is $U_0(x)=\sin(2\pi x_2)(e_1+\rho e_3)$, as in §1.1. It points perpendicular to the direction in which it varies, so its self-advection vanishes. The formula permits every real tilt, while the paper chooses $\rho>0$ small to obtain the desired positive, unequal couplings for the first amplification.
notes.TorusEuler.stationaryShearFlow: The explicit flow is $X_0(t,a)=a+tU_0(a)$. The second coordinate stays fixed, so the stationary shear remains constant along each trajectory. This supplies the flow used to launch the first wave in §1.1. The inverse and Jacobian properties are verified separately from the formula for the particle positions.
notes.TorusEuler.stationaryShearFlow_jacobian_: For $0\le t\le1$ and $|\rho|\le1$, both the label derivative of $X_0(t,\cdot)$ and its inverse have norm at most $1+4\pi$. The inverse derivative is evaluated at the transported particle $X_0(t,a)$. This supplies the deformation part of the base induction bound in §7.2 from the explicit formula (6.2).
notes.TorusEuler.stationaryShearFlow_jacobians: The stationary shear flow has deformation $D_aX_0=\operatorname{Id}+t\cos(2\pi a_2)B_\rho$ and inverse $\operatorname{Id}-t\cos(2\pi a_2)B_\rho$, as in (6.2). The formal statement evaluates the inverse-flow derivative at the transported particle, exactly where it represents the inverse deformation. The formulas hold for every real time and shear parameter.
notes.TorusEuler.stationaryShearFlow_origin: The explicit stationary shear flow satisfies $X_0(t,0)=0$ at every real time because the sine profile vanishes at the origin. Section 6.1 uses this to identify the central wave equations with the equations over the fixed gradient $B_\rho$. The identity itself needs no short-time or small-parameter assumption.
notes.TorusEuler.stationaryShearFlow_second: Along the stationary shear flow, the second coordinate remains equal to the initial label $a_2$ for all times. This explains why the sine profile is constant on each trajectory and yields the explicit flow formula (6.2). The formal identity holds without any restriction on the shear parameter or on time.
notes.TorusEuler.stationaryShearGradient: The central gradient is $B_\rho=2\pi(e_1+\rho e_3)\otimes e_2$, the rank-one matrix in (6.1). It reads the second component of a vector and sends it into the span of $e_1$ and $e_3$. Section 6.1 uses this matrix for the first wave, its initial couplings and the explicit deformation of the parent.
notes.TorusEuler.stationaryShearGradient_coupl: The central gradient has the two entries $\nu=2\pi$ and $\eta=2\pi\rho$ in the coordinate frame, giving $\varepsilon=\rho$ as in §1.1. These identities hold for every real tilt. They provide positive couplings only after imposing the paper's choice $\rho>0$; smallness is a further amplification requirement.
notes.TorusEuler.stationaryShearGradient_origi: At the origin, differentiating the stationary sine shear removes its cosine factor and gives the constant linear map used for the initial coupling calculation. This identifies the actual periodic velocity with the local model in §1.1. The identity holds for every real tilt and does not require the later smallness assumptions.
notes.TorusEuler.stationaryShearGradient_sq: The central shear matrix satisfies $B_\rho^2=0$: its image has zero second component, which is the only component it reads. Consequently $\operatorname{Id}-cB_\rho$ is the exact inverse of $\operatorname{Id}+cB_\rho$. This is the identity behind (6.2), valid for every real shear parameter.
notes.TorusEuler.stationaryShear_advection: The self-advection $(U_0\cdot\nabla)U_0$ vanishes everywhere because the shear depends only on $x_2$ and has no second component. This verifies the elementary Euler calculation in §6.1 and permits zero pressure and residual. The formal identity holds for every real shear parameter and at every spatial point.
notes.TorusEuler.stationaryShear_base_T1: The stationary shear is smooth, periodic, odd and divergence free, with its frequencies inside the band $2\lambda_0^5$ whenever $\lambda_0\ge1$. This establishes (T1) for the base stage of §7.2. The statement gives band inclusion; the separate Fourier calculation identifies its exact nonzero modes as $\pm e_2$.
notes.TorusEuler.stationaryShear_mFourierCoeff: The Fourier coefficient of the stationary sine shear is nonzero exactly at $e_2$ and $-e_2$. This gives the precise support asserted in §6.1, from which the initial frequency-band estimate follows. The formal calculation uses the complex Fourier coefficients of the real shear and holds for any real value of $\rho$.
notes.TorusEuler.stationaryShear_second: The second component of $U_0$ vanishes at every point, for every real shear parameter. This is the elementary property behind the two observations in §6.1: self-advection vanishes, and particles keep their second coordinate. The statement refers to the paper’s coordinate $x_2$, independently of how coordinates are represented in the formalization.
notes.TorusEuler.strongLabelMomentum_of_integr: Differentiating the integrated equation with $L=-\int_0^t g\,ds$ gives (4.11), using $K_t-\Omega=2(D_aX)^T\partial_tD_aX$. This formal result assumes that the derivative of the integrated pressure gradient is the negative strong pressure gradient. It therefore supplies the differentiation step, not a proof that an arbitrary original scalar potential has the needed time regularity.
notes.TorusEuler.terminalCurl_tendsto_atTop_of: Lower vorticity bounds on every sufficiently late activation interval, tending to infinity, give $|\operatorname{curl}u(t,0)|\to\infty$ once the corresponding derivative errors between $u$ and $U_j$ tend to zero. Proposition 8.2 uses the whole intervals, so the conclusion covers every approach to $T_\infty$ from below. It is stronger than divergence only at the activation times.
notes.TorusEuler.terminalProjectedHigherTimeDe: Differentiating the integrated mean equation isolates the highest time derivative of the mean velocity under the projected kinetic operator. The right side contains forcing derivatives, lower velocity derivatives and differentiated coefficients with binomial factors. The auxiliary note writes the equivalent differentiated differential equation; this formal identity retains the coefficient $\Omega$ from the integrated equation, so the displayed formulas differ before rearrangement.
notes.TorusEuler.terminalTimeConvolution_le: The factorially weighted sum of the binomial product terms is at most the product of the two weighted sums. The entries are nonnegative and $T>0$. After canceling the binomial factors, the pairs with total order at most $q$ form a subset of all pairs through order $q$. This gives the product bound used in the auxiliary time estimates.
notes.TorusEuler.terminalTimeJetWeight_mul_cho: The identity $(T^n/n!)\binom ni=(T^i/i!)(T^{n-i}/(n-i)!)$ holds for $i\le n$. It explains why factorial weights are used in the time norms: the binomial coefficients from differentiating a product disappear. The auxiliary profile estimates then reduce product bounds to products of nonnegative sums.
notes.TorusEuler.terminalTime_cutoff_tail_rate: At cutoff scale $\Lambda=\lambda^5$, sufficient expansion depth makes the tail at most $\tfrac12\lambda^{-1}$. The displayed arithmetic condition is $5m+5+\psi\le3P$, together with control of the fixed cutoff constant by $\lambda$. The auxiliary note eventually meets this condition at every fixed derivative order, allowing the other half of the correction allowance for the mean.
notes.TorusEuler.terminalVelocityBound_of_exte: A continuous velocity on the closed time interval and one spatial period is bounded. Any velocity agreeing with it before the terminal time inherits that bound. This supplies the bounded-velocity part of Proposition 8.2 from the continuous limit $w$ in Section 8; the argument uses compactness and requires no Euler equation.
notes.TorusEuler.terminal_poincare_pointwise: For a continuously differentiable path with $f(T)=0$, the bound $|f(t)|^2\le(T-t)\int_0^T|f'|^2\,ds$ gives the terminal Poincaré estimate behind §1.2. The proof first obtains the sharper integral over $[t,T]$ displayed in the paper, then enlarges the integration interval. This distinction matters when comparing the linked proof step with the stated conclusion.
notes.TorusEuler.theorem11: This formal result extracts the existence conclusion from the numbered Theorem 1.1: a smooth periodic Euler solution with all the stated singularity and off-origin limit properties. The numbered theorem also explicitly states uniqueness of the maximal classical velocity and its lifetime. That additional comparison is omitted from this shorter existence conclusion.
notes.TorusEuler.theorem11_of_continuation_and: This route to Theorem 1.1 assumes that a finite vorticity integral permits a longer smooth Euler solution. Together with central blow-up, that assumption forces divergence of the integral; the other terminal hypotheses complete the conclusion. The formal statement does not prove the continuation criterion itself. The main Section 8 proof instead obtains divergence directly from quantitative activation bounds.
notes.TorusEuler.timeDerivative: The time derivative is computed at fixed spatial position within $[0,T_*)$. It is the usual derivative at interior times and the right derivative at time zero. Theorem 1.1 applies its off-origin spatial-limit conclusion to this field as well as to the velocity. The formula does not assert differentiability at or after the excluded terminal time.
notes.TorusEuler.torusLInf: The torus $L^\infty$ norm is the essential supremum over the centered fundamental cell. It may be infinite for a general field. For the continuous periodic fields before $T_*$, it agrees with the spatial supremum used in Theorem 1.1. Applied to the velocity gradient and curl, it gives the quantities in the two divergent time integrals.
notes.TorusEuler.torusLInf_curl_le: The familiar inequality $\|\operatorname{curl}u\|_\infty\le C\|\nabla u\|_\infty$ follows because curl is a fixed linear combination of first derivatives. The constant is independent of the velocity. Corollary 8.3 applies this estimate to the smooth Euler solution to transfer divergence of the vorticity integral to divergence of the gradient integral.
notes.TorusEuler.trace_endpointPhysicalMean_eq: If $X$ preserves volume, $v$ is divergence free in label coordinates and $B=D_aXv$, then $\mathbf d\cdot B=0$. The statement assumes the necessary spatial derivatives and inverse deformation. This identifies the divergence condition in the endpoint formulation with the mean equation (5.11), using the volume-preserving change of variables.
notes.TorusEuler.transportedProfile: This defines $f^\natural$ by taking the inverse-flow label at a spatial point and substituting its phase $k_*\cdot a$ into $f(t,a,s)$. It is the evaluation used in §3.1 to turn profiles into physical fields. No periodicity or support condition is built into the formula; these are supplied when constructing a smooth field on the torus.
notes.TorusEuler.transportedProfile_chainRule: This proves (3.1): spatial differentiation splits into a label derivative and $\kappa\partial_s$, while differentiation along the parent trajectory gives only the profile's time derivative. The inverse label map must satisfy its transport equation and the indicated joint derivatives must exist. The formal statement also includes interval endpoints with the corresponding one-sided time derivatives.
notes.TorusEuler.transportedProfile_on_traject: Along the parent trajectory, evaluating $f^\natural$ returns $f(t,a,k_*\cdot a)$, the formula used for the leading oscillation in §3.1. Only the inverse relation between the flow and label map is needed. The statement is therefore an evaluation identity before any differentiation, periodicity argument or amplitude evolution is used.
notes.TorusEuler.tsupport_radialEnvelope_subse: For $\ell_*>0$, the closed support of $g$ lies in $\lVert a\rVert\le2\ell_*$. This is the localization required in §5.1 and in the transverse support estimates. The further choice $\ell_*\le\mathsf D^{-3}$ with $\mathsf D\ge2$ then places that support inside the centered periodic cell.
notes.TorusEuler.unitTorus_sup_le_holderHalf_a: Averaging on a ball of radius $\varepsilon^2$ gives $\|v\|_\infty\le\varepsilon H+\varepsilon^{-3}\|v\|_{L^2}$ when $H$ bounds the half-Hölder seminorm. This is the interpolation step in Lemma A.2 that absorbs the lower-order supremum term. The power three comes from the spatial dimension, and the formal statement uses normalized measure on the unit torus.
notes.TorusEuler.vorticityForm: The coefficient is $\Omega=F^T(M^T-M)F$, where the application in §4 takes $F=D_aX$. This is the vorticity contribution to the label energy and integrated momentum equation. The formula is algebraic and does not assume that the parent solves Euler or that the supplied deformation is invertible.
notes.TorusEuler.waveBump: The formal construction fixes a particular even bump by applying a smooth transition to $1-64s^2$. This supplies the choice of $\psi$ in the proof of Lemma 3.1, where the paper permits any bump with the stated support and normalization. The profile-family theorem then supplies the smoothness and uniform estimates needed from that choice.
notes.TorusEuler.waveCorrection_longitudinal_o: If $\partial_s(\kappa\cdot C)=-\mathbf d\cdot V$ and $C$ has zero phase mean, integration gives $\kappa\cdot C=-\partial_s^{-1}(\mathbf d\cdot V)$. This is the final step in (3.6). The formal statement assumes the derivative identity and continuity; the preceding geometric calculation establishes that identity for the actual divergence correction.
notes.TorusEuler.wavePotential: This is $Q[V]=-\partial_s^{-1}(\kappa\times V/|\kappa|^2)$ in (3.5). At each label, phase integration supplies the potential whose fast curl will recover the transverse oscillation. A nonzero covector and transversality are needed for that recovery; continuity, periodicity and zero mean ensure that the potential itself is a periodic phase profile.
notes.TorusEuler.wavePotentialTimeSource: This is the vector inside the phase primitive in (5.33): the three cross-product terms divided by $|\kappa|^2$, together with the correction from differentiating that denominator. It depends only on $M$, $\kappa$, $V$, and $f$. The accompanying derivative theorem supplies the nonvanishing and differential-equation assumptions that give it this interpretation.
notes.TorusEuler.wavePotential_fast_curl: For a continuous transverse profile and nonzero covector, $\kappa\times\partial_sQ[V]=V$. This is the algebraic cancellation used in §3.1 to complete the localized velocity by a curl. The pointwise identity needs neither periodicity nor zero phase mean; those assumptions are needed separately for the potential to be a periodic profile.
notes.TorusEuler.wavePotential_firstWaveLeadin: For the selected first-wave seed, envelope and profile family, the potential has the form $gP_h(\mathbf a\times\kappa)/|\kappa|^2$. This realizes the expression following (3.6). The formal statement concerns the first wave with $0<h\le1$; it does not claim the identity for every arbitrary seed, envelope and profile introduced earlier in §3.1.
notes.TorusEuler.wavePotential_frequency_scale: Rescaling the wave vector by a positive frequency rescales its vector potential by the inverse frequency. This separates the factor $\lambda^{-1}$ from the normalized coefficients $\kappa/\lambda$ and $\lambda^2/|\kappa|^2$ in the proof of Lemma 5.5. Product, derivative, and phase primitive estimates are then needed to bound the curl correction.
